# Pirkei Avot — פִּרְקֵי אָבוֹת

Translated from the Hebrew (Torat Emet) by a model pipeline; every unit reviewed. Provenance at the end.

## Chapter 1 — פֶּרֶק א (Pirkei Avot 1:1–1:18)

### Reading text

<sup>1:1</sup> Moses received Torah from Sinai and handed it down to Joshua; Joshua to the elders; the elders to the prophets; and the prophets handed it down to the members of the Great Assembly. They said three things: Be deliberate in judgment; raise up many disciples; and make a fence for the Torah.

<sup>1:2</sup> Shimon the Righteous was of the remnants of the Great Assembly. He used to say: On three things the world stands: on the Torah, and on the Temple service, and on acts of kindness.

<sup>1:3</sup> Antigonos of Sokho received from Shimon the Righteous. He used to say: Do not be like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a gratuity, but be like servants who serve the master not on condition of receiving a gratuity; and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.

<sup>1:4</sup> Yose son of Yoezer of Tzereda and Yose son of Yochanan of Jerusalem received from them. Yose son of Yoezer of Tzereda says: Let your house be a meeting place for the sages; and be covered in the dust of their feet; and drink their words with thirst.

<sup>1:5</sup> Yose son of Yochanan of Jerusalem says: Let your house be open wide; and let the poor be members of your household; and do not talk too much with the woman. They said this of one's own wife; how much more so of the wife of his fellow. From here the sages said: Whenever a man talks too much with the woman, he brings evil upon himself, and neglects words of Torah, and in the end inherits Gehinnom.

<sup>1:6</sup> Yehoshua son of Perachya and Nittai the Arbelite received from them. Yehoshua son of Perachya says: Make for yourself a teacher; and acquire for yourself a friend; and judge every person favorably.

<sup>1:7</sup> Nittai the Arbelite says: Keep far from a bad neighbor, and do not associate with a wicked person, and do not despair of retribution.

<sup>1:8</sup> Judah son of Tabbai and Shimon son of Shetach received from them. Judah son of Tabbai says: Do not make yourself like those who arrange the pleas before the judges. When litigants stand before you, let them be in your eyes like the wicked; and when they depart from before you, let them be in your eyes like the innocent, once they have accepted the judgment upon themselves.

<sup>1:9</sup> Shimon son of Shetach says: Be thorough in examining the witnesses, and be careful with your words, lest from them they learn to lie.

<sup>1:10</sup> Shemaiah and Avtalyon received from them. Shemaiah says: Love work, hate lordship, and do not make yourself known to the ruling power.

<sup>1:11</sup> Avtalyon says: Sages, be careful with your words, lest you incur the liability of exile and be exiled to a place of evil waters, and the disciples who come after you drink and die, and so it turns out that the name of Heaven is profaned.

<sup>1:12</sup> Hillel and Shammai received from them. Hillel says: Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them near to the Torah.

<sup>1:13</sup> He used to say: One who spreads his name far loses his name; and one who does not add will cease; and one who does not learn deserves to die; and one who makes use of the crown passes away.

<sup>1:14</sup> He used to say: If I am not for myself, who is for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?

<sup>1:15</sup> Shammai says: Make your Torah fixed. Say little and do much, and receive every person with a pleasant countenance.

<sup>1:16</sup> Rabban Gamliel used to say: Make for yourself a teacher, and withdraw from doubt, and do not make a habit of tithing by estimates.

<sup>1:17</sup> Shimon his son says: All my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing good for the body except silence. And it is not expounding that is the main thing, but action. And whoever multiplies words brings sin.

<sup>1:18</sup> Rabban Shimon son of Gamliel says: On three things the world stands: on justice, and on truth, and on peace, as it is said (Zechariah 8): Judge truth and a judgment of peace in your gates.

### Chapter 1 by mishnah

#### Pirkei Avot 1:1

> משֶׁה קִבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי, וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ, וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ לִזְקֵנִים, וּזְקֵנִים לִנְבִיאִים, וּנְבִיאִים מְסָרוּהָ לְאַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה. הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים, הֱווּ מְתוּנִים בַּדִּין, וְהַעֲמִידוּ תַלְמִידִים הַרְבֵּה, וַעֲשׂוּ סְיָג לַתּוֹרָה:

**Moses received Torah from Sinai and handed it down to Joshua; Joshua to the elders; the elders to the prophets; and the prophets handed it down to the members of the Great Assembly. They said three things: Be deliberate in judgment; raise up many disciples; and make a fence for the Torah.**

Literal: Moses received Torah from-Sinai, and-handed-it to-Joshua, and-Joshua to-elders, and-elders to-prophets, and-prophets handed-it to-men-of assembly the-great. They said three things: Be deliberate in-the-judgment, and-raise-up disciples many, and-make fence to-the-Torah.

Grammar:

- The chain of tradition has one verb, מָסַר 'hand over', and drops it after the first link: 'Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets'.
- מְסָרוּהָ (3rd plural with the 3rd feminine singular suffix, 'handed it') states the verb again in the last link, as it was stated for Moses: the chain opens and closes with מָסַר.
- הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים introduces three plural imperatives: הֱווּ (Qal of הָיָה, Mishnaic form), הַעֲמִידוּ (Hifil of the I-guttural root עמד, 'cause to stand') and עֲשׂוּ (Qal of the III-ה root עשה).
- קִבֵּל is Piel of קבל, 'received', and in Mishnaic Hebrew is the standard verb for receiving a tradition.
- The third saying is a metaphor: סְיָג is a hedge round a field or a vineyard.

Note: 'Torah' is without the article, as in the Hebrew, and not 'the Torah'. 'From Sinai' is kept literal; Bartenura glosses it as 'from the One who was revealed at Sinai'. 'Members of the Great Assembly' follows decisions.md for אַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה. 'Be deliberate' renders מְתוּנִים, from a root meaning 'slow, patient'; both Bartenura and Rambam read it as waiting before deciding a case.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: unlike the other tractates of the Mishnah this one is not built on a commandment but on ethics and character traits; the sages of the nations also wrote such books. The mishnah therefore begins with Moses at Sinai, to say that these teachings are not the sages' invention but were received from Sinai.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'from Sinai' means from the One who was revealed at Sinai. The English keeps 'from Sinai' and adopts this sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the elders are those who outlived Joshua (Josh 24:31, שֶׁהֶאֱרִיכוּ יָמִים אַחֲרֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ), and these elders passed it to other elders until the first of the prophets, Eli the priest and Samuel of Ramah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they were one hundred and twenty elders: Zerubbabel, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, of the days of Ezra and the return from exile in the Second Temple; among them were Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi and Nehemiah son of Hachaliah. They were called 'Great' because they restored the crown to its former state: Moses said 'the great, mighty and awesome God', Jeremiah and Daniel left out 'mighty' and 'awesome', and they restored them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they said many things, but these three are those on which the keeping of the Torah rests.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if a case comes before you once, twice, three times, do not say 'I have already studied it'; wait (מַמְתִּינִים) before you decide. The English 'deliberate' takes this.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: against Rabban Gamliel's rule, teach Torah to everyone without examining him (unless his bad conduct is known); or: one who raised disciples in youth should raise them in old age (Eccl 11:6).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a fence so that one does not come to touch a Torah prohibition, e.g. secondary degrees of forbidden unions and the Sabbath rest-decrees; compare Lev 18:30, 'make a guard for my guard'.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: he has already explained the nature of the tradition; his aim here is to explain the words of the pious and moralists, to urge the acquiring of useful traits, and to warn about some vices; for the rest he explains only words.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: let them delay the decision and not rule quickly until they understand it, since new facts may appear that were not seen at first thought.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the 'fence' is the decrees and enactments that keep a man far from transgressions, as in 'you shall keep my charge' (Lev 18:30): make a guard for my guard.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'raise up many disciples' follows Beit Hillel, who teach everyone, against Beit Shammai who teach only the worthy.

Apparatus:

- Spelling: Vilna reads סייג for סְיָג.
- Source of the closing image: compare Lev 18:30 (cited by Bartenura and Rambam).
- סְיָג: Vilna reads סייג (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 1:2

> שִׁמְעוֹן הַצַּדִּיק הָיָה מִשְּׁיָרֵי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, עַל שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים הָעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד, עַל הַתּוֹרָה וְעַל הָעֲבוֹדָה וְעַל גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים:

**Shimon the Righteous was of the remnants of the Great Assembly. He used to say: On three things the world stands: on the Torah, and on the Temple service, and on acts of kindness.**

Literal: Shimon the-Righteous was from-remnants-of assembly the-great. He was saying: On three things the-world stands: on the-Torah, and-on the-service, and-on bestowal-of kindnesses.

Grammar:

- הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: the pronoun, the past of הָיָה and a participle express a habitual saying ('he used to say').
- עַל ... עוֹמֵד: the sentence is a list of three pillars; each is introduced by עַל, and the last two by וְעַל.
- גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים is a construct chain: 'the bestowing of kindnesses'.
- מִשְּׁיָרֵי has a partitive מִ: 'one of the remnants', and not 'from (them)'.

Note: הָעֲבוֹדָה is rendered 'the Temple service'; Bartenura (עֲבוֹדַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת) and Rambam (the sacrifices) agree. 'Stands' keeps the Hebrew verb; Bartenura glosses it 'the world was created only for these three'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: מִשִּׁיּוּרֵי: after all the others died the tradition remained in his hand; he was High Priest after Ezra.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'he used to say' means this was constantly on his lips; so throughout the tractate.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: the world was created only for the sake of these three things.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: had Israel not accepted the Torah, heaven and earth would not have been created (Jer 33:25; Shabbat 88a).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the service of the sacrifices; the world stands on it (Taanit 27b); Noah's offerings were the ground of the promise not to bring a flood.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'the world is built of kindness' (Ps 89:3); acts of kindness: gladdening brides and grooms, comforting mourners, visiting the sick, burying the dead.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the continuing repair of the world rests on wisdom (the Torah), on virtues of character (acts of kindness) and on keeping the commandments (the sacrifices).

Apparatus:

- Spelling and parse: none.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:3

> אַנְטִיגְנוֹס אִישׁ סוֹכוֹ קִבֵּל מִשִּׁמְעוֹן הַצַּדִּיק. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, אַל תִּהְיוּ כַעֲבָדִים הַמְשַׁמְּשִׁין אֶת הָרַב עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס, אֶלָּא הֱווּ כַעֲבָדִים הַמְשַׁמְּשִׁין אֶת הָרַב שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס, וִיהִי מוֹרָא שָׁמַיִם עֲלֵיכֶם:

**Antigonos of Sokho received from Shimon the Righteous. He used to say: Do not be like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a gratuity, but be like servants who serve the master not on condition of receiving a gratuity; and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.**

Literal: Antigonos man-of Sokho received from-Shimon the-Righteous. He was saying: Not be-you like-servants the-serving [acc.] the-master on condition-of to-receive gratuity, but be-you like-servants the-serving [acc.] the-master that-not on condition-of to-receive gratuity, and-let-be fear-of Heaven upon-you.

Grammar:

- The saying is built on antithesis: אַל תִּהְיוּ ... אֶלָּא הֱווּ, with the same words repeated, the second time with שֶׁלֹּא.
- עַל מְנָת (לְ) is an idiom for 'on condition (of)'; לְקַבֵּל is a Piel infinitive.
- הַמְשַׁמְּשִׁין is Piel participle plural with the article, and את marks the definite object הָרַב (a Mishnaic use with שמש).
- וִיהִי is the jussive 'and let there be'; the Mishnaic Hebrew uses it with a subject מוֹרָא שָׁמַיִם 'fear of Heaven'.
- The verb forms: תִּהְיוּ is imperfect used as a prohibition with אַל; הֱווּ is the imperative.

Note: פְּרָס is rendered 'gratuity' because both commentators define it against שָׂכָר 'wage': a gift from one who owes nothing. אִישׁ סוֹכוֹ is 'of Sokho' (literally 'man of Sokho').

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: פְּרָס is from the language of ערך 'valuation' (Targum: purseneh); it is what one gives to one who served him though he owes nothing, as a father gives a small son. Even for such a hope one should not serve one's Maker, but only from love.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even if you serve from love, serve also from fear: the lover is zealous in positive commandments, the one who fears is careful about prohibitions, and so one's service is complete.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: פְּרָס is a reward given by one who owes no favour, unlike שָׂכָר which is due by law; one should serve God without hope of a reward, from love; but love does not remove the commandment of fear, hence 'let the fear of Heaven be upon you'.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah's text reads אֶלָּא הֱווּ כַעֲבָדִים הַמְשַׁמְּשִׁין אֶת הָרַב עַל מְנָת שֶׁלֹּא לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס, 'on condition of not receiving a gratuity'; he holds that this reading of the books is the main one: serve as a bought slave serves, with no gratuity, out of love, as one serves a friend from long ago.

Apparatus:

- Spelling: none.
- Variant (Rabbeinu Yonah's text): עַל מְנָת שֶׁלֹּא לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס, 'on condition of not receiving a gratuity', for שֶׁלֹּא עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס; he defends it as the reading of the books. His lemma also reads וִיהֵא for וִיהִי.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:4

> יוֹסֵי בֶן יוֹעֶזֶר אִישׁ צְרֵדָה וְיוֹסֵי בֶן יוֹחָנָן אִישׁ יְרוּשָׁלַיִם קִבְּלוּ מֵהֶם. יוֹסֵי בֶן יוֹעֶזֶר אִישׁ צְרֵדָה אוֹמֵר, יְהִי בֵיתְךָ בֵית וַעַד לַחֲכָמִים, וֶהֱוֵי מִתְאַבֵּק בַּעֲפַר רַגְלֵיהֶם, וֶהֱוֵי שׁוֹתֶה בְצָמָא אֶת דִּבְרֵיהֶם:

**Yose son of Yoezer of Tzereda and Yose son of Yochanan of Jerusalem received from them. Yose son of Yoezer of Tzereda says: Let your house be a meeting place for the sages; and be covered in the dust of their feet; and drink their words with thirst.**

Literal: Yose son-of Yoezer man-of Tzereda and-Yose son-of Yochanan man-of Jerusalem received from-them. Yose son-of Yoezer man-of Tzereda says: Let-be your-house house-of meeting for-the-sages, and-be covering-yourself in-dust-of their-feet, and-be drinking in-thirst [acc.] their-words.

Grammar:

- Pairs (זוּגוֹת): from Yose ben Yoezer on, teachers are named two by two, so קִבְּלוּ is plural; Bartenura says the first of each pair was the nasi and the second av beit din.
- בֵּית וַעַד is 'a house of meeting' for the sages; בֵּית is construct and וַעַד an absolute noun.
- מִתְאַבֵּק is a Hithpael participle ('covering oneself in dust'); with וֶהֱוֵי it makes a continuing action: 'be (continually) covered'.
- וֶהֱוֵי: the conjunction וְ before a ḥatef vowel takes the matching full vowel, so וֶ before הֱ; the saying has three parallel commands (יְהִי, וֶהֱוֵי, וֶהֱוֵי).
- אֶת marks the definite object דִּבְרֵיהֶם, as in Biblical Hebrew; the word order puts בְצָמָא first, before the object.

Note: מִתְאַבֵּק is rendered as the Hebrew image, 'covered in the dust of their feet', and not as the metaphor 'sit at their feet'. Bartenura gives two readings of it: (1) follow them closely, so that you are covered with the dust they raise; (2) sit on the ground at their feet while the teacher sits on the bench. The English keeps the image and takes (1), the first and more literal.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: in this chapter the sages are named in pairs, each pair receiving from the earlier pair; the first of each pair was the nasi, the second the av beit din.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: when the sages want to gather, let your house be ready for it, so that they say 'let us meet at so-and-so's house'; you will learn something from them, like one who enters a perfumer's shop and carries out a good smell.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: first reading, that you walk behind them and are filled with the dust they raise; second reading, that you sit on the ground at their feet. The English adopts the first and records the second in the apparatus.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: like a thirsty man who drinks eagerly, and not like a sated man who loathes even good food.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: בֵּית וַעַד is בֵּית מוֹעֵד: make your house ready so that the sages always gather there, so that when someone asks 'where shall we meet?' he is told 'in so-and-so's house'.

Apparatus:

- Second reading of מִתְאַבֵּק (Bartenura): sit on the ground at their feet.
- Variant: in 1:4.16-17 Vilna omits אִישׁ צְרֵדָה in the second mention of the name; the base text has it.
- Commentary lemma: Rabbeinu Yonah names the second sage יוֹסֵף בֶּן יוֹחָנָן (Yosef) for יוֹסֵי בֶן יוֹחָנָן.
- אִישׁ צְרֵדָה: Vilna reads — (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 1:5

> יוֹסֵי בֶן יוֹחָנָן אִישׁ יְרוּשָׁלַיִם אוֹמֵר, יְהִי בֵיתְךָ פָתוּחַ לִרְוָחָה, וְיִהְיוּ עֲנִיִּים בְּנֵי בֵיתֶךָ, וְאַל תַּרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה עִם הָאִשָּׁה. בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ אָמְרוּ, קַל וָחֹמֶר בְּאֵשֶׁת חֲבֵרוֹ. מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאָדָם מַרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה עִם הָאִשָּׁה, גּוֹרֵם רָעָה לְעַצְמוֹ, וּבוֹטֵל מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְסוֹפוֹ יוֹרֵשׁ גֵּיהִנֹּם:

**Yose son of Yochanan of Jerusalem says: Let your house be open wide; and let the poor be members of your household; and do not talk too much with the woman. They said this of one's own wife; how much more so of the wife of his fellow. From here the sages said: Whenever a man talks too much with the woman, he brings evil upon himself, and neglects words of Torah, and in the end inherits Gehinnom.**

Literal: Yose son-of Yochanan man-of Jerusalem says: Let-be your-house open to-breadth, and-let-be poor sons-of your-house, and-not multiply talk with the-woman. Of-his-wife they-said, light and-heavy of-wife-of his-fellow. From-here said sages: All time that-man multiplying talk with the-woman, causing evil to-himself, and-neglecting from-words-of Torah, and-his-end inheriting Gehinnom.

Grammar:

- The mishnah has a saying of Yose (three imperatives) and then a comment in the voice of the sages ('they said', 'from here the sages said'). Bartenura notes that the comment is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who edited the mishnayot.
- קַל וָחֹמֶר is the argument a fortiori ('light and heavy'), here without a verb: 'how much more so'.
- עַל / בְּ: בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ אָמְרוּ uses ב to mean 'concerning'; the verb is plural with no stated subject ('they said' = 'people said / the sages said').
- אָדָם is 'a person', but the context is a man speaking with a woman; the English says 'a man'.
- גּוֹרֵם, בּוֹטֵל and יוֹרֵשׁ are participles that state a general result: 'is causing, is neglecting, is inheriting'.
- שִׂיחָה is the direct object of תַּרְבֶּה / מַרְבֶּה (Hifil of רבה, 'make much'): 'make much talk', i.e. talk too much; it is indefinite, so it has no אֶת.

Note: הָאִשָּׁה is rendered 'the woman', with the article, because Bartenura reads the article as the reason the warning is first about one's own wife (בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ). Rambam says talk with women is mostly about sexual matters, and gives that as the reason; Bartenura gives the cases of Korach and the wife's contempt. The two do not conflict on the English, and the English does not choose between them. 'Neglects words of Torah' follows both commentators: he is drawn to idle things and wastes his time. 'Open wide' (לִרְוָחָה) is the wide-open house; Bartenura: open to the four directions, as Abraham's was.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: like the house of Abraham, which was open to the four corners of the world, so that guests would not have to go round to find the door.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: let him not buy slaves to serve him; it is better that Israelites benefit from his property than the accursed seed of Canaan.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since he says 'the woman' and not 'a woman', we learn that they said it of one's own wife. Some explain it of a wife in her impurity only, but the mishnah indicates even a pure wife (Chagigah 5b: even idle talk between husband and wife is reported at the judgment), unless he must appease her for a religious reason.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Rabbi (who arranged the mishnayot) wrote this on the basis of Yose's words; when a man tells his wife his troubles, she teaches him to stir up strife (Korach), or she scorns him in her heart; both bring evil on himself.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he is drawn to idle things and does not engage in Torah.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: let there be an open gate for travellers, so that anyone on the road who needs something, or is hungry or thirsty, may enter at once.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: his servants should be the poor and weak, which is better than buying slaves; the sages used to blame those who bought slaves and praise those whose household was the poor.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: talk with women is mostly about intercourse, so excessive talk with them is forbidden; 'evil to himself' means he acquires base traits and much desire.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: it is clear that he wastes his time on other affairs.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: because such talk brings him to rebellion and he becomes liable to punishment.

Apparatus:

- Spelling: 1:5.23 Vilna reads וחומר; 1:5.44 Vilna reads גיהנום; the base text has the pointed forms.
- Reading of לִרְוָחָה: 'for relief', so that the house is open to give relief to the needy (a second sense of רְוָחָה).
- Commentary lemmas: Rambam reads וְסוֹפוֹ יוֹרֵד לְגֵיהִנֹּם, 'and in the end goes down to Gehinnom', for יוֹרֵשׁ גֵּיהִנֹּם; Rabbeinu Yonah reads כָּל הַמַּרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה, 'whoever talks much', for כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאָדָם מַרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה, and names the sage יוֹסֵף בֶּן יוֹחָנָן.
- וָחֹמֶר: Vilna reads וחומר (spelling)
- גֵּיהִנֹּם: Vilna reads גיהנום (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 1:6

> יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה וְנִתַּאי הָאַרְבֵּלִי קִבְּלוּ מֵהֶם. יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה אוֹמֵר, עֲשֵׂה לְךָ רַב, וּקְנֵה לְךָ חָבֵר, וֶהֱוֵי דָן אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם לְכַף זְכוּת:

Grammar:

- קִבְּלוּ is plural because there are two teachers, again named as a pair.
- עֲשֵׂה and קְנֵה are imperatives of final-ה verbs; לְךָ repeated after each verb is an ethical dative ('for yourself').
- וֶהֱוֵי דָן is the imperative of הָיָה with a participle: 'be one who judges', a continuing practice.
- לְכַף זְכוּת is an idiom: the scale of a balance tipped toward merit; the English 'favorably' gives the sense.
- The three commands are short and parallel, each with an object: רַב, חָבֵר, כָּל הָאָדָם.

Note: 'Make for yourself a teacher' is taken in Rambam's sense: treat him as your teacher even if he is not fit. Bartenura quotes Rambam and then gives his own hearing of the words, that one should take one regular teacher; it is recorded. 'Acquire' is kept: Rambam stresses that the verb is קנה 'buy', not 'make'. 'Judge every person favorably' is the idiom; both commentators limit it (for an unknown man; a known wicked man may be judged otherwise), but the saying is kept in its brevity.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: Rambam explains that even if he is not fit to be your teacher, make him your teacher; Bartenura's own view is that he should take one teacher to learn from always, and not learn today from one and tomorrow from another (though Avodah Zarah 19a says one who learns from one teacher sees no blessing, which refers to reasoning only).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even if you must buy him at a high price and spend money to win his love; this is not said of a teacher, who must teach free of charge.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: when the matter is in the scale with no tilt either way, such as a man of unknown conduct who does something that can be judged for merit or for guilt, the measure of piety is to judge for merit; but one known to be wicked may be judged for guilt.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: even if he is not fit to be your teacher, set him up as your teacher and imagine him a teacher, and you will gain learning from it; learning from another is firmer than learning alone, even if he is your equal or below you.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: he says 'acquire', not 'make' or 'join': one must acquire a friend who loves him, through whom his deeds and affairs are put right (as 'a companion or death'), and strive for him with all his heart; he then lists the kinds of friend: of use, of pleasure and of virtue.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: when you do not know whether a man is righteous or wicked and he does something that may be taken well or badly, take it well. A man known to be righteous who is seen doing what looks wrong must be judged favourably if there is any possibility, and you may not suspect him; but of a known wicked man who does what looks good, be on guard. For the unknown man and an undecided act, the way of piety is to judge for merit.

Apparatus:

- The sages in the chain: Yehoshua son of Perachya and Nittai the Arbelite received from Yose son of Yoezer and Yose son of Yochanan (1:4-5).
- The phrase 'to the scale of merit' (לְכַף זְכוּת) is the idiom; Jastrow (כַּף 7) gives 'scale of the balance', and Bartenura's כַּף מֹאזְנַיִם is the pan of a balance.

Grammar:

- הַרְחֵק is a Hifil imperative: 'make yourself distant'.
- Two prohibitions use אַל with the imperfect (Hitpael): אַל תִּתְחַבֵּר and אַל תִּתְיָאֵשׁ.
- The three clauses are parallel and short; the saying moves from neighbor to companion to the wicked's fate.
- הָאַרְבֵּלִי is a gentilic: 'the man of Arbel'.

Note: וְאַל תִּתְיָאֵשׁ מִן הַפֻּרְעָנוּת: Bartenura and Rambam both read 'do not give up hope that the wicked will be punished'; Rambam adds that punishment may come swiftly in this world.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: keep away so that you do not learn from his deeds, and so that you are not caught in his downfall: 'woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbor'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: whoever clings to the wicked receives a reward like theirs even if he does not act as they do, like one who enters a tanner's house and carries the bad smell out with him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not say 'this wicked man prospers, I will cling to him'; know that retribution will come quickly, 'for his calamity comes suddenly'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: do not join the wicked in any kind of love or fellowship, so that you do not learn from his deeds. And when you sin, or see a sinner, do not feel secure and say that God will punish him only in the world to come; do not despair of swift punishment for that sin.

- Vilna reads הפורענות (full spelling) for base הַפֻּרְעָנוּת.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:8

Grammar:

- The saying has two parallel temporal clauses with וּכְשֶׁ: 'when they stand ... when they depart'.
- יִהְיוּ ... כִרְשָׁעִים and כְזַכָּאִין compare in similes: before the verdict, treat each as a likely wrongdoer; afterwards, as innocent.
- בַעֲלֵי דִינִין is an idiom: 'masters of judgment', that is, the parties to a case; a Mishnaic plural ending in -ין.
- The first clause begins with אַל plus the imperfect, a prohibition; עַצְמְךָ is 'yourself' (lit. 'your bone, your self').
- קִבְּלוּ מֵהֶם: Piel perfect, 'received from them', the standard formula of transmission in this chapter.

Note: כְעוֹרְכֵי הַדַּיָּנִין: Bartenura gives two readings, 'those who arrange the litigants' pleas before the judges' (so also Rambam: those who coach litigants) and 'the great ones of the judges'; the English follows the first. A third reading Bartenura heard: do not act as a senior judge to compel litigants to appear.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: like those who arrange and set out the pleas of the litigants before the judges, for it is forbidden to reveal the law to one litigant. His second reading, 'like the great judges', is recorded here as an alternative and is not adopted.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: let your heart not incline to either party by saying 'so-and-so is a man of standing and would not make a false claim'; if you think so, you will not be able to see his guilt.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not suspect the one found liable of being a thief; say he perhaps erred. If one has sworn, do not say he swore falsely.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the 'arrangers of the judges' are people who learn pleas until they are expert, and compose questions and answers for litigants; the mishnah warns not to resemble them, i.e. not to teach a litigant a plea that will help him.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads דינים (standard plural) for base דִינִין.
- הַדַּיָּנִין: Vilna reads הדיינין (spelling)
- דִינִין: Vilna reads דינים (word)

- The third clause is a prohibition: אַל with the Hitpael imperfect of יָדַע, 'do not make yourself known'.
- לָרָשׁוּת: the definite 'the authority' is expressed by ה assimilated into ל.

The English 'lordship' keeps both. לָרָשׁוּת: the commentators agree it means the ruling power (שררה, שלטנות).

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: they were righteous converts, descended from Sennacherib; Avtalyon was named 'father of the little ones' because he was head of a court. This concerns the names, not the sense of the saying.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even one who has a livelihood must engage in work, for idleness leads to boredom.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: his second reading, to distance yourself from exercising authority over a community, is the sense kept in 'lordship'; his first reading, do not say 'I am too great to work', is recorded in the note.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not make yourself known to the authority in order to gain rabbinic office through it, or lest they remove you from the will of your Maker, as happened to Doeg the Edomite; authority is called רשות because the power is in its hand to do as it wishes.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: רשות is rulership; these three qualities protect faith and the world: without work one is driven to theft and sin; seeking office brings trials; nearness to power corrupts, as Doeg shows.

Grammar:

- הִזָּהֲרוּ is a Nifal imperative plural: the נ of the Nifal is assimilated into the doubled ז.
- After שֶׁמָּא 'lest' a chain of consequences follows: תָחוּבוּ, then four verbs joined by וְ (וְתִגְלוּ, וְיִשְׁתּוּ, וְיָמוּתוּ, וְנִמְצָא), and last the participle מִתְחַלֵּל.
- חֲכָמִים is a vocative: 'O sages'.
- תָחוּבוּ חוֹבַת is a cognate object, verb and noun from the root חוב ('incur a liability'); גָּלוּת וְתִגְלוּ then repeats the root גלה.
- נִמְצָא plus participle: 'it turns out that (the name of Heaven) is being profaned'.
- מַיִם הָרָעִים: figurative: the evil waters are heretical teachings that the disciples would 'drink'.

Note: מַיִם הָרָעִים: the English keeps the metaphor and gives the sense in the note; Bartenura and Rambam both take the 'evil waters' as heresy (מִינוּת, אפיקורסות). Bartenura sees the exile as the way the sages' words fall among heretics, who mis-read them.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not leave room in your words for the heretics (מִינִים) to err.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even if there are no heretics where you are, sin may bring exile to a place of people who interpret the Torah against the halakhah ('מראים פנים בתורה שלא כהלכה'); they are the 'evil waters'. They will draw improper meanings from your words, and the disciples who come after you will drink these heretical words and die in their guilt.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: those false opinions remain in the world, as happened with Antigonos of Socho and Zadok and Boethus, from whom the Sadducees and Boethusians arose.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'evil waters' is a figure for heresy; be careful in your words among the crowd so that they cannot be read another way, for heretics would read them according to their own belief, the disciples would turn to heresy and the name of Heaven would be profaned, as happened with Antigonos, Zadok and Boethus.

Apparatus:

- The mishnah as printed here has no variant readings recorded in the pack.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:12

> הִלֵּל וְשַׁמַּאי קִבְּלוּ מֵהֶם. הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן, אוֹהֵב שָׁלוֹם וְרוֹדֵף שָׁלוֹם, אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה:

Grammar:

- הֱוֵי מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן: מִ is partitive, 'one of'. תַּלְמִידָיו 'his disciples' carries a suffix that anticipates the possessor named by שֶׁל: 'his disciples, of Aaron', a common Mishnaic construction.
- Four participles, אוֹהֵב, רוֹדֵף, אוֹהֵב, מְקָרְבָן, follow the imperative as a list of Aaron's qualities.
- שָׁלוֹם is repeated: 'love peace and pursue peace': a pair of verbs of increasing effort.
- הַבְּרִיּוֹת is 'creatures': here human beings generally, not only Israel; מְקָרְבָן has the feminine suffix -ן on 'them'.

Note: הַבְּרִיּוֹת: literally 'the creatures'; rendered 'people' because the context (bringing them to the Torah) is of human beings. מְקָרְבָן: the suffix ן is a feminine plural form on a collective noun (בְּרִיּוֹת is feminine plural).

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura (citing Avot de-Rabbi Natan): Aaron would go to each of two quarrelling people and say that the other regrets it, until they kissed; and he would befriend one who had sinned, who would feel shame and return to the good, as in Malachi 2:6.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: Aaron would greet one who he knew had sinned, befriend him and speak much with him, until the man was ashamed and returned to good, and became one of his disciples; so the prophet says 'he walked with Me in peace and uprightness, and turned many from iniquity'.

Apparatus:

- Quotation of Malachi 2:6 (בְּשָׁלוֹם וּבְמִישׁוֹר הָלַךְ אִתִּי) appears in Bartenura, not in the mishnah.
- No variant readings are recorded in the pack for this mishnah.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:13

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, נָגֵד שְׁמָא, אָבֵד שְׁמֵהּ. וּדְלֹא מוֹסִיף, יָסֵף. וּדְלֹא יָלֵיף, קְטָלָא חַיָּב. וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּתָגָא, חָלֵף:

**He used to say: One who spreads his name far loses his name; and one who does not add will cease; and one who does not learn deserves to die; and one who makes use of the crown passes away.**

Literal: he was saying: drawing-out name, lost his-name. and-who-not adding, will-cease. and-who-not learning, death liable. and-who-makes-use of-crown, passes-away.

Grammar:

- This saying is in Aramaic, except for the opening formula הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר; the Aramaic relative is דְּ- (Hebrew שֶׁ-) and the emphatic ending is -ָא (שְׁמָא, קְטָלָא, תָּגָא).
- Four short clauses, each a relative clause (a participle in the first three, the perfect אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ in the last) followed by its consequence; the first and the last are an inverted pair (name drawn out, name lost; crown used, one passes).
- וּדְלֹא מוֹסִיף יָסֵף: a sound-play between two roots, מוֹסִיף from יסף 'add' and יָסֵף, which Bartenura reads as יָסוּף from סוף 'come to an end' (or, in his second reading, יֵאָסֵף 'be gathered (to his people)', from אסף): 'who does not add will cease'.
- קְטָלָא חַיָּב: the adjective חַיָּב is predicate with the noun it governs, 'liable (to) death'.

Note: נָגֵד is taken as 'draw out, extend', so one who stretches his name afar through power and the title of rabbi. Bartenura 1:13:3 gives a second reading, יֵאָסֵף ('be gathered to his people', i.e. die before his time); the English takes the first, יָסוּף ('cease'). In the last clause the English takes the first of Bartenura's explanations: the one who uses the crown of Torah as a tool. The jastrow lemma for 4 is a verb with a general sense ('draw a line') and the sense paths given for 2, 3, 15 and 17 are the nearest the pack offers.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one whose name is drawn out far through authority and lordship will soon lose it, for lordship buries its owner. נָגֵד is 'drawing', as the Targum has מִשְׁכוּ, נְגִידוּ.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who does not add to his learning.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: what he has already learned will cease from his mouth and he will forget his study. The other reading, יֵאָסֵף ('be gathered to his people', die untimely), is recorded in apparatus.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: this is worse than 'does not add', hence 'liable to death', that is, it is fitting that he be killed, as in Pesachim 49: an unlearned person may be torn like a fish.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who uses the crown of Torah, like a man using his tools, passes from the world; תָּגָא is a crown. He records two other explanations (תג"א as תלמיד גברא אחרינא, and use of the Ineffable Name), which are not adopted.

Apparatus:

- Bartenura on 1:13:3 records a variant reading יֵאָסֵף for יָסֵף.
- Bartenura on 1:13:5 gives two other explanations of בְּתָגָא: an acronym תג"א (תלמיד גברא אחרינא, 'another man's disciple'), and a reading יִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ with the Ineffable Name.
- Vilna reads שמיה (1:13.7), יסיף (1:13.10), חייב (1:13.14), and ודישתמש (1:13.15): spelling and form only.
- שְׁמֵהּ: Vilna reads שמיה (spelling)
- יָסֵף: Vilna reads יסיף (spelling)
- חַיָּב: Vilna reads חייב (spelling)
- וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ: Vilna reads ודישתמש (word)

| אֲנִי | am I | אֲנִי |  | pronoun (personal pronoun, 1st person, common, singular) |  |
| וְאִם | and if | ו: and + אִם |  | conjunction + conjunction (conditional conjunction) |  |
| לֹא | not | לֹא |  | particle (negative particle) |  |
| עַכְשָׁיו | now | עַכְשָׁיו |  | adverb (temporal adverb) | 1 |
| אֵימָתָי | when — interrogative: 'at what time' | אֵימָתָי |  | adverb (interrogative adverb, temporal) | 1 |

Grammar:

- Three rhetorical questions, each with a conditional first half; the answer to each is understood.
- אֵין אֲנִי לִי: אֵין negates the existence of the subject 'I' for the benefit 'to me'; the verbless clause has no verb 'to be'.
- לִי comes twice in the same sense, 'for me': 'if I am not for me, who is for me?'. The English renders the first 'for myself' because its subject is also 'I'; לְעַצְמִי 'for my self' in the next clause sharpens it.
- וּכְשֶׁאֲנִי לְעַצְמִי: כְּשֶׁ- is the Mishnaic 'when', compounded from כ + שֶׁ.
- אֵימָתַי is the Mishnaic interrogative 'when', and עַכְשָׁיו the Mishnaic 'now'.

Note: The English keeps the three clauses short and unpaired. 'Who is for me?' is left open: Bartenura reads it as 'who will earn merit for me' and Rambam as 'who will rouse my soul', so the English does not choose between them. אֵימָתַי is read by Bartenura as 'after death' and in the other explanation 'in old age'; the English leaves it as plain 'when'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if I do not earn merit for myself, who will earn it on my behalf.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even if I have earned merit for myself, what is that merit and what is it worth against what I am obliged to do.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'now' means in this world.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: after death one can no longer earn merit; another explanation: if not now in youth, when, perhaps in old age it will not come to hand.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: if I do not rouse my own soul upward, who will, since I have no outside rouser. And in the next clause, 'what am I': what has come of me, I am not complete even after doing this. He takes 'now' to be youth, since habits harden later (Prov 22:6).

Apparatus:

- Rambam applies the third clause to youth (Prov 22:6, 'train a youth in his way').
- Bartenura gives two senses of אֵימָתַי: after death, and in old age.

#### Pirkei Avot 1:15

> שַׁמַּאי אוֹמֵר, עֲשֵׂה תוֹרָתְךָ קֶבַע. אֱמֹר מְעַט וַעֲשֵׂה הַרְבֵּה, וֶהֱוֵי מְקַבֵּל אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם בְּסֵבֶר פָּנִים יָפוֹת:

**Shammai says: Make your Torah fixed. Say little and do much, and receive every person with a pleasant countenance.**

- Three imperatives, each with a different construction: עֲשֵׂה and אֱמֹר are plain imperatives, וֶהֱוֵי with a participle gives a continuous 'be receiving'.
- עֲשֵׂה תוֹרָתְךָ קֶבַע: a double accusative of result, 'make your Torah (into) something fixed'.
- אֱמֹר מְעַט וַעֲשֵׂה הַרְבֵּה: an antithesis, with מְעַט and הַרְבֵּה as adverbs.

Note: קֶבַע is rendered 'fixed' in the sense of a permanent, not a passing, occupation. Bartenura also records a second reading: that you hold yourself to the same standard in your Torah as for others. סֵבֶר פָּנִים is a phrase for a look or expression of the face; 'pleasant countenance' is Rambam's 'gently and with welcome words'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: your main occupation is Torah, day and night; when weary of study, do work. The other way round (work as main, Torah when work allows) is excluded. He adds a second explanation: do not be strict with yourself and lenient with others, or the reverse.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: as Abraham said 'I will fetch a morsel of bread' and then took a tender and good calf (Gen 18).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: when you bring guests in, do not give with your face to the ground, for such giving is counted as nothing; Shammai's three warnings correspond to Jeremiah's wise, strong and rich.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: Torah study is the root and chief thing and all other occupations follow it; if there is time, good, and if not, no harm. The righteous say little and do much, as Abraham; the wicked say much and do nothing, as Ephron.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: to deal with people gently and with pleasant, welcome words.

Apparatus:

- Gen 18:5 (וְאֶקְחָה פַת לֶחֶם) and 18:7 (וַיִּקַּח בֶּן בָּקָר רַךְ וָטוֹב) are cited by Bartenura and Rambam for 'say little, do much'.
- Vilna reads אמור (1:15.6) for אֱמֹר: spelling only.
- אֱמֹר: Vilna reads אמור (spelling)

- וְלֹא הַמִּדְרָשׁ הוּא הָעִקָּר: the pronoun הוּא stands as copula between subject and predicate.
- וְכָל הַמַּרְבֶּה: כָּל with the articular participle makes a general statement, 'every one who multiplies'.
- The last clause echoes Proverbs 10:19, בְּרֹב דְּבָרִים לֹא יֶחְדַּל פֶּשַׁע, as Rambam notes.

Note: לַגּוּף: 'body' is read as the person; Bartenura's gloss is the person who hears his own shame and is silent. The mishnah's מִדְרָשׁ is rendered 'study', and Rambam and Bartenura both read it as speech about Torah that must lead to action. The last clause is read by Rambam as about speech in general and by Rabbeinu Yonah as about Torah rulings; the English leaves the words general.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who hears his own shame and is silent.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even exposition and speaking in Torah, than which there is no better trait, is rewarded chiefly for the action; one who expounds and does not carry it out is better off silent.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Eve multiplied words ('neither shall you touch it'), added a touch not forbidden, and the serpent pushed her to touch it and then to eat; Solomon: 'do not add to his words' (Prov 30).
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'in many words transgression does not cease' (Prov 10:19); a man who speaks much is bound to say something improper; few words mark the wise, many the fool.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: first of a wise man's four classes of speech, all harm and no benefit, such as cursing and foul speech.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: second class, harm on one side and benefit on the other, such as praise that angers an enemy.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: third class, neither benefit nor harm, such as idle talk about buildings and foods.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: fourth class, wholly beneficial; the wise man speaks only in that class and is silent in the others, which gives the sense of 'silence' as the best course for the body.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: the first of five classes under the Law, speech that is commanded, namely reciting and studying Torah.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: second class, forbidden speech: false witness, slander, cursing, foul speech and evil speech.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: third class, repulsive speech, idle talk (שיחה בטלה), which the pious avoided.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: fourth class, beloved speech, praising virtues and condemning vices; he says this is called דרך ארץ.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: fifth class, permitted speech about livelihood, food and clothing, to be kept short; and for מדרש he cites 'fair are words from those who do them', that deeds must agree with words and few words carry much.

Apparatus:

- Proverbs 10:19 (בְּרֹב דְּבָרִים לֹא יֶחְדַּל פֶּשַׁע) is cited by Rambam.
- Vilna reads העיקר (1:17.18) for הָעִקָּר: spelling only.
- Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma reads טוֹב מִשְּׁתִיקָה, 'better than silence', for the base טוֹב אֶלָּא שְׁתִיקָה.
- הָעִקָּר: Vilna reads העיקר (spelling)

Grammar:

- עַל שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים הָעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד: the preposition עַל means 'upon' (the world rests on); the participle עוֹמֵד is 'stands, endures'.
- The three items are each introduced with עַל and the article: הַדִּין, הָאֱמֶת, הַשָּׁלוֹם.
- שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר introduces the verse (Zech 8:16) as a proof text; the mishnah reads the verse as naming the three things, truth, judgment, and peace.
- אֱמֶת וּמִשְׁפַּט שָׁלוֹם שִׁפְטוּ: the two nouns are the objects of the plural imperative שִׁפְטוּ 'judge', put before it for emphasis; מִשְׁפַּט is in the construct, 'a judgment of peace'.
- בְּשַׁעֲרֵיכֶם: 'in your gates', the place of the court.

Note: הָעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד: Bartenura says that here 'the world' means the settlement of human beings, not the world of the previous mishnah (1:2). The English keeps 'the world'. Rambam reads the three things as the political order (justice), the intellectual virtues (truth), and the moral virtues (peace); this is recorded but not adopted. The verse is translated from the Hebrew of the mishnah, the three items answering to 'truth', 'judgment', 'peace'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the settlement of human beings endures; this is not the 'world stands' of the earlier mishnah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: justice is to acquit the innocent and convict the guilty.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: truth is that no man lie to his fellow.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: peace between kingdoms and between a man and his fellow.
- Rambam (records): Rambam: justice is conduct of the state with uprightness; truth is the intellectual virtues and peace the moral virtues, and when the three are found, existence is as perfect as it can be.

Apparatus:

- Zechariah 8:16: אֱמֶת וּמִשְׁפַּט שָׁלוֹם שִׁפְטוּ בְּשַׁעֲרֵיכֶם.
- Vilna reads טז (the verse number 16) where the base has the chapter number ח at 1:18.19; the citation is Zech 8:16.
- —: Vilna reads טז (word)

## Chapter 2 — פֶּרֶק ב (Pirkei Avot 2:1–2:16)

### Reading text

<sup>2:1</sup> Rabbi says: Which is the upright path that a person should choose for himself? Whatever is a glory to those who do it and a glory to him from people. Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, for you do not know the reward given for the commandments. Reckon the loss from a commandment against its reward, and the gain from a transgression against its loss. Look at three things and you will not come to transgression: know what is above you: an eye that sees and an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.

<sup>2:2</sup> Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehuda the Patriarch, says: Torah study is excellent together with a worldly occupation, for the toil of both makes sin forgotten. And any Torah study that has no work with it in the end comes to nothing and draws sin along. And all who labor with the community should labor with them for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their fathers supports them and their righteousness stands forever. And you, I credit to you a great reward as if you had done it.

<sup>2:3</sup> Be wary of the authorities, for they do not draw a person near except for their own needs. They appear as friends when it is to their benefit, and they do not stand by a person in his hour of need.

<sup>2:4</sup> He used to say: Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His will. Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before your will. Hillel says: Do not separate yourself from the community, and do not trust yourself until the day of your death, and do not judge your fellow until you reach his place, and do not say a thing that cannot be heard, for in the end it will be heard. And do not say, 'When I am free I will study': perhaps you will not be free.

<sup>2:5</sup> He used to say: No boor fears sin, and no unlearned person is pious, and no shy person learns, and no short-tempered person teaches, and not everyone who does much business becomes wise. And in a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.

<sup>2:6</sup> He also saw a skull floating on the surface of the water. He said to it: 'Because you drowned others, they drowned you, and in the end those who drowned you will be drowned.'

<sup>2:7</sup> He used to say: The more flesh, the more worms. The more property, the more anxiety. The more wives, the more witchcraft. The more maidservants, the more lewdness. The more male slaves, the more robbery. The more Torah, the more life. The more sitting in study, the more wisdom. The more counsel, the more understanding. The more charity, the more peace. One who has acquired a good name has acquired it for himself. One who has acquired for himself words of Torah has acquired for himself the life of the world to come.

<sup>2:8</sup> Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai received from Hillel and from Shammai. He used to say: If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself, for to this end you were created. Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai had five disciples, and these are they: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach. He used to enumerate their praises: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, happy is she who bore him. Rabbi Yose the Priest, a pious man. Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, a fearer of sin. And Rabbi Elazar son of Arach, a spring gathering strength. He used to say: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Eliezer son of Hyrcanus in the other pan, he would outweigh them all. Abba Shaul says in his name: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus also with them, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach in the other pan, he would outweigh them all.

<sup>2:9</sup> He said to them: Go out and see which is the right way that a person should cling to. Rabbi Eliezer says: A good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: A good companion. Rabbi Yose says: A good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who sees what is to come. Rabbi Elazar says: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words. He said to them: Go out and see which is the evil way that a person should keep far from. Rabbi Eliezer says: An evil eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: An evil companion. Rabbi Yose says: An evil neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who borrows and does not repay. One who borrows from a person is as one who borrows from the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 37): The wicked one borrows and does not repay, but the Righteous One is gracious and gives. Rabbi Elazar says: An evil heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words.

<sup>2:10</sup> They said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: Let your fellow's honor be as dear to you as your own, and do not be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. And warm yourself at the fire of the sages, and beware of their coals, lest you be burned; for their bite is the bite of a fox, their sting is the sting of a scorpion, their whisper is the whisper of a fiery serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.

<sup>2:11</sup> Rabbi Yehoshua says: The evil eye, the evil impulse, and hatred of people remove a person from the world.

<sup>2:12</sup> Rabbi Yose says: Let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own. Prepare yourself to learn Torah, for it is not an inheritance to you. And let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.

<sup>2:13</sup> Rabbi Shimon says: Be careful in reciting the Shema and in the Prayer. And when you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine, but a plea for mercy and supplication before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Joel 2): “For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in kindness, and relenting of the evil.” And do not be wicked in your own eyes.

<sup>2:14</sup> Rabbi Elazar says: Be diligent in learning Torah, and know what to answer an Epicurean. And know before whom you toil. And faithful is the master of your work to pay you the reward of your labor.

<sup>2:15</sup> Rabbi Tarfon says: The day is short, the work is great, the laborers are lazy, the reward is abundant, and the master of the house is pressing.

<sup>2:16</sup> He used to say: It is not for you to finish the work, and you are not free to desist from it. If you have learned much Torah, they give you much reward. And faithful is the master of your work to pay you the reward of your labor. And know that the granting of the reward of the righteous is in the world to come.

### Chapter 2 by mishnah

#### Pirkei Avot 2:1

> רַבִּי אוֹמֵר, אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיָּבֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם, כֹּל שֶׁהִיא תִפְאֶרֶת לְעוֹשֶׂיהָ וְתִפְאֶרֶת לוֹ מִן הָאָדָם. וֶהֱוֵי זָהִיר בְּמִצְוָה קַלָּה כְבַחֲמוּרָה, שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ מַתַּן שְׂכָרָן שֶׁל מִצְוֹת. וֶהֱוֵי מְחַשֵּׁב הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה כְּנֶגֶד שְׂכָרָהּ, וּשְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה כְנֶגֶד הֶפְסֵדָהּ. וְהִסְתַּכֵּל בִּשְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאִי אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵרָה, דַּע מַה לְּמַעְלָה מִמְּךָ, עַיִן רוֹאָה וְאֹזֶן שׁוֹמַעַת, וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ בַסֵּפֶר נִכְתָּבִין:

**Rabbi says: Which is the upright path that a person should choose for himself? Whatever is a glory to those who do it and a glory to him from people. Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, for you do not know the reward given for the commandments. Reckon the loss from a commandment against its reward, and the gain from a transgression against its loss. Look at three things and you will not come to transgression: know what is above you: an eye that sees and an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.**

Literal: Rabbi saying, which-is path upright that-he-chooses for-him the-person: all that-it glory to-its-doers and-glory to-him from the-person. And-be careful in-commandment light like-in-weighty, that-there-is-not you knowing giving-of reward-of-them of commandments. And-be reckoning loss-of commandment against reward-its, and-reward-of transgression against loss-its. And-look in-three things and-not you coming to-hands-of transgression: know what above from-you: eye seeing and-ear hearing and-all deeds-your in-the-book being-written.

Grammar:

- אֵיזוֹהִי is the Mishnaic interrogative 'which is it', agreeing with the feminine דֶרֶךְ.
- The saying is built of parallel imperatives with וֶהֱוֵי: be careful (זָהִיר), be reckoning (מְחַשֵּׁב); then the closing triad, introduced by וְהִסְתַּכֵּל.
- שֶׁיָּבֹר is a relative clause with a modal yiqtol: 'that a person should choose'; יָבֹר is from the geminate root ברר.
- The last clause is a nominal series: 'an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book': these are the three things.

Note: 'Glory' renders תִפְאֶרֶת in both parts; both normative commentators read the path as the middle one, which is a glory to the doer and to people. 'Upright' for יְשָׁרָה: 'straight, right'. The reckoning clauses follow Bartenura (what a commandment costs against its reward; the pleasure of a sin against what it costs); Rambam's reading is recorded in the apparatus. The three things: the eye, the ear and the book of deeds, as Rabbeinu Yonah counts them: he asks why three are named when on the plain reading they are one, and answers by dividing them into deeds, speech and memory.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura glosses שֶׁיָּבֹר as שֶׁיִּבְרֹר, 'that he choose': the verb is 'to choose'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura reads the path as the middle way in every trait: not stingy, which brings no glory from people, and not overspending, which does not bring glory to the one who does it; generosity between the two is a glory to both.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says the Torah does not state the reward for fulfilling positive commandments, whereas the punishments for the prohibitions are stated; so one cannot tell a light commandment from a weighty one.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'reckon' what you lose in goods and money because of a commandment against the reward it brings in this world or the next, which will exceed the loss.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the שְׂכַר of a transgression is the pleasure you take in it, to be set against the loss that will come from it.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the upright path is the good actions, the middle traits, by which a person acquires a worthy disposition and good conduct with people; this is 'a glory to the doer and a glory to him from people'. Be as careful with a commandment thought light (rejoicing on a festival, learning the holy tongue) as with one known to be weighty, because the Torah states the punishments of the prohibitions in eight grades but not the reward of the positive commandments. He reads 'reckon the loss of a commandment against its reward' as inferring a positive commandment's reward from the penalty for neglecting it, and 'the reward of a transgression' as the reward for refraining from it, measured by its punishment.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: the Holy One sees and knows all human deeds and remembers them as if written before Him. He asks why the mishnah counts three things when, read plainly, they are one (God knows all and repays); he answers that it is a likeness: as a man is ashamed to act or speak improperly before kings and sages, so he should think at all times that he stands before the Holy One; he then counts the three apart (2:1:8–9).

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads שיבור (base שֶׁיָּבֹר), לעושה (base לְעוֹשֶׂיהָ; Vilna's form is singular 'its doer') and עבירה for עֲבֵרָה (2:1.36, 2:1.46): spelling only, except that the singular לעושה differs in number.
- Rambam reads the reckoning clauses differently: הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה is the penalty for neglecting a positive commandment, from which its reward is inferred (Sabbath rest, punished by stoning when broken, outweighs circumcision, punished by karet), and שְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה is the reward for refraining from a transgression, measured by its punishment. The English follows Bartenura: the cost of doing a commandment against its reward, the pleasure of a sin against its cost.
- שֶׁיָּבֹר: Vilna reads שיבור (spelling)
- לְעוֹשֶׂיהָ: Vilna reads לעושה (spelling)
- עֲבֵרָה: Vilna reads עבירה (spelling)
- עֲבֵרָה: Vilna reads עבירה (spelling)
- וְאֹזֶן: Vilna reads ואוזן (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:2

> רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא אוֹמֵר, יָפֶה תַלְמוּד תּוֹרָה עִם דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, שֶׁיְּגִיעַת שְׁנֵיהֶם מְשַׁכַּחַת עָוֹן. וְכָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵין עִמָּהּ מְלָאכָה, סוֹפָהּ בְּטֵלָה וְגוֹרֶרֶת עָוֹן. וְכָל הָעֲמֵלִים עִם הַצִּבּוּר, יִהְיוּ עֲמֵלִים עִמָּהֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, שֶׁזְּכוּת אֲבוֹתָם מְסַיַּעְתָּן וְצִדְקָתָם עוֹמֶדֶת לָעַד. וְאַתֶּם, מַעֲלֶה אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם שָׂכָר הַרְבֵּה כְּאִלּוּ עֲשִׂיתֶם:

**Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehuda the Patriarch, says: Torah study is excellent together with a worldly occupation, for the toil of both makes sin forgotten. And any Torah study that has no work with it in the end comes to nothing and draws sin along. And all who labor with the community should labor with them for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their fathers supports them and their righteousness stands forever. And you, I credit to you a great reward as if you had done it.**

Literal: Rabban Gamliel son-his of Rabbi Yehuda the-Patriarch saying: good study-of Torah with way-of land, that-toil-of both-of-them causes-to-forget iniquity. And-all Torah that-there-is-not with-it work, end-its void and-dragging iniquity. And-all the-labourers with the-community, let-them-be labouring with-them for-the-sake-of Heaven, that-merit-of their-fathers supporting-them and-their-righteousness standing for-ever. And-you, raising I upon-you reward much as-if you-did.

Grammar:

- יָפֶה תַלְמוּד תּוֹרָה: the predicate comes first, 'excellent is Torah study'.
- שֶׁיְּגִיעַת ... מְשַׁכַּחַת: a שֶׁ-clause of reason, 'for the toil of both ... makes forgotten'.
- The middle saying turns on יִהְיוּ עֲמֵלִים 'let them labor' (jussive) and the participles מְסַיַּעְתָּן and עוֹמֶדֶת.
- וְאַתֶּם ... מַעֲלֶה אֲנִי: the speaker turns to address the labourers directly: 'and as for you, I count to you ...'.

Note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ is translated 'a worldly occupation' following Bartenura's gloss (work or trade) and Rambam (earning a living). 'Their fathers' are the fathers of the community, per Bartenura. In the last clause the English leaves the object of 'you had done' unexpressed, as the Hebrew does. The title נָשִׂיא is 'the Patriarch'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura glosses דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ as 'work or trade'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Torah drains a person's strength and work breaks the body, and so the evil impulse is idle in him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if one says that constant toil in Torah would make sin forgotten without work, the mishnah says Torah without work ends in nothing, since one cannot do without sustenance and ends by robbing people and forgetting his study.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: let them be occupied with the community for the sake of Heaven, and not to take a crown by saying 'I did so and so for the community'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the merit and the lasting righteousness are those of the fathers of the community; it is this which helps those who work with them, and not the quality of the workers' own effort.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: although the good outcome does not come from your deeds but from the merit of the community's fathers, I count it to you as if you had brought about the salvation, since you labor for Heaven's sake. He adds another reading, about those who press the community to charity or the redeeming of captives.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ is earning a living; Torah without it leads to robbing people. He takes the last clause as God's word to those who work with the community, who are sometimes kept from a commandment by communal business: God counts it as if they had done it.

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads מסייעתן (base מְסַיַּעְתָּן) and כאילו (base כְּאִלּוּ): spelling only.
- Bartenura's and Rabbeinu Yonah's lemmata read עוֹסְקִין 'occupied' for עֲמֵלִים 'labour' (וְכָל הָעוֹסְקִין עִם הַצִּבּוּר יִהְיוּ עוֹסְקִין עִמָּהֶם), and Rabbeinu Yonah reads וְכָל הַתּוֹרָה for וְכָל תּוֹרָה.
- מְסַיַּעְתָּן: Vilna reads מסייעתן (spelling)
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)

Grammar:

- הֱווּ is the plural imperative of הָיָה, 'be', in the Mishnaic form; the Aramaic-style plural endings in זְהִירִין, מְקָרְבִין, נִרְאִין, כְּאוֹהֲבִין, עוֹמְדִין follow.
- שֶׁאֵין מְקָרְבִין: the plural participle has no stated subject; it is 'they', the authorities.
- לוֹ לָאָדָם: a Mishnaic doubling of the object, 'to him, that is, the person'.
- The saying is a pair of contrasts: 'appear as friends when it benefits them' against 'do not stand by a person in his distress'.

Note: 'Authorities' for הָרָשׁוּת: the ruling powers. Bartenura applies it to dealing with the authorities on behalf of the community; Rambam to governments. The English keeps both applications open. In the second clause, 'they' are the authorities.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: you who deal with community affairs, although you must make yourselves known to the authorities to attend to the people's business, be careful with them.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: הָרְשׁוּת are the governments of old, and the mishnah speaks of their traits and warns against them.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads לצורך (base לְצֹרֶךְ): spelling only.
- לְצֹרֶךְ: Vilna reads לצורך (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:4

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, עֲשֵׂה רְצוֹנוֹ כִרְצוֹנְךָ, כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹנְךָ כִרְצוֹנוֹ. בַּטֵּל רְצוֹנְךָ מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנוֹ, כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל רְצוֹן אֲחֵרִים מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנֶךָ. הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר, אַל תִּפְרֹשׁ מִן הַצִּבּוּר, וְאַל תַּאֲמִין בְּעַצְמְךָ עַד יוֹם מוֹתְךָ, וְאַל תָּדִין אֶת חֲבֵרְךָ עַד שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ לִמְקוֹמוֹ, וְאַל תֹּאמַר דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִשְׁמֹעַ, שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמַע. וְאַל תֹּאמַר לִכְשֶׁאִפָּנֶה אֶשְׁנֶה, שֶׁמָּא לֹא תִפָּנֶה:

**He used to say: Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His will. Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before your will. Hillel says: Do not separate yourself from the community, and do not trust yourself until the day of your death, and do not judge your fellow until you reach his place, and do not say a thing that cannot be heard, for in the end it will be heard. And do not say, 'When I am free I will study': perhaps you will not be free.**

Literal: He he-used saying: do will-his like-your-will, so-that he-will-do your-will like-his-will. Annul your-will from-before his-will, so-that he-will-annul will-of others from-before your-will. Hillel saying: not you-separate from the-community, and-not you-trust in-yourself until day-of your-death, and-not you-judge [object-marker] your-fellow until that-you-reach his-place, and-not you-say thing that-not possible to-hear that-its-end to-be-heard. And-not you-say when-I-am-free I-will-study, lest not you-will-be-free.

Grammar:

- הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: a perfect of הָיָה with a participle, the habitual past ('used to say'); the unnamed subject is the speaker last named, Rabban Gamliel (2:2).
- עֲשֵׂה ... בַּטֵּל: two imperatives, each followed by a כְּדֵי שֶׁ purpose clause with the roles of God and the speaker reversed.
- Hillel's sayings are a string of אַל + yiqtol prohibitions; the verbs תִּפְרֹשׁ, תַּאֲמִין, תָּדִין, תֹּאמַר are all second masculine singular.
- שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמַע: the Nifal infinitive after ל gives 'is bound to be heard'.

Note: 'He' in the first saying is the speaker last named, Rabban Gamliel of 2:2. The suffix of רְצוֹנוֹ is God, per Bartenura. The saying of Hillel on 'a thing that cannot be heard' is ambiguous. The English, 'for in the end it will be heard', gives Bartenura's second reading: do not say a secret thinking no one can hear it, for in the end it will be heard. Bartenura says this reading goes with the base text's שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ. His first reading, which is Rambam's, goes with his lemma וְסוֹפוֹ: do not say what cannot be understood at first hearing. It is recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: spend your money on the wishes of Heaven as if you were spending it on your own wishes; if you do, He will do your will as He does His, that is, He will treat you generously.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura first reads 'the will of others' as thwarting the plans of all who rise against you for ill; he then says he heard that this is only a respectful way of saying 'so that He will set aside His will before yours', as in the Talmud's statement that a decree of seventy years is annulled for one who does a commandment properly.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: instead share in their trouble, for whoever separates himself from the community does not see the community's comfort.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Yohanan the High Priest served for eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if you see your fellow come to a test and fail, do not judge him guilty until you come to a test like his and are saved.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not make statements that cannot be understood at first, relying on the listener eventually understanding them, for people may err and become heretics through you; on this reading his text has וְסוֹפוֹ. Another reading: do not reveal a secret even when alone, saying no one will hear, for in the end it will be heard ('a bird of the air will carry the voice'); the text שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ fits this reading. Rashi reads שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר without אִי and applies it to Torah: do not put off hearing what you can hear now.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'when I am free' of my business, I will engage in Torah.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: as explained in his fourth chapter, one should separate from the community only according to its corruption. And a person, however worthy his disposition and however strong, should not stop repeating good deeds to strengthen it, nor trust that the virtue cannot leave him; it can, hence 'until the day of your death'.
- Rambam (records): Rambam: a thing that cannot be heard is one whose plain meaning seems very far-fetched; the saying warns against speech that needs a distant interpretation and close study before the listener can understand it.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'when I am free' means free of this business, like the earlier saying of Shammai to make your Torah fixed.

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads תפרוש, תאמן and לשמוע (bases תִּפְרֹשׁ, תַּאֲמִין, לִשְׁמֹעַ): spelling only.
- Bartenura's lemma reads וְסוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמֵעַ for שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמַע. He says the reading שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ belongs to his second interpretation (a secret will in the end be heard), and that Rashi reads דָּבָר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לִשְׁמֹעַ, without אִי: do not say of a word of Torah that you can hear now that you will hear it later.
- Bartenura's first reading, and Rambam's: do not say a thing that cannot be understood at first hearing, relying on the listener to understand it in the end after close study; people may misread it.
- תִּפְרֹשׁ: Vilna reads תפרוש (spelling)
- תַּאֲמִין: Vilna reads תאמן (spelling)
- לִשְׁמֹעַ: Vilna reads לשמוע (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:5

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, אֵין בּוּר יְרֵא חֵטְא, וְלֹא עַם הָאָרֶץ חָסִיד, וְלֹא הַבַּיְשָׁן לָמֵד, וְלֹא הַקַּפְּדָן מְלַמֵּד, וְלֹא כָל הַמַּרְבֶּה בִסְחוֹרָה מַחְכִּים. וּבְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין אֲנָשִׁים, הִשְׁתַּדֵּל לִהְיוֹת אִישׁ:

**He used to say: No boor fears sin, and no unlearned person is pious, and no shy person learns, and no short-tempered person teaches, and not everyone who does much business becomes wise. And in a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.**

Literal: He he-used saying: there-is-not boor fearing-of sin, and-not people-of the-land pious, and-not the-shy learning, and-not the-hot-tempered teaching, and-not all the-increasing in-business making-wise. And-in-place that-there-are-not men, strive to-be man.

Grammar:

- Five parallel negations, one with אֵין and four with וְלֹא: 'no boor ..., no unlearned person ..., no shy person ..., no short-tempered person ...'; the fifth, וְלֹא כָל, is 'not everyone who ...': it limits, it does not deny.
- אֵין בּוּר יְרֵא חֵטְא: the existential negative אֵין governs the first clause; the rest use וְלֹא.
- יְרֵא חֵטְא is a construct chain, 'one fearing of sin'.
- The closing line shifts to an imperative, הִשְׁתַּדֵּל, with a play on אֲנָשִׁים and אִישׁ.

Note: עַם הָאָרֶץ is 'an unlearned person' by the decisions; the literal 'people of the land' is given here. בּוּר is 'boor' (empty, uncultivated). Bartenura reads בּוּר as worse than the unlearned person: empty of everything, even of business sense. אִישׁ in the last clause is 'a man' in the sense of a person of worth; Bartenura takes it as sitting at the head and giving rulings.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: בּוּר is empty of every thing and does not know even good business practice; he is worse than the עַם הָאָרֶץ. He cites the Targum of Genesis 47:19 for בּוּר as 'waste'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the עַם הָאָרֶץ may fear sin, since he knows business, but he cannot be pious (חָסִיד).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who is ashamed to ask, lest they mock him, stays in his doubts.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the teacher who is strict with students when they ask him will not teach properly; he must show a pleasant face in the law.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura quotes Deuteronomy 30:13, 'nor is it beyond the sea': Torah is not found among those who go overseas.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'in a place where there are no men' means to sit at the head and give rulings.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: בּוּר has neither wisdom nor good traits; the עַם הָאָרֶץ has no intellectual virtues but some moral ones; the exacting person is one who takes offense at everything and gets angry; הִשְׁתַּדֵּל means to train yourself to acquire the virtues, and teach yourself when there are no wise men to teach you.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads הביישן (base הַבַּיְשָׁן): spelling only.
- Bartenura and Rambam read the saying about business with Deuteronomy 30:12-13 ('It is not in heaven ... nor is it beyond the sea'); the mishnah does not quote the verse.
- הַבַּיְשָׁן: Vilna reads הביישן (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:6

> אַף הוּא רָאָה גֻלְגֹּלֶת אַחַת שֶׁצָּפָה עַל פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם. אָמַר לָהּ, עַל דַּאֲטֵפְתְּ, אַטְפוּךְ. וְסוֹף מְטִיפַיִךְ יְטוּפוּן:

**He also saw a skull floating on the surface of the water. He said to it: 'Because you drowned others, they drowned you, and in the end those who drowned you will be drowned.'**

Literal: Also he he-saw skull one that-floating upon face-of the-water. He-said to-her: because that-you-made-float, they-made-float-you; and-end-of your-floaters they-will-float.

Grammar:

- The second half of the mishnah is Aramaic: עַל דַּאֲטֵפְתְּ אַטְפוּךְ וְסוֹף מְטִיפַיִךְ יְטוּפוּן. The Aramaic relative דְּ replaces Hebrew שֶׁ.
- The skull is feminine (גֻלְגֹּלֶת), so the speaker addresses it with the feminine suffixes -תְּ, -ךְ and -ַיִךְ.
- The saying uses the root טוּף four times as a play: the Afel (causative) in אֲטֵפְתְּ 'you made float', אַטְפוּךְ 'they made you float' and מְטִיפַיִךְ 'those who made you float', then the Peal (simple) יְטוּפוּן 'they will float'.
- אַף הוּא opens the mishnah as a link to the preceding sayings of Hillel.

Note: The Aramaic clause is a measure-for-measure saying: Bartenura reads the skull as that of a wicked man who threw people into the river; Rambam gives it the moral that evil deeds return on the head of the doer. The English 'drowned' stands for the Aramaic 'made float', which Bartenura glosses as casting people on the river. The last verb is read as passive in sense: 'will be drowned'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: you were wicked and cast people into the river, and by the same measure they measured to you.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: it was not given to them to kill you, but to a court, and the Holy One, blessed be He, delivered you to them (and they too will be punished).
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: you were killed because you killed another, and the one who killed you will himself be killed; evil deeds return on the head of their doer, as 'by the measure a person measures, they measure to him'.

Apparatus:

- Aramaic text of the saying: עַל דַּאֲטֵפְתְּ אַטְפוּךְ, וְסוֹף מְטִיפַיִךְ יְטוּפוּן.
- Variant: Vilna reads גולגלת (base גֻלְגֹּלֶת): spelling only.
- Rabbeinu Yonah's text reads בְּסוֹף מְטִיפַיִךְ יְטִיפוּן (Afel), 'in the end others will make those who drowned you float', for יְטוּפוּן (Peal) 'they will float'.
- גֻלְגֹּלֶת: Vilna reads גולגלת (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:7

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, מַרְבֶּה בָשָׂר, מַרְבֶּה רִמָּה. מַרְבֶּה נְכָסִים, מַרְבֶּה דְאָגָה. מַרְבֶּה נָשִׁים, מַרְבֶּה כְשָׁפִים. מַרְבֶּה שְׁפָחוֹת, מַרְבֶּה זִמָּה. מַרְבֶּה עֲבָדִים, מַרְבֶּה גָזֵל. מַרְבֶּה תוֹרָה, מַרְבֶּה חַיִּים. מַרְבֶּה יְשִׁיבָה, מַרְבֶּה חָכְמָה. מַרְבֶּה עֵצָה, מַרְבֶּה תְבוּנָה. מַרְבֶּה צְדָקָה, מַרְבֶּה שָׁלוֹם. קָנָה שֵׁם טוֹב, קָנָה לְעַצְמוֹ. קָנָה לוֹ דִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, קָנָה לוֹ חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

**He used to say: The more flesh, the more worms. The more property, the more anxiety. The more wives, the more witchcraft. The more maidservants, the more lewdness. The more male slaves, the more robbery. The more Torah, the more life. The more sitting in study, the more wisdom. The more counsel, the more understanding. The more charity, the more peace. One who has acquired a good name has acquired it for himself. One who has acquired for himself words of Torah has acquired for himself the life of the world to come.**

Literal: he was saying: increasing-flesh, increasing-worm; increasing-property, increasing-anxiety; increasing-wives, increasing-witchcraft; increasing-maidservants, increasing-lewdness; increasing-slaves, increasing-robbery; increasing-Torah, increasing-life; increasing-sitting, increasing-wisdom; increasing-counsel, increasing-understanding; increasing-charity, increasing-peace. acquired name good, acquired for-himself. acquired for-him words-of Torah, acquired for-him life-of the-world the-coming
