| הַבָּא | that is to come — הַבָּא: 'the coming', the qal participle of בוא with the article; Jastrow בָּא III: עוֹלָם הַבָּא 'the world to come'. | ה: the + בָּא | בוא | article + verb (qal, participle active, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- מַרְבֶּה is a hifil masculine singular participle ('one who increases'). The saying runs on one pattern, מַרְבֶּה X מַרְבֶּה Y, and the English gives it as 'the more X, the more Y'; the participle carries no 'if' or 'then'.
- The first five pairs set a possession against its cost (flesh and worms, property and anxiety, wives and witchcraft, maidservants and lewdness, slaves and robbery); the next four set a good against its reward (Torah and life, study and wisdom, counsel and understanding, charity and peace). The list is closed by two sentences with קָנָה, the perfect used for a general truth.
- דְאָגָה (anxiety), כְשָׁפִים (sorceries, plural of כֶּשֶׁף) and זִמָּה (lewdness) are all biblical words (Prov 12:25; 2 Kgs 9:22; Lev 18:17); the pack's BDB entries for זִמָּה and עֶבֶד are proper names with the same consonants, and Jastrow's entry for רָבָה is only a cross-reference.
- In קָנָה לוֹ, the preposition with suffix לוֹ is a dative of advantage ('for himself'); in לְעַצְמוֹ the noun 'bone, self' is used as the reflexive.
- הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא is a noun with an article plus a participle with an article, 'the world that comes'; decisions.md fixes it as 'the world to come'.

Note: מַרְבֶּה is given as 'the more ...' to keep the brevity of the sayings. בָּשָׂר is rendered 'flesh' as in Bartenura (one who eats and drinks until he is fat); the English does not decide whether the worms of the grave or of the body are meant. יְשִׁיבָה: 'sitting', that is, sitting in session or in the academy (Bartenura: many disciples gather to hear his reasoning); I keep the literal word. In this reading the clause is 'more sitting, more wisdom', and Bartenura notes that others read 'one who increases yeshivah increases wisdom', which is what our text has. צְדָקָה: 'charity' (giving), the sense of the later usage; Bartenura quotes Isaiah 32:17, where the word is 'righteousness', so the English keeps 'charity' while the wider sense is recorded here.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who eats and drinks until he is fat and fleshy increases worms on himself in the grave, and the worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh. He adds that this tanna teaches that every increase is harmful to a person except increase of Torah, wisdom and charity.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the anxiety is lest the king's household (the government) rob him or bandits come upon him and kill him. He cites a pious man who prayed to be saved from 'scattering of the soul', which meant having many goods scattered in many places so that one must scatter one's mind to think of this place and that.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the order of the list is a sequence of causes: first a man adorns himself, eats and drinks and grows fleshy; then he seeks wealth; with wealth enough to support many women he takes many wives; each wife needs a maidservant; and a large household needs fields and vineyards and slaves to work them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'more Torah, more life' because it is written (Deuteronomy 30:20) 'for it is your life and the length of your days'.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura comments on the order 'the more wisdom, the more yeshivah': one who increases wisdom gives reasons for his words and his arguments settle in the hearts of the hearers, so that disciples gather to him (2:7:6). The base text has the reverse order, which Bartenura records as the reading of others; the English follows the base text.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: many disciples gather to hear his arguments. He notes the reading 'more sitting, more wisdom' (the reading of our text): one who has many disciples is sharpened by them, and they increase and add to his wisdom.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'increases counsel' means one who takes counsel often.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'understanding' is to understand one thing from another, from the counsel that his advisers give him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the support for charity and peace is Isaiah 32:17, 'and the work of righteousness shall be peace'.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: one who gives charity is loved by those who benefit from his money and so increases peace in the world; one who advises others to give also has it counted to his credit.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: a good name is for himself and he will not leave it to others, unlike the one who increases property, who at death leaves it and goes without any of the desirable things he gained from it.

Apparatus:

- No variant readings are recorded between the witnesses for this mishnah.
- Bartenura (2:7:6) knows both orders, 'increases wisdom, increases sitting' and 'increases sitting, increases wisdom'; the base text has the second.
- Isaiah 32:17 and Deuteronomy 30:20 are quoted by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.

#### Pirkei Avot 2:8

> רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי קִבֵּל מֵהִלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמָּאי. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, אִם לָמַדְתָּ תוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה, אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמְךָ, כִּי לְכָךְ נוֹצָרְתָּ. חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ לְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי, וְאֵלּוּ הֵן, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקְנוֹס, וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה, וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַכֹּהֵן, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵל, וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ. הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שִׁבְחָן. רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקְנוֹס, בּוֹר סוּד שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְאַבֵּד טִפָּה. רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה, אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַכֹּהֵן, חָסִיד. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵל, יְרֵא חֵטְא. וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ, מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם, וֶאֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקְנוֹס בְּכַף שְׁנִיָּה, מַכְרִיעַ אֶת כֻּלָּם. אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ, אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקְנוֹס אַף עִמָּהֶם, וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ בְּכַף שְׁנִיָּה, מַכְרִיעַ אֶת כֻּלָּם:

**Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai received from Hillel and from Shammai. He used to say: If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself, for to this end you were created. Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai had five disciples, and these are they: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach. He used to enumerate their praises: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, happy is she who bore him. Rabbi Yose the Priest, a pious man. Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, a fearer of sin. And Rabbi Elazar son of Arach, a spring gathering strength. He used to say: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Eliezer son of Hyrcanus in the other pan, he would outweigh them all. Abba Shaul says in his name: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus also with them, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach in the other pan, he would outweigh them all.**

Literal: Rabban Yohanan son-of Zakkai received from-Hillel and-from-Shammai. he was saying: if you-learned Torah much, not you-hold goodness for-yourself, for for-this you-were-formed. five disciples were to-him, to-Rabban Yohanan son-of Zakkai, and-these they: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Hyrcanus, and-Rabbi Yehoshua son-of Hananiah, and-Rabbi Yose the-Priest, and-Rabbi Shimon son-of Netanel, and-Rabbi Elazar son-of Arach. he was counting their-praise: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Hyrcanus, cistern plastered that-not-he losing drop. Rabbi Yehoshua son-of Hananiah, happy she-who-bore-him. Rabbi Yose the-Priest, pious. Rabbi Shimon son-of Netanel, fearing-of sin. and-Rabbi Elazar son-of Arach, spring the-gathering-strength. he was saying: if they-be all sages-of Israel in-pan-of scales, and-Eliezer son-of Hyrcanus in-pan second, tipping ACC all-of-them. Abba Shaul saying in-his-name: if they-be all sages-of Israel in-pan-of scales, and-Rabbi Eliezer son-of Hyrcanus also with-them, and-Rabbi Elazar son-of Arach in-pan second, tipping ACC all-of-them

Grammar:

- קִבֵּל (piel of קבל) is the technical verb of transmission: 'received (the tradition)'. It has no stated object in the mishnah.
- אִם לָמַדְתָּ תּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה: a conditional with the perfect (אִם plus qatal), and הַרְבֵּה, the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, used as an adverb after the object; אַל תַּחֲזִיק is a negative command with hifil yiqtol of חזק.
- חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ: possession is expressed by הָיָה plus ל ('five disciples were to him'); the following לְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי repeats the owner by name.
- הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שִׁבְחָן and הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: הָיָה with a participle is the habitual past ('used to enumerate', 'used to say'); the suffix -ָן in שִׁבְחָן is the Mishnaic 3rd person plural, used for masculine as for feminine referents: 'their praises'.
- Each praise is a nominal clause without a verb: name, then predicate (בּוֹר סוּד ..., אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ, חָסִיד, יְרֵא חֵטְא, מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר); יְרֵא חֵטְא is a construct chain of adjective and noun.
- מַכְרִיעַ אֶת כֻּלָּם: hifil participle of כרע, 'tilts the scale against them all'; the weighing is expressed by a conditional with the plural יִהְיוּ and the dual מֹאזְנַיִם, 'a pair of scales'.

Note: קִבֵּל מֵהִלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמָּאי: the English leaves the object unsaid, as in the Hebrew; the sense is 'received the tradition'. אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמְךָ: 'do not claim credit for yourself' (Bartenura: do not say 'I have learned much Torah'; he left no Scripture, Mishnah, halakhah or aggadah unlearned). The literal 'do not hold goodness for yourself' is kept in the literal line. בּוֹר סוּד: סוּד is the passive participle of סוד 'to plaster': 'a plastered cistern'. Bartenura says that this is the reading, not בּוֹר סִיד 'a cistern of lime' (the Vilna spelling), and explains 'like a cistern coated with lime'; Rambam: 'like a lined cistern that does not lose its water'. The English follows the base text as both explain it. חָסִיד: 'a pious man'; Bartenura: one who acts beyond the line of the law. יְרֵא חֵטְא: 'a fearer of sin'; Bartenura: one who is strict with himself and forbids himself permitted things for fear of sin. מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר: 'a spring gathering strength': Bartenura says his heart is wide and he adds arguments and reasons from his own mind. אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ: Bartenura reads 'in his name' as in the name of Rabban Yohanan; and he writes that Abba Shaul does not dispute the first teacher, but both sayings are the Rabban's, and both are true, since for knowledge and memory Rabbi Eliezer outweighs all and for sharpness and argument Rabbi Elazar son of Arach does.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'do not claim credit' means do not say 'I have learned much Torah'. Rabban Yohanan said this because he left no Scripture, Mishnah, halakhah or aggadah that he had not learned (Sukkah 28a, Bava Batra 134a).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the reading is בּוֹר סוּד, not בּוֹר סִיד ('a cistern of lime'); that is, like a cistern coated (plastered) with lime.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'does not lose a drop' means that he does not forget a single thing from his learning.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'happy is she who bore him': he is blessed with good traits so that everyone says 'happy is the woman who bore him'. Another explanation: his mother caused him to be wise, going round all the study-houses of her city and asking them to pray that the child in her womb should be wise, and from the day he was born she did not take his cradle out of the study-house, so that only words of Torah should enter his ears.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: חָסִיד is one who acts beyond the line of the law.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a fearer of sin is one who is strict with himself and forbids himself things that are permitted, out of fear that he might come to sin; otherwise what is the distinction, for even an unlearned person can be a fearer of sin?
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'a spring gathering strength': his heart is broad and he adds argument and reasoning from his own mind.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'in his name' means in the name of Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he has found it written that Abba Shaul does not disagree with the first teacher, that both statements were said by Rabban Yohanan, and both are true: for breadth of knowledge and memory, Rabbi Eliezer tips the scale; for keenness and argument, Rabbi Elazar son of Arach does.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: Rabbi Eliezer was praised for memory, as like a lined cistern that does not lose its water; Rabbi Yehoshua for the excellence of his character traits, by which a man is happy, honored and loved by most of the world, hence 'happy is she who bore him'; Rabbi Yose for his good character and his intellectual virtues; Rabbi Shimon for fear of sin, which is diligence and effort in the affairs of the good and guarding oneself from evil; Rabbi Elazar son of Arach for good understanding, every deep matter being light for him and his insight adding to the matter.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'happy' said without more means that he was blessed in all the blessed traits, great in wisdom and in order in his traits and in all his affairs.

Apparatus:

- 2:8.25 word: Vilna omits לוֹ; base לוֹ.
- 2:8.60 spelling: Vilna reads סיד ('lime'); base סוּד ('plastered'). Bartenura prefers סוּד over סִיד; both give the image of a lime-coated cistern that loses no water (Bartenura, Rambam).
- 2:8.66 2:8.67 word: Vilna omits בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה after the name in the second list; base has it.
- 2:8.72 word: Vilna omits הַכֹּהֵן in the second list; base has it.
- 2:8.103 spelling: Vilna reads כולם; base כֻּלָּם.
- 2:8.123 2:8.124 word: Vilna omits בֶּן עֲרָךְ in the last clause; base has it.
- 2:8.129 spelling: Vilna reads כולם; base כֻּלָּם.
- Bartenura reports (2:8:9) that Abba Shaul and the first teacher are not in dispute; the English reads the two weighings as complementary.

#### Pirkei Avot 2:9

> אָמַר לָהֶם, צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם. רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר, עַיִן טוֹבָה. רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר, חָבֵר טוֹב. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, שָׁכֵן טוֹב. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד. רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר, לֵב טוֹב. אָמַר לָהֶם, רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם, שֶׁבִּכְלָל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם. אָמַר לָהֶם צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם. רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר, עַיִן רָעָה. רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר, חָבֵר רָע. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, שָׁכֵן רָע. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, הַלֹּוֶה וְאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם. אֶחָד הַלֹּוֶה מִן הָאָדָם, כְּלֹוֶה מִן הַמָּקוֹם בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים לז) לֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם, וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן. רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר, לֵב רָע. אָמַר לָהֶם, רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם, שֶׁבִּכְלָל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם:

**He said to them: Go out and see which is the right way that a person should cling to. Rabbi Eliezer says: A good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: A good companion. Rabbi Yose says: A good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who sees what is to come. Rabbi Elazar says: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words. He said to them: Go out and see which is the evil way that a person should keep far from. Rabbi Eliezer says: An evil eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: An evil companion. Rabbi Yose says: An evil neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who borrows and does not repay. One who borrows from a person is as one who borrows from the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 37): The wicked one borrows and does not repay, but the Righteous One is gracious and gives. Rabbi Elazar says: An evil heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words.**

Literal: he-said to-them: go-out and-see which-is way straight that-will-cling in-it the-person. Rabbi Eliezer saying: eye good. Rabbi Yehoshua saying: companion good. Rabbi Yose saying: neighbor good. Rabbi Shimon saying: the-one-seeing ACC the-born. Rabbi Elazar saying: heart good. he-said to-them: seeing I ACC words-of Elazar son-of Arach from-your-words, that-in-generality-of his-words your-words. he-said to-them: go-out and-see which-is way evil that-will-keep-far from-it the-person. Rabbi Eliezer saying: eye evil. Rabbi Yehoshua saying: companion evil. Rabbi Yose saying: neighbor evil. Rabbi Shimon saying: the-borrowing and-not-he paying. one the-borrowing from the-person like-borrowing from the-Place blessed-be He, as-it-is-said (Psalms 37): borrows wicked and-not he-will-pay, and-righteous gracious and-giving. Rabbi Elazar saying: heart evil. he-said to-them: seeing I ACC words-of Elazar son-of Arach from-your-words, that-in-generality-of his-words your-words

Grammar:

- The question is asked twice: אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם and אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם. אֵיזוֹהִי is 'which is' (the feminine of the Mishnaic interrogative, agreeing with דֶרֶךְ, which is feminine); שֶׁיִּדְבַּק and שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק are relative clauses with the imperfect (qal of דבק, hitpael of רחק) of purpose or fitness.
- The answers are nominal clauses in a fixed frame: name + אוֹמֵר + noun + adjective (עַיִן טוֹבָה, חָבֵר טוֹב, שָׁכֵן טוֹב, לֵב טוֹב), and the opposites with רָע/רָעָה. The adjective agrees with the noun in gender, so עַיִן, which is feminine, takes טוֹבָה and רָעָה.
- הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'the one who sees the born' has a qal participle with the article and a nifal participle with the article (the object marker אֶת before it); the idiom means to see what will come to be. Its answer-partner is הַלֹּוֶה וְאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם, a participle plus a negative participial clause with אֵין and a suffix.
- רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר ... מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם: the participle comes before the pronoun, the usual Mishnaic order ('I see'); the comparative מִן means 'rather than'. שֶׁבִּכְלָל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם is a nominal clause with a fronted prepositional phrase.
- Rabbi Shimon's second saying quotes Psalm 37:21 (לֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם, וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן), introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר, 'as it is said'; the verse is in biblical Hebrew with participles (חוֹנֵן, 'gracious', and נוֹתֵן, 'giving').

Note: עַיִן טוֹבָה / עַיִן רָעָה: a 'good eye' is contentment with what one has (Bartenura, Rambam); Rabbeinu Yonah, who is not normative, reads it as generosity. The English keeps the idiom and gives the sense here. הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'one who sees what is to come': Bartenura says he looks at what will be and weighs the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the gain of a transgression against its loss; Rambam says he reflects on the outcome of his affairs. The literal is 'one who sees that which is born'. רוֹאֶה אֲנִי: 'I prefer', literally 'I see'; Rambam says it means 'chooses and discerns'. אֶחָד הַלֹּוֶה ... כְּלֹוֶה: 'one who borrows ... is as one who borrows': the comparison makes the debt to a person a debt to God. הַמָּקוֹם: 'the Omnipresent', literally 'the Place' (decisions.md). וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן: in Psalm 37:21 this is the righteous person who gives to others; Bartenura (and Rambam) read the 'righteous one' as God, who is gracious to the lender and gives him what the borrower did not repay, so that the borrower remains a debtor to the Omnipresent. The English follows them: 'the Righteous One'. Bartenura (2:9:6) explains why the evil way is asked about separately: the opposite of every good trait is not necessarily evil, so a second question was needed.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a good eye is one who is content with what he has, does not seek superfluous things, and is not envious when he sees that his fellows have more than he.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a good companion is one who rebukes him when he sees him doing something improper.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a good neighbor is to be found near him by day and by night, whereas a good companion is not near him at all times.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who sees what is to be looks ahead at what will come, and so weighs the loss of a commandment against its reward and the reward of a transgression against its loss.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the heart moves all the other powers and is the source of all actions; although actions have their own organs, the power that rouses all movements is in the heart, so Rabbi Elazar said 'a good heart', and so Rabban Yohanan preferred his words.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the second question was needed because he did not understand from their first answers that the evil way is the opposite of the good way, since not everything good has an evil opposite: ḥasidut is good, but one who is not pious and stands on the law of the Torah is not evil; and the seeking of surplus might not be called evil as it harms no one.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the one who borrows and does not repay is the opposite of 'one who sees what is to be', for if he does not repay he will find no one to lend to him and will be left hungry. He did not simply say 'one who does not see what is to be', because one who does not foresee might still avoid mishap by saving himself when it comes.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'the righteous one' is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the righteous one of the world, gracious and giving to the lender what the borrower borrowed from him and did not repay, so that the borrower remains a debtor to the Omnipresent.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: a good eye is contentment with what a person has, one of the virtues of character, and an evil eye is its opposite, the belittling of things and eagerness for more; 'sees what is to be' is the thought a man gives to the outcome of his affairs and livelihood; the borrower who does not repay is a counter-example, a mean trait; 'the righteous one is gracious and gives' is God, who repays the lender; 'I see his words' is 'I choose and discern'; and a good heart means good actions, the middle path of the virtues, and includes contentment, love of the good and the other virtues, while an evil heart includes all the vices.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: the speaker of 'he said to them' is Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai to his disciples.

Apparatus:

Grammar:

- הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים: 'they' are the five disciples, each of whom said three things (Rabbeinu Yonah; Bartenura: three things on conduct and character, always on their lips); the three of Rabbi Eliezer follow (Bartenura counts them in 2:10:2; Rambam holds that the third, on the sages' fire, is a saying he reported from another).
- יְהִי and תְּהִי are jussive and imperfect of הָיָה used as imperatives; וֶהֱוֵי is the imperative with a conjunction. The pairs וֶהֱוֵי מִתְחַמֵּם and וֶהֱוֵי זָהִיר govern a participle and an adjective: 'be warming yourself', 'be careful'.
- שֶׁלֹּא תִכָּוֶה: שֶׁלֹּא with the nifal imperfect of כוה, 'that you not be burned'.
- The ending -ָן in גַּחַלְתָּן, נְשִׁיכָתָן, עֲקִיצָתָן, לְחִישָׁתָן and אוּרָן (and שִׁבְחָן in 2:8) is the 3rd person plural suffix of Mishnaic Hebrew ('their'), used for masculine as for feminine referents; here it refers to the sages (חֲכָמִים).
- Each of the three comparisons is a construct chain, 'the bite of a fox', 'the sting of a scorpion', 'the whisper of a saraph', in which the second member names a creature whose attack is feared.

Note: הֵם: the disciples of Rabban Yohanan, each of whom said three things (Rabbeinu Yonah; Bartenura's 'these three things were always on their lips'); the English keeps 'They'. אוּרָן: אוּר 'fire' (with shureq), distinct from אוֹר 'light'; the English 'fire' is the plain sense. שׁוּעָל: 'fox' (Bartenura describes its teeth as thin and crooked, so the bite is hard to heal). לְחִישָׁה: 'whisper, spell'; Bartenura glosses it as דִּבּוּרָן, 'their speech'. שָׂרָף: 'saraph, fiery serpent'. כְּנֶגֶד, rendered 'at', is literally 'opposite'; Rabbeinu Yonah glosses 'near'. The English takes שֶׁלֹּא תִכָּוֶה as 'lest you be burned' and the following שֶׁ clause as the reason.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they spoke about conduct (derekh eretz), moral discipline and character traits, because on what is forbidden and permitted, exempt and liable, they said many things; or else, these three things were always on their lips.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'when will your fellow's honor be as dear as your own? When you are not easily angered, for otherwise you cannot avoid slighting your fellow's honor.' That is one saying; repenting a day before death is the second; warming yourself at the sages' fire is the third.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since no one knows when he will die, he should repent today in case he dies tomorrow.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'be careful of their coals' means do not treat them lightly.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'lest you be burned' means lest you be punished through them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the bite of a fox is hard to heal because its teeth are thin, crooked and twisted, and the physician must cut the flesh with a scalpel and widen the bite.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the sting of a scorpion is more severe than the bite of a snake.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: לְחִישָׁתָן means their speech (דִּבּוּרָן).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the whisper of a saraph is like the breath that comes from the mouth of the saraph, which burns while it whispers. Another explanation: this saraph does not accept a charm, unlike other snakes (Psalm 58:6, 'that will not hear the voice of charmers'); so a disciple of the sages, if you provoke him and then come to appease him, does not accept appeasement.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'do not be easily angered' means do not prepare yourself for anger and irritability; the sages exaggerated in condemning anger, the strongest saying being that whoever is angry is as one who worships an idol.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: a man does not know when he will die, so all his days should be in repentance. He also says that 'warm yourself at the fire of the sages' is not among this sage's own sayings but something he heard from another and reported, so it is not counted among his own words; its meaning is that when you associate with the wise you should draw near only as they draw you near, as one who warms himself at a fire sits at a distance and benefits from its heat, and is burned if he comes too close.

Apparatus:

- 2:10.17 spelling: Vilna reads לכעוס; base לִכְעֹס.
- A stray 'שלשה' appears in the Vilna witness with no counterpart in the base (the base reads שְׁלשָׁה at 2:10.3).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (2:10:9) notes that the copyist thinks a word is missing at 'and all their words'.
- Psalm 58:6 is quoted by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.
- —: Vilna reads שלשה (word)
- לִכְעֹס: Vilna reads לכעוס (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:11

> רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר, עַיִן הָרָע, וְיֵצֶר הָרָע, וְשִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת, מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:

**Rabbi Yehoshua says: The evil eye, the evil impulse, and hatred of people remove a person from the world.**

Grammar:

- The three subjects are joined by 'and' and take the plural participle מוֹצִיאִין (hifil of יצא, with -ין, the Aramaic-style plural of Mishnaic Hebrew): 'they take a person out of the world'.
- עַיִן הָרָע and יֵצֶר הָרָע both have the adjective with the article after a noun without it (the noun is definite by its qualifier); contrast עַיִן רָעָה in 2:9, with no article, 'an evil eye'.
- שִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת is a construct chain: 'the hatred of the creatures'; whether the genitive is subjective (others' hatred) or objective (one's hatred of them) is open, as Bartenura's two readings show.
- מִן הָעוֹלָם: 'from the world' means out of life; Rambam reads it as a death before one's time.

Note: עַיִן הָרָע: Bartenura gives two readings, the same as 'an evil eye' (discontent with one's lot) or malevolent gaze at a friend's money or children that causes harm. The English keeps the ambiguity of 'the evil eye'. שִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת: 'hatred of people' is likewise ambiguous: baseless hatred (Bartenura), loathing human company (Rambam, whom Bartenura reports) or the hatred a harsh man brings on himself (Bartenura's own hearing). יֵצֶר הָרָע: 'the evil impulse'; 'inclination' is equally correct.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'the evil eye' is like 'an evil eye': a man not content with what he has who goes after other things. Some explain it as one who casts an evil eye on his fellow's money or sons and harms him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'hatred of people' is baseless hatred. He reports that Rambam explains it as one who loathes the society of people and loves to sit alone; and he himself has heard it of a harsh man who brings on himself the hatred of people so that all hate him.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: eagerness for money, excess of desire and evil of the soul (a disease of black bile) lead a man to loathe the sight of his fellows, to prefer the company of beasts and to live in deserts and wilds; for them this is not asceticism but the evil of their desire and envy of others, and without doubt such things kill a man before his time.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'the evil eye' means one who is not content with his portion and who looks at his fellow's wealth with an envious eye.

Apparatus:

- No variant readings are recorded between the witnesses for this mishnah.

Grammar:

- The first saying has the same frame as Rabbi Eliezer's in 2:10: יְהִי X חָבִיב עָלֶיךָ כְּשֶׁלָּךְ, with מָמוֹן in place of כָּבוֹד. כְּשֶׁלָּךְ is the preposition כּ with the genitive particle שֶׁל and the suffix: 'like yours'.
- הַתְקֵן is a hifil imperative of תקן, 'make ready, fit'; with עַצְמְךָ it is reflexive, 'prepare yourself'. The infinitive construct לִלְמֹד gives the purpose.
- שֶׁאֵינָהּ יְרֻשָּׁה לָךְ: אֵין with the feminine suffix -ָהּ (referring to תּוֹרָה) is the negative of a nominal clause; שֶׁ introduces the reason.
- וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יִהְיוּ: the plural 3rd person imperfect of הָיָה used as a jussive, 'let all your deeds be'.

Note: מָמוֹן: 'money, property' (Jastrow); the English uses 'money' to keep it apart from נְכָסִים 'property' (2:7). שֶׁאֵינָהּ יְרֻשָּׁה לָךְ: 'it is not an inheritance to you', literally 'it is not an inheritance for you': it does not pass to you from your family (Bartenura, Rabbeinu Yonah). לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם: 'for the sake of Heaven' (decisions.md); שֵׁם is Jastrow שֵׁם II 'name'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'prepare yourself' means that you should not say, since my father and grandfather were wise, the Torah goes back to its lodging and I need not seek it.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even when you are engaged in eating and drinking and worldly occupation, intend not to give your body pleasure but to be healthy so as to do the will of your Maker.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam refers to his earlier discussions, in his eighth chapter on the readiness a person must make to prepare himself for the virtues and in his fifth chapter on the saying that all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: you will not attain it unless you labor in it, because it is not like the inheritance of fathers that the son receives without effort.

Apparatus:

- 2:12.12 spelling: Vilna reads ללמוד; base לִלְמֹד.
- 2:12.15 spelling: Vilna reads ירושה; base יְרֻשָּׁה.
- לִלְמֹד: Vilna reads ללמוד (spelling)
- יְרֻשָּׁה: Vilna reads ירושה (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:13

> רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי זָהִיר בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּבַתְּפִלָּה. וּכְשֶׁאַתָּה מִתְפַּלֵּל, אַל תַּעַשׂ תְּפִלָּתְךָ קֶבַע, אֶלָּא רַחֲמִים וְתַחֲנוּנִים לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (יואל ב) כִּי חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם הוּא אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד וְנִחָם עַל הָרָעָה. וְאַל תְּהִי רָשָׁע בִּפְנֵי עַצְמְךָ:

**Rabbi Shimon says: Be careful in reciting the Shema and in the Prayer. And when you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine, but a plea for mercy and supplication before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Joel 2): “For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in kindness, and relenting of the evil.” And do not be wicked in your own eyes.**

Literal: Rabbi Shimon says be careful in-reading-of Shema and-in-the-prayer. And-when you praying, not make your-prayer fixed-routine, but mercies and-supplications before the-Place blessed He, that-it-was-said (Joel 2) for gracious and-compassionate He, long-of nostrils and-great-of kindness and-relenting upon the-evil. And-not be wicked in-the-face-of yourself.

Grammar:

- הֱוֵי and תְּהִי are both forms of הָיָה: the contracted imperative 'be!' and the jussive-type imperfect after אַל, 'do not be'.
- אַל תַּעַשׂ is a prohibition: אַל with the imperfect. אֶלָּא 'but' sets the right prayer against the wrong one, with the verb 'make' understood.
- קֶבַע is the opposite of תַּחֲנוּנִים: a fixed act versus a plea; רַחֲמִים וְתַחֲנוּנִים are the two things the prayer should be.
- The mishnah quotes Joel 2:13 as it stands there: כִּי חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם הוּא, without אֵל (the Vilna text adds אֵל, as in Jonah 4:2). אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם is a construct chain: אֶרֶךְ is the construct of the adjective אָרֵךְ 'long', 'long of nostrils (anger)', meaning patient.
- חַנּוּן, רַחוּם, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, רַב חֶסֶד and the nifal participle וְנִחָם are a series of attributes of God, all predicates of הוּא.
- בִּפְנֵי עַצְמְךָ, literally 'in the face of your self', is an idiom whose sense is disputed; see the note.

Note: The last clause is ambiguous. Bartenura gives three readings: do not do what will make you condemn yourself; Rambam's 'do not be wicked in your own eyes', that is, do not regard yourself as wicked, or you will turn wholly to evil; and his own, do not separate from the community and stand 'by yourself'. The English follows Rambam, who is the commentator also listed as normative, and keeps the Hebrew idiom 'in your own eyes'. The sense of the pause on 'a plea for mercy' is that prayer is a petition, not a duty to be discharged.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: read the Shema at its proper time, and likewise pray each prayer at its proper time (לִקְרוֹתוֹ בְּעוֹנָתוֹ).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'fixed' is like a man who carries a debt and says 'when shall I be rid of this burden?'; or like one who recites a set portion as a mere reading, not in the language of supplication of one who begs for mercy.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: God wants supplications, and through them He shows mercy at once.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: do not do anything that will today or tomorrow make you condemn yourself. He also cites Rambam (do not hold yourself a wicked man) and his own hearing: do not be wicked by separating from the community and standing by yourself. The English takes Rambam's reading; the others are recorded.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: when a man thinks himself lacking and inferior, he will not make much of any fault he commits; and 'fixed' prayer is prayer that is a burden to him, which he treats like a task he was told to do and be rid of.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not be so wicked in your own eyes that you cannot repent; nor righteous in your own eyes: a man should see himself as half guilty and half innocent.

Apparatus:

- Joel 2:13: כִּי חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם הוּא אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד וְנִחָם עַל הָרָעָה. The base text quotes Joel exactly, without אֵל. Bartenura's lemma (כִּי אֵל חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם הוּא) and the Vilna text read אֵל, as in Jonah 4:2 (כִּי אַתָּה אֵל חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם); Rabbeinu Yonah cites the verse in Jonah's wording, and his copyist notes that by our mishnah's reading the verse is Joel 2:13.
- Vilna reads בקרית for בִּקְרִיאַת (2:13.6); Vilna adds אל in the quotation (כי אל חנון ורחום הוא); Vilna's reference adds the verse number (יואל ב, יג).
- בִּקְרִיאַת: Vilna reads בקרית (word)
- —: Vilna reads יג (word)
- —: Vilna reads אל (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:14

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי שָׁקוּד לִלְמֹד תּוֹרָה, וְדַע מַה שֶּׁתָּשִׁיב לְאֶפִּיקוֹרוֹס. וְדַע לִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָמֵל. וְנֶאֱמָן הוּא בַעַל מְלַאכְתְּךָ שֶׁיְּשַׁלֶּם לָךְ שְׂכַר פְּעֻלָּתֶךְ:

**Rabbi Elazar says: Be diligent in learning Torah, and know what to answer an Epicurean. And know before whom you toil. And faithful is the master of your work to pay you the reward of your labor.**

Literal: Rabbi Elazar says be diligent to-learn Torah, and-know what-that-you-answer to-Epicurean. And-know before whom you toiling. And-faithful he master-of your-work that-he-will-pay to-you reward-of your-labor.

Grammar:

- Three imperatives in a row (הֱוֵי, וְדַע, וְדַע) give the saying its three parts; the second and third are in the same form, 'know!'.
- מַה שֶּׁתָּשִׁיב is 'what you should answer': מַה plus the relative שֶׁ and the imperfect used as a duty.
- לִפְנֵי מִי is 'before whom', with מִי as an interrogative inside the object clause.
- בַּעַל מְלַאכְתְּךָ is a construct chain 'master of your work'; the word בַּעַל is the owner, and the image is of an employer who pays a worker.
- The last clause begins with וְנֶאֱמָן הוּא, a predicate placed first for emphasis.

Note: אֶפִּיקוֹרוֹס is kept as 'Epicurean' with its sense a scoffer at the Torah: Bartenura derives it from הֶפְקֵר, 'ownerless, license', as one who treats the Torah as ownerless. Rambam understands it of idolaters, Rabbeinu Yonah of one who denies the oral Torah; the translation does not narrow it. The English wording of the last sentence follows the Hebrew order; the שֶׁ clause is read as 'to pay'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: אֶפִּיקוֹרוֹס is a word of hefker: one who scorns the Torah and treats it as ownerless; or one who treats himself as ownerless and does not care for his soul. The English keeps 'Epicurean' with the sense of a scorner.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: know before whom you toil, in this answer you give the Epicurean, so that your heart is not tempted to incline to his view.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: שְׁקִידָה comes from 'for I am watchful (שֹׁקֵד) over My word', meaning quick and eager; or it means habit and constancy, as in 'to watch (לִשְׁקֹד) at my doors daily'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: you must learn what to answer the Epicureans among the idolaters and refute them; with an Israelite Epicurean one does not speak at all, for argument only makes him scorn more and he has no remedy. And though you learn the nations' opinions, guard that none of them rises in your heart, and know that He before whom you labor knows the secret of your heart.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: God is the master of your work, so do not do the work of Torah deceitfully; and He pays reward faithfully.

Apparatus:

- The saying has no direct biblical quotation. Rambam's proof texts on the sense of שְׁקִידָה are Jer 1:12 (כִּי שֹׁקֵד אֲנִי עַל דְּבָרִי) and Prov 8:34 (לִשְׁקֹד עַל דַּלְתֹתַי יוֹם יוֹם).
- Vilna reads ללמוד for לִלְמֹד (2:14.6) and פעולתך for פְּעֻלָּתֶךְ (2:14.24).
- Rabbeinu Yonah's lemmas read מה שתשיב את אפקורוס (for לְאֶפִּיקוֹרוֹס) and ומי הוא בעל מלאכתך (for וְנֶאֱמָן הוּא בַעַל מְלַאכְתְּךָ): 'and who is the master of your work, who will pay you'.
- לִלְמֹד: Vilna reads ללמוד (spelling)
- פְּעֻלָּתֶךְ: Vilna reads פעולתך (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 2:15

> רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן אוֹמֵר, הַיּוֹם קָצָר וְהַמְּלָאכָה מְרֻבָּה, וְהַפּוֹעֲלִים עֲצֵלִים, וְהַשָּׂכָר הַרְבֵּה, וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת דּוֹחֵק:

**Rabbi Tarfon says: The day is short, the work is great, the laborers are lazy, the reward is abundant, and the master of the house is pressing.**

Literal: Rabbi Tarfon says the-day short, and-the-work abundant, and-the-laborers lazy, and-the-reward much, and-master-of the-house pressing.

Grammar:

- The saying is five short nominal clauses with no verb 'to be': subject then predicate, each joined by וְ.
- הַרְבֵּה is a hifil infinitive absolute that works as an adverb or predicate, 'much'; here it stands for the amount of the reward.
- מְרֻבָּה is a pual participle, feminine to agree with מְלָאכָה.
- בַּעַל הַבַּיִת is 'master of the house', a householder who hires workers; as a metaphor it stands for God.

Note: The saying is a parable (so Rambam). The day is a man's short life (Bartenura), the work is the Torah, which is long, and the master of the house is God, who presses the worker. The English keeps the parable's images and does not spell out the interpretation.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the life of this world is short.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the work is the Torah, which is 'longer than the earth in measure' (Job 11:9).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the master of the house presses, as it is said (Joshua 1) 'and you shall meditate on it day and night'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: this is a parable for the shortness of years, the abundance of wisdom, men's laziness in seeking it, the great reward, and the many warnings of the Torah to seek wisdom and learning.

Apparatus:

- Job 11:9 (Torah longer than the earth in measure, as cited by Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah); Joshua 1:8 (וְהָגִיתָ בּוֹ יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה).
- Vilna reads מרובה for מְרֻבָּה (2:15.7).
- מְרֻבָּה: Vilna reads מרובה (spelling)

And-faithful he master-of your-work that-he-pays to-you reward-of your-labor. And-know giving-of their-reward of righteous for-the-future to-come.

- לֹא עָלֶיךָ ... לִגְמֹר: 'not upon you to finish'; the infinitive construct with ל gives the duty or burden. The second clause has the same negative with 'free'.
- בֶן חוֹרִין is an idiom: 'free man'; לִבָּטֵל is the nifal infinitive, 'to be idle, to be exempt'.
- נוֹתְנִים is a participle plural with no subject, an impersonal 'they give'.
- לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא, literally 'for the future that comes', is the mishnaic term for the world to come.

Note: לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא is translated 'in the world to come', since Bartenura and Rambam both say it means לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא; the literal sense is 'for the time that is to come'. נוֹתְנִים 'they give' is an impersonal plural: 'one gives you', that is, you are given. The last clause is a nominal clause, the object of וְדַע, with לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא as its predicate: 'that the giving of their reward, of the righteous, is in the time to come'; the English supplies 'that' and 'is'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the Holy One, blessed be He, did not hire you (שְׂכָרְךָ) to finish all of it, so that you would lose your wages if you did not finish it. And lest you say 'I will not learn and will take no wages', it says 'you are not free to be idle': against your will the yoke is laid on you to work.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא means 'to the world to come' (לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא).
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: it means the world to come, and he has already explained the matter in the tenth chapter of Sanhedrin (the Helek).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not think 'I am not broad of heart and cannot finish it, so what is the gain of my toil?'; since you toil in Torah you have fulfilled your Creator's commandment.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not say that since you need not finish, you will learn only an hour a day; you are a slave bought for it, to meditate on it day and night.

Apparatus:

- Joshua 1:8 is cited by Rabbeinu Yonah on 'not free to desist' (וְהָגִיתָ בּוֹ יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה).
- Vilna reads לגמור for לִגְמֹר, ליבטל for לִבָּטֵל, and פעולתך for פְּעֻלָּתֶךָ.
- לִגְמֹר: Vilna reads לגמור (spelling)
- לִבָּטֵל: Vilna reads ליבטל (spelling)
- פְּעֻלָּתֶךָ: Vilna reads פעולתך (spelling)

## Chapter 3 — פֶּרֶק ג (Pirkei Avot 3:1–3:18)

### Reading text

<sup>3:1</sup> Akavya son of Mahalalel says: Consider three things and you will not come to the point of transgression. Know where you came from, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning. Where you came from: from a putrid drop. And where you are going: to a place of dust, maggot and worm. And before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning: before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

<sup>3:2</sup> Rabbi Hanina, the deputy of the priests, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear of it, each man would have swallowed his fellow alive. Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion says: Two who sit with no words of Torah between them, this is a seat of scoffers, as it is said (Psalm 1): "and in the seat of scoffers he has not sat." But two who sit with words of Torah between them, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the LORD and for those who esteem his name." I know this only of two. From where do we learn that even for one who sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets a reward for him? As it is said (Lamentations 3): "He sits alone and murmurs, for he has taken it upon himself."

<sup>3:3</sup> Rabbi Shimon says: Three who ate at one table and did not say words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate of sacrifices to the dead, as it is said (Isaiah 28): "For all the tables are full of vomit and filth, with no place." But three who ate at one table and said words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Ezekiel 41): "And he spoke to me: This is the table that is before the LORD."

<sup>3:4</sup> Rabbi Hanina son of Hakhinai says: One who is awake at night, or who walks on the road alone, and who turns his heart to idleness: this one is answerable with his life.

<sup>3:5</sup> Rabbi Nehunya son of Hakanah says: Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation. And whoever throws off from himself the yoke of Torah, they place upon him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation.

<sup>3:6</sup> Rabbi Halafta son of Dosa, of Kefar Hananiah, says: Ten who sit and occupy themselves with Torah, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Psalm 82): "God stands in the congregation of God." And from where even five? As it is said (Amos 9): "and his bundle upon the earth he has founded." And from where even three? As it is said (Psalm 82): "In the midst of judges he judges." And from where even two? As it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and so on." And from where even one? As it is said (Exodus 20): "In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you."

<sup>3:7</sup> Rabbi Elazar of Bartota says: Give Him what is His, for you and what is yours are His. And so David says: “For everything comes from You, and from Your hand we have given to You.” Rabbi Shimon says: One who walks on the road and reviews his learning, and interrupts his learning and says, “How fine is this tree, and how fine is this furrow!”, Scripture accounts it to him as if he were forfeiting his life.

<sup>3:8</sup> Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yannai, in the name of Rabbi Meir, says: Whoever forgets a single thing from his learning, Scripture accounts it to him as if he were forfeiting his life, as it is said: “Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes saw.” One might think this holds even if his learning was too hard for him; the teaching says: “and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.” Thus he is not forfeiting his life until he sits and removes them from his heart.

<sup>3:9</sup> Rabbi Hanina son of Dosa says: Anyone whose fear of sin comes before his wisdom, his wisdom endures. But anyone whose wisdom comes before his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure. He used to say: Anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom endures. But anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom does not endure.

<sup>3:10</sup> He used to say: Anyone with whom the spirit of people is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. And anyone with whom the spirit of people is not pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him. Rabbi Dosa son of Harkinas says: Morning sleep, midday wine, the chatter of children, and sitting in the synagogues of the unlearned remove a person from the world.

<sup>3:11</sup> Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in says: One who profanes the sacred things, and one who despises the festivals, and one who shames his fellow in public, and one who breaks the covenant of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, and one who brazenly flouts the Torah, contrary to the halakha: even though he has Torah and good deeds, he has no share in the world to come.

<sup>3:12</sup> Rabbi Yishmael says: Be yielding to a superior, and composed with the young, and receive every person with joy.

<sup>3:13</sup> Rabbi Akiva says: Laughter and levity accustom a person to lewdness. The Masoretic tradition is a fence for the Torah; tithes are a fence for wealth; vows are a fence for abstinence; a fence for wisdom is silence.

<sup>3:14</sup> He used to say: Beloved is a human being, for he was created in the image. Extra love was made known to him, that he was created in the image, as it is said (Genesis 9): 'For in the image of God He made the human being.' Beloved are Israel, for they were called children of the Omnipresent. Extra love was made known to them, that they were called children of the Omnipresent, as it is said (Deuteronomy 14): 'You are children of the LORD your God.' Beloved are Israel, for a desirable vessel was given to them. Extra love was made known to them, that a desirable vessel was given to them, by which the world was created, as it is said (Proverbs 4): 'For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake my Torah.'

<sup>3:15</sup> Everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given; the world is judged with goodness, and all is according to the abundance of deeds.

<sup>3:16</sup> He used to say: Everything is given as a pledge, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, the shopkeeper extends credit, the ledger is open, and the hand writes; and whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow. The collectors make their rounds constantly, every day, and exact payment from a person with his knowledge and without his knowledge. They have what to rely on, and the judgment is a judgment of truth. And everything is prepared for the banquet.

<sup>3:17</sup> Rabbi Elazar son of Azariah says: If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He used to say: Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are many and whose roots are few; and the wind comes and uproots it and overturns it on its face, as it is said (Jeremiah 17): 'He shall be like a bare shrub in the desert plain, and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, a salt land, uninhabited.' But anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are few and whose roots are many, so that even if all the winds in the world come and blow against it, they do not move it from its place, as it is said (ibid.): 'He shall be like a tree planted by water, and by a stream it sends out its roots, and it shall not see when heat comes; its leaf shall be fresh, and in a year of drought it shall not worry, and it shall not cease from yielding fruit.'

<sup>3:18</sup> Rabbi Eliezer son of Hisma says: Bird offerings and the openings of the menstruant, these very things are the essentials of the laws. Astronomical cycles and gematria are the desserts of wisdom.

### Chapter 3 by mishnah

#### Pirkei Avot 3:1

> עֲקַבְיָא בֶן מַהֲלַלְאֵל אוֹמֵר, הִסְתַּכֵּל בִּשְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאִי אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵרָה. דַּע מֵאַיִן בָּאתָ, וּלְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ, וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִתֵּן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן. מֵאַיִן בָּאתָ, מִטִּפָּה סְרוּחָה, וּלְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ, לִמְקוֹם עָפָר רִמָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה. וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִתֵּן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן, לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:

**Akavya son of Mahalalel says: Consider three things and you will not come to the point of transgression. Know where you came from, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning. Where you came from: from a putrid drop. And where you are going: to a place of dust, maggot and worm. And before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning: before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.**

Grammar:

- The saying has the form of a question and an answer: one imperative, דַּע 'know', governs three questions, and each is then answered in turn.
- אִי אַתָּה בָא is the Mishnaic negative with a participle (a future: 'you will not come'); אִי stands for אֵין.
- עָתִיד is an adjective (the pattern qatil), 'ready, destined', and takes the infinitive לִתֵּן: 'you are destined to give'.
- מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים is a double superlative ('King of the kings of kings'): the construct chain piles up the title.
- מֵאַיִן, וּלְאָן and וְלִפְנֵי מִי are three interrogative phrases, each repeated in the answer; the third answer reuses the whole question.

Note: דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן is rendered 'account and reckoning' (literally 'judgment and account'): the pair is a fixed idiom for a full accounting, and Bartenura reads the third item as the judgment before the King. Bartenura (3:1:1) reads the three items as three remedies: the putrid drop against pride, dust and worm against desire for wealth, the account against sin. The adjective סְרוּחָה is 'putrid'; Bartenura explains that the drop is called putrid because it is about to spoil once outside the womb.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says the drop is 'putrid' because it is about to rot once outside the womb, and that the one who looks at his origin is saved from pride, the one who looks at the place of dust, maggot and worm is saved from desire for wealth, and the one who looks at the coming account is saved from sin. The English follows his sense of the three items.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads עבירה for עֲבֵרָה, and ליתן for לִתֵּן (twice): spellings only.
- Rabbeinu Yonah on 3:1 links the first consideration (whence you came) to lowliness of spirit, which saves from pride (Proverbs 16:5, cited there as 16:4), the second (dust and worm) to contempt for pleasures and wealth, as in Ecclesiastes, and the third to the shame of the soul before the King of kings.
- עֲבֵרָה: Vilna reads עבירה (spelling)
- לִתֵּן: Vilna reads ליתן (spelling)
- לִתֵּן: Vilna reads ליתן (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:2

> רַבִּי חֲנִינָא סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי מִתְפַּלֵּל בִּשְׁלוֹמָהּ שֶׁל מַלְכוּת, שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא מוֹרָאָהּ, אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ חַיִּים בְּלָעוֹ. רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶן תְּרַדְיוֹן אוֹמֵר, שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, הֲרֵי זֶה מוֹשַׁב לֵצִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים א) וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵצִים לֹא יָשָׁב. אֲבָל שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְיֵשׁ בֵּינֵיהֶם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שְׁכִינָה שְׁרוּיָה בֵינֵיהֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מלאכי ג) אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב יְיָ וַיִּשְׁמָע וַיִּכָּתֵב סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנָיו לְיִרְאֵי יְיָ וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ. אֵין לִי אֶלָּא שְׁנַיִם, מִנַּיִן שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קוֹבֵעַ לוֹ שָׂכָר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איכה ג) יֵשֵׁב בָּדָד וְיִדֹּם כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו:

**Rabbi Hanina, the deputy of the priests, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear of it, each man would have swallowed his fellow alive. Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion says: Two who sit with no words of Torah between them, this is a seat of scoffers, as it is said (Psalm 1): "and in the seat of scoffers he has not sat." But two who sit with words of Torah between them, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the LORD and for those who esteem his name." I know this only of two. From where do we learn that even for one who sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets a reward for him? As it is said (Lamentations 3): "He sits alone and murmurs, for he has taken it upon himself."**

Literal: Rabbi Hanina deputy-of the-priests says be praying in-welfare-of-it of kingdom that-were-it-not fear-of-it man ACC his-fellow alive swallowed-him Rabbi Hanina son-of Teradion says two who-sit and-there-is-not between-them words-of Torah behold this seat-of scoffers that-it-is-said Psalms 1 and-in-seat-of scoffers not he-sat but two who-sit and-there-is between-them words-of Torah Shekhinah dwelling between-them that-it-is-said Malachi 3 then spoke fearers-of YHWH man to his-fellow and-listened YHWH and-heard and-was-written book-of remembrance before-him for-fearers-of YHWH and-for-esteemers-of his-name there-is-not to-me except two from-where that-even one who-sits and-occupies in-the-Torah that-the-Holy-One blessed he fixes for-him reward that-it-is-said Lamentations 3 he-sits alone and-is-silent for he-took upon-him

Grammar:

- The verse has three sayings: Rabbi Hanina the deputy on prayer for the government, Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion on Torah study in company, and its extension to one who studies alone.
- שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא introduces a contrafactual clause; the apodosis is the perfect בְּלָעוֹ (בָּלַע with the suffix -וֹ, resuming רֵעֵהוּ): 'would have swallowed him'.
- שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן ... is a casus pendens: 'Two who sit and there is not between them ... this is ...'; הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause.
- וְיֵשׁ and וְאֵין are the existential particles ('there is' and 'there is not') followed by a subject in the construct: 'words of Torah'.
- מִנַּיִן is the standard Talmudic question, 'from where (do we learn)'; the answers are verses, quoted by their source.

Note: סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים is 'the deputy of the priests'; the English keeps the title. מַלְכוּת is 'the government' (the sages read the ruling power, including foreign rule: Bartenura 3:2:1). The sentence 'each man would have swallowed his fellow alive' (Bartenura 3:2:2 cites Habakkuk 1:14, 'like the fish of the sea') is a contrafactual. The last verse, נָטַל עָלָיו, is read in the Mishnah as 'he has taken it upon himself': Bartenura 3:2:5 reads 'as though the whole giving of the Torah were for him alone'; וְיִדֹּם is rendered 'murmurs': Bartenura (3:2:4) and Rambam (3:2:2) read it as the soft voice of one who studies in a whisper; Rabbeinu Yonah reads silent study in thought. In Lamentations 3:28 the verse is more likely 'Let him sit alone and be silent, for he has laid it upon him' (God has laid it on him).

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says the 'government' here includes even the governments of the nations of the world; the English follows with the general word 'the government'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura cites Habakkuk 1:14 ('and you make man like the fish of the sea'): as among fish the greater swallows the lesser, so would men without the fear of government (Avodah Zarah 4a). The English follows this reading of 'swallow'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says, 'Behold here are two': the verse, 'each man to his fellow', shows two speakers. The English follows this proof.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: וְיִדֹּם is 'a term of a still, thin voice' (קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַּקָּה), the way one who studies alone studies in a whisper. The English follows with 'murmurs'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura reads כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו as 'as if the giving of the whole Torah had been for him alone'; the English follows with 'he has taken it upon himself'.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam (anchored here by the pack, but commenting on 3:1) says that looking at whence one came brings humility, looking at one's end brings contempt for worldly affairs, and looking to the greatness of the One who commands (הַמְצַוֶּה) brings haste to obey His commandments; one who holds these three will not sin at all. This bears on 3:1, not on the plain sense of 3:2.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam says that 'seat of scoffers' means any seat in which words of Torah are not spoken, as the end of Psalm 1:1-2 shows: because his delight was in the Torah of the LORD he did not sit in a seat of scoffers where there is no Torah. The English follows this reading.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam quotes the Talmud (Berakhot 6a): one who sits and studies has the Shekhinah with him (Exodus 20:21); two have their words written in the Book of Remembrance; and he explains וְיִדֹּם as 'quiet speech, the soft voice' (Aramaic שתיק), and כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו as 'as if the giving of the whole Torah had been for him alone'. The English follows him.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: the one who is silent and meditates in Torah is as if he took upon himself the yoke of Torah in thought; he cites the Rama's reading, that one who studies alone is as if he fulfilled the whole Torah, with וְיִדֹּם as speech.

Apparatus:

- Psalm 1:1 (the last clause, וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵצִים לֹא יָשָׁב).
- Malachi 3:16 (אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ ...): the Mishnah quotes the verse to its end; the proof is in אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ, two speakers.
- Lamentations 3:28 (יֵשֵׁב בָּדָד וְיִדֹּם כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו).
- Vilna reads ה for יְיָ (three times), ולחושבי for וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי, שאפילו for שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ, וידום for וְיִדֹּם; Vilna omits שְׁרוּיָה ('dwells') at 3:2.48.
- 3:2.34 תהלים, 3:2.51 מלאכי and 3:2.88 איכה are the source names of the quoted verses; 3:2.35, 3:2.52 and 3:2.89 are letter numerals for the chapters.
- Vilna adds the verse number after each source: (תהלים א) א, (מלאכי ג) טז, (איכה ג) כח.
- —: Vilna reads א (word)
- שְׁרוּיָה: Vilna reads — (word)
- —: Vilna reads טז (word)
- יְיָ: Vilna reads ה (word)
- יְיָ: Vilna reads ה (word)
- יְיָ: Vilna reads ה (word)
- וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי: Vilna reads ולחושבי (spelling)
- שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ: Vilna reads שאפילו (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads כח (word)
- וְיִדֹּם: Vilna reads וידום (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:3

> רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, שְׁלשָׁה שֶׁאָכְלוּ עַל שֻׁלְחָן אֶחָד וְלֹא אָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּאִלּוּ אָכְלוּ מִזִּבְחֵי מֵתִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (ישעיה כח) כִּי כָּל שֻׁלְחָנוֹת מָלְאוּ קִיא צֹאָה בְּלִי מָקוֹם. אֲבָל שְׁלשָׁה שֶׁאָכְלוּ עַל שֻׁלְחָן אֶחָד וְאָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּאִלּוּ אָכְלוּ מִשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (יחזקאל מא) וַיְדַבֵּר אֵלַי זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי ה':

**Rabbi Shimon says: Three who ate at one table and did not say words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate of sacrifices to the dead, as it is said (Isaiah 28): "For all the tables are full of vomit and filth, with no place." But three who ate at one table and said words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Ezekiel 41): "And he spoke to me: This is the table that is before the LORD."**

Grammar:

- The saying sets two sentences in opposition: three who ate and did not speak words of Torah, and three who ate and did (אֲבָל, 'but'); both have the form 'three who ... as if they ate ...'.
- שֶׁאָכְלוּ is a relative clause with a perfect: 'who ate'; the sentence is a casus pendens with כְּאִלּוּ opening the main clause.
- מִשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם uses the Mishnaic double genitive: 'from his table, of the Place'.
- מָקוֹם is a name of God, 'the Place' (the Omnipresent), here without the article; בְּלִי מָקוֹם in Isaiah can be read 'with no place', and the sages read it as 'without the Place'.
- The two scripture proofs are quoted with their sources (Isaiah 28:8, Ezekiel 41:22), the second ending with 'the table that is before the LORD'.

Note: מָקוֹם בָּרוּךְ הוּא is translated 'the Omnipresent, blessed be He' by the project's decision; the literal sense of מָקוֹם is 'the Place'. מִזִּבְחֵי מֵתִים is 'sacrifices to the dead', the sacrifices of idols (Bartenura and Rambam; Psalm 106:28). In Isaiah 28:8 בְּלִי מָקוֹם means 'with no room'; Bartenura reads it as 'without the Place', for they did not mention the name of the Place at the table, so the English 'with no place' keeps both readings.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (records): Bartenura adds a legal note, 'I heard': saying the grace after meals at the table counts as saying words of Torah over it. The English keeps 'words of Torah' and records his sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says 'sacrifices to the dead' are offerings to idols, as in Psalm 106:28 ('and they were joined to Baal-peor and ate sacrifices to the dead'). The English follows.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says idolatry is called צֹאָה 'filth', as in Isaiah 30:22: 'You shall say to it, Get out (צֵא)'. The English keeps 'filth' and follows.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura reads בְּלִי מָקוֹם as 'because they did not mention the name of the Place, blessed be He, at the table'. The English 'with no place' keeps the plain sense and records this reading here.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: as soon as one speaks words of Torah, the table is called 'the table that is before the LORD'. Some say the proof is from the head of the verse, 'the altar of wood, three cubits (אַמּוֹת)': read not אַמּוֹת but אִמּוֹת, 'mothers' (sources), three, for Torah, Prophets and Writings (or Scripture, Mishnah and Talmud), which a man must speak of at the table; so Rashi explained. The English follows the first reading.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam says 'sacrifices to the dead' is the offering of idol worship, as Scripture calls it, and Isaiah calls it 'vomit and filth' to scorn it. The English follows.

Apparatus:

- Isaiah 28:8 (כִּי כָּל שֻׁלְחָנוֹת מָלְאוּ קִיא צֹאָה בְּלִי מָקוֹם).
- Ezekiel 41:22 (the last words: זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי יְיָ); the Mishnah's text of Ezekiel runs וַיְדַבֵּר אֵלַי.
- Vilna reads כאילו for כְּאִלּוּ (twice) and צואה for צֹאָה.
- 3:3.19 ישעיה and 3:3.47 יחזקאל are the source names; 3:3.20 כח and 3:3.48 מא are letter numerals (28 and 41), and the pack's lemma links for them (כֹּחַ, מָא) are not the sense here.
- Vilna adds the verse number after each source: (ישעיה כח) ח, (יחזקאל מא) כב.
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads ח (word)
- צֹאָה: Vilna reads צואה (spelling)
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads כב (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:4

> רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶן חֲכִינַאי אוֹמֵר, הַנֵּעוֹר בַּלַּיְלָה וְהַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ יְחִידִי וְהַמְפַנֶּה לִבּוֹ לְבַטָּלָה, הֲרֵי זֶה מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:

**Rabbi Hanina son of Hakhinai says: One who is awake at night, or who walks on the road alone, and who turns his heart to idleness: this one is answerable with his life.**

Literal: Rabbi Hanina son-of Hakhinai says the-one-awake at-night and-the-one-walking on-the-road alone and-the-one-turning his-heart to-idleness behold this incurring-liability with-his-life

Grammar:

- Three participles with the article (הַנֵּעוֹר, הַמְהַלֵּךְ, הַמְפַנֶּה) head the sentence; Bartenura reads the third as the condition of the first two: one who is awake at night or walks alone, and turns his heart to idle things.
- הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause ('this one ...'), resuming the subject.
- הַנֵּעוֹר is a Nifal participle of עור, 'is awake'; מְהַלֵּךְ and מְפַנֶּה are Piel participles. The Piel of פנה is 'to clear, make room': he frees his heart for idleness.
- מִתְחַיֵּב is a Hitpael participle: 'makes himself liable'. The Vilna spelling is מתחייב.
- בְּנַפְשׁוֹ 'with his life': he puts his own life at risk (Bartenura: demons by night, robbers on the road).
- יְחִידִי, 'alone, by himself', is the Mishnaic adverbial form of יָחִיד.

Note: מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ is rendered 'is answerable with his life'. The English follows Bartenura: the night (3:4:1-2) is the time of demons and the lone traveller is in danger from robbers and other harm, and the one in either case who turns his heart to idle thoughts is guilty, for words of Torah would have guarded him. Read grammatically as three separate subjects, each participle with its own article, the saying would make the waking and the journey liable by themselves; the commentators do not read it so.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the one awake at night and the one walking alone on the road are guilty when he thinks idle things in his heart (וּמְחַשֵּׁב בְּלִבּוֹ דִּבְרֵי הֲבַאי): the third clause is the condition of the first two. The English follows.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: night is the time of demons, and one who walks alone on the road is in danger from robbers and many evils; had he thought of words of Torah, it would have guarded him. Hence he is liable with his life only when his heart is turned to idleness. The English follows.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads מתחייב for מִתְחַיֵּב: spelling only.
- מִתְחַיֵּב: Vilna reads מתחייב (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:5

> רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה אוֹמֵר, כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עֹל תּוֹרָה, מַעֲבִירִין מִמֶּנּוּ עֹל מַלְכוּת וְעֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ. וְכָל הַפּוֹרֵק מִמֶּנּוּ עֹל תּוֹרָה, נוֹתְנִין עָלָיו עֹל מַלְכוּת וְעֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ:

**Rabbi Nehunya son of Hakanah says: Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation. And whoever throws off from himself the yoke of Torah, they place upon him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation.**

Grammar:

- The saying is two parallel conditional sentences: כָּל + participle, then a plural participle (מַעֲבִירִין, נוֹתְנִין) as an impersonal passive.
- The two sentences are antithetic and in the same order: the one who takes the yoke of Torah has the other yokes removed (מַעֲבִירִין), the one who throws it off has them placed on him (נוֹתְנִין).
- הַמְקַבֵּל and הַפּוֹרֵק are articular participles used as the subject after כָּל, 'whoever takes / whoever throws off'; קִבֵּל עָלָיו and פָּרַק מִמֶּנּוּ are the opposite idioms for a yoke.
- עֹל תּוֹרָה is a construct chain 'the yoke of Torah'; the same pattern, עֹל מַלְכוּת, עֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, follows.
- דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ ('the way of the land') is an idiom for the ordinary business of life, and in Avot often for the worldly occupation of earning a living.

Note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ is rendered 'worldly occupation' by the project's decision, following Bartenura (3:5:2: the toil and labour of earning a living); Rambam (3:5:3) reads 'the toil of the times'. מַלְכוּת is 'the government': Bartenura says the burden of the king and officials, Rambam the toil of the king and his armies. The Vilna spelling is עול for עֹל. The pack's lemma link for עֹל (עַל) is a different word; the sense is 'yoke'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura glosses עֹל מַלְכוּת as the burden of the king and the officers. The English follows with 'the yoke of the government'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura glosses דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ as the toil and labour of earning a living, since the work of the one who studies is blessed. The English follows with 'worldly occupation'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says 'throws off the yoke of Torah' means one who says, 'The yoke of Torah is hard and I cannot bear it'. The English follows with 'throws off'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam glosses עֹל תּוֹרָה as persistence in reading (הַתְמָדַת הַקְּרִיאָה). The English keeps 'the yoke of Torah' and follows him.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam glosses עֹל מַלְכוּת as the toil of the king and his troops. The English follows with 'the yoke of the government'.
- Rambam (records): Rambam glosses עֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ as 'the toil of the time (zeman)': in reward for taking the yoke of Torah, God spares him the toil of the age. The English follows Bartenura's 'worldly occupation' instead and records this.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads עול for עֹל (four times) and ועול for וְעֹל (twice): spelling only.
- עֹל: Vilna reads עול (spelling)
- עֹל: Vilna reads עול (spelling)
- וְעֹל: Vilna reads ועול (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:6

> רַבִּי חֲלַפְתָּא בֶן דּוֹסָא אִישׁ כְּפַר חֲנַנְיָה אוֹמֵר, עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְעוֹסְקִין בַּתּוֹרָה, שְׁכִינָה שְׁרוּיָה בֵינֵיהֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים פב) אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל. וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ חֲמִשָּׁה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (עמוס ט) וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ. וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ שְׁלשָׁה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים פב) בְּקֶרֶב אֱלֹהִים יִשְׁפֹּט. וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ שְׁנַיִם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מלאכי ג) אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי ה' אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב ה' וַיִּשְׁמָע וְגוֹ'. וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ אֶחָד, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמות כ) בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ:

**Rabbi Halafta son of Dosa, of Kefar Hananiah, says: Ten who sit and occupy themselves with Torah, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Psalm 82): "God stands in the congregation of God." And from where even five? As it is said (Amos 9): "and his bundle upon the earth he has founded." And from where even three? As it is said (Psalm 82): "In the midst of judges he judges." And from where even two? As it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and so on." And from where even one? As it is said (Exodus 20): "In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you."**

Literal: Rabbi Halafta son-of Dosa man-of village-of Hananiah says ten who-sit and-occupy in-the-Torah Shekhinah dwelling between-them that-it-is-said Psalms 82 God standing in-congregation-of God and-from-where even five that-it-is-said Amos 9 and-his-bundle upon earth he-founded-it and-from-where even three that-it-is-said Psalms 82 in-midst-of judges he-judges and-from-where even two that-it-is-said Malachi 3 then spoke fearers-of the-LORD man to his-fellow and-listened the-LORD and-heard and-so-on and-from-where even one that-it-is-said Exodus 20 in-every the-place which I-cause-to-be-remembered ACC my-name I-will-come to-you and-I-will-bless-you

Grammar:

- The verse is a descending ladder: ten, five, three, two, one, each given a scripture proof introduced by וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ 'and from where even'.
- The first sentence has the same casus pendens as 3:2: 'Ten who sit ... the Shekhinah dwells among them'.
- שְׁכִינָה שְׁרוּיָה בֵּינֵיהֶם: a feminine noun with a passive participle of שרה, 'dwelling', with the suffix בֵּינֵיהֶם 'among them'.
- The proof texts are cut off at the point of the proof: the quotation from Malachi ends with וְגוֹ' ('and so on'), and Exodus 20:21 is quoted from בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם.
- אֲגֻדָּה ('bundle') is read as a hand with five fingers (Rambam, Rabbeinu Yonah) or as a bundle of three elements or three stalks of hyssop (Bartenura); the verse is a wordplay on the number in the proof.

Note: The proof of the five rests on אֲגֻדָּתוֹ, 'his bundle': Rambam and Rabbeinu Yonah read a bundle as what one binds in one hand, which has five fingers. Bartenura's own text reverses the two middle proofs: five from 'in the midst of judges he judges' (three judges and two litigants) and three from 'his bundle' (fire, air and water around the earth, or three stalks of hyssop); he gives the order of this text as the reading of 'some books', with the hand of five fingers. The English keeps 'his bundle'. In the first proof the congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten (Rambam; Bartenura from the spies, Numbers 14:27). In the third, אֱלֹהִים is 'judges' (a court of three: Rambam, Bartenura), and the English follows them. 'Kefar Hananiah' is a place, as in the pack. The pack's lemma link for אֵל (the particle אַל) does not fit; the word is אֵל 'God', in 'the congregation of God'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (records): Bartenura says 'we read: ten who sat in judgment' (עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים בַּדִּין). The English follows the printed text (Torah study) and records his reading.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura says a congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten, as in Numbers 14:27, where the ten spies minus Joshua and Caleb are 'this evil congregation'. The English follows.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura (his heading reads 'and from where even five' with this verse): 'in the midst of judges he judges' gives three judges and two litigants, five. The English follows the base text, which proves three from this verse, as Bartenura himself explains in the reading of 'some books' (3:6:4); his own order is recorded here.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura's text reads 'even three' with 'his bundle': fire, air and water, three, surround the foundation of the earth; or a bundle of hyssop of three stalks. He adds that some books read 'even five' with this verse, for a man binds with one hand of five fingers, and the whole of the fingers is called a bundle; the head of the verse, 'who builds His upper chambers in the heavens', means that the Shekhinah descends when a bundle studies Torah; and then 'even three' from 'in the midst of judges', for judges are three. The English follows the 'some books' reading, which is the base text.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: נָטַל עָלָיו is a term of covering (לְשׁוֹן סְכָךְ), as the Targum renders וְסַכֹּתָ 'and you shall cover' by וְתַטֵּל: the Shekhinah covers him. The comment belongs to the verse of 3:2 (Lamentations 3:28), not to the plain sense of 3:6.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: a congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten, and a court not fewer than three, who are called אֱלֹהִים for judgment; an אֲגֻדָּה is what a man binds with one hand, which has five fingers, so the five fingers are called a bundle. The English follows all three points: 'congregation', 'judges' and 'his bundle'.

Apparatus:

- Psalm 82:1 (אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל).
- Amos 9:6 (וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ).
- Psalm 82:1 (בְּקֶרֶב אֱלֹהִים יִשְׁפֹּט).
- Malachi 3:16 (אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב יְיָ וַיִּשְׁמָע ...).
- Exodus 20:21 (בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ).
- Vilna omits בֶן דּוֹסָא (3:6.3-4) and תהלים פב (3:6.37-38); reads אפילו for אֲפִלּוּ, ואגודתו for וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ, ישפוט for יִשְׁפֹּט and וגומר for וְגוֹ'.
- Vilna adds the verse number after the sources: (תהלים פב) א, (עמוס ט) ו, (מלאכי ג) טז, (שמות כ) כ.
