#### Pirkei Avot 3:7

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אִישׁ בַּרְתּוֹתָא אוֹמֵר, תֶּן לוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאַתָּה וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלּוֹ. וְכֵן בְּדָוִד הוּא אוֹמֵר (דברי הימים א כט) כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, הַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְשׁוֹנֶה, וּמַפְסִיק מִמִּשְׁנָתוֹ וְאוֹמֵר, מַה נָּאֶה אִילָן זֶה וּמַה נָּאֶה נִיר זֶה, מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:

**Rabbi Elazar of Bartota says: Give Him what is His, for you and what is yours are His. And so David says: “For everything comes from You, and from Your hand we have given to You.” Rabbi Shimon says: One who walks on the road and reviews his learning, and interrupts his learning and says, “How fine is this tree, and how fine is this furrow!”, Scripture accounts it to him as if he were forfeiting his life.**

Literal: my-master Elazar man-of Bartota saying give to-him from-his-own that-you and-yours his. and-so in-David he saying (Chronicles I 29) for from-you the-all and-from-your-hand we-gave to-you. my-master Shimon saying the-walker on-the-road and-repeating and-interrupting from-his-repetition and-saying how fine tree this and-how fine furrow this, raising upon-him the-written as-if incurring-liability in-his-soul.

Grammar:

- אוֹמֵר is a participle: in Avot the attribution formula is 'X says', not a past tense.
- תֶּן is the imperative of נתן: the first nun of the root drops in the imperative, as in biblical תֵּן; the segol of תֶּן is the short form before a closely joined word (Bartenura's heading has תֵּן).
- שֶׁ is the Mishnaic relative; before the pronoun in שֶׁאַתָּה וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלּוֹ it is causal ('for you and yours are His'). שֶׁלּוֹ is the possessive 'of-him'.
- The saying has two parts: a positive injunction (Rabbi Elazar of Bartota) and a verse from Chronicles that supports it. Rabbi Shimon's saying is a separate sentence; the long participial subject is resumed by מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו.
- הַמְהַלֵּךְ is a Piel participle; שׁוֹנֶה, מַפְסִיק and אוֹמֵר are participles that continue the subject. The subject hangs until the main verb מַעֲלֶה.
- מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ: the Hitpael participle of חיב, 'be held liable'; the idiom means to be liable to forfeit his life.

Note: Rabbi Elazar's 'Give Him what is His' is given as an imperative to the reader; the object of 'give' is God, as Bartenura reads it. The 'furrow' of the field is Bartenura's reading of ניר (the BDB lemma offered, a proper name, is not a fit and no sense is given). 'Forfeiting his life' renders מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, literally 'liable with/in his soul', that is, liable to a penalty of life; the same phrase recurs in 3:8.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not refrain from engaging in what is Heaven's, whether with your body or your money, for you are not giving from your own, neither from your body nor from your property: you and your property are His.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the same holds for any idle talk; the mishnah speaks of this case because travellers talk about what they see. Some say it is to teach that even though one blesses 'blessed is He who has such in His world', it still counts against him because he interrupted his learning.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: ניר is the furrow of the plow, as in 'break up your fallow ground' (Jeremiah 4:3, נִירוּ לָכֶם נִיר).

Apparatus:

- Quotation: 1 Chronicles 29:14, כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ; the Vilna text abbreviates דברי הימים as ד"ה and adds the verse number יד (14) to the citation.
- Spelling: Vilna reads כאילו and מתחייב where the base text has כְּאִלּוּ and מִתְחַיֵּב.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) takes the first saying to cover both body and property, and reads the Rabbi Shimon saying as a warning about interrupting study for idle remarks; one text-tradition has Rabbi Yaakov in place of Rabbi Shimon.
- דברי הימים: Vilna reads ד"ה (word)
- —: Vilna reads יד (word)
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)
- מִתְחַיֵּב: Vilna reads מתחייב (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:8

> רַבִּי דּוֹסְתַּאי בְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר, כָּל הַשּׁוֹכֵחַ דָּבָר אֶחָד מִמִּשְׁנָתוֹ, מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים ד) רַק הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ וּשְׁמֹר נַפְשְׁךָ מְאֹד פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ. יָכוֹל אֲפִלּוּ תָקְפָה עָלָיו מִשְׁנָתוֹ, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר (שם) וּפֶן יָסוּרוּ מִלְּבָבְךָ כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, הָא אֵינוֹ מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ עַד שֶׁיֵּשֵׁב וִיסִירֵם מִלִּבּוֹ:

**Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yannai, in the name of Rabbi Meir, says: Whoever forgets a single thing from his learning, Scripture accounts it to him as if he were forfeiting his life, as it is said: “Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes saw.” One might think this holds even if his learning was too hard for him; the teaching says: “and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.” Thus he is not forfeiting his life until he sits and removes them from his heart.**

Literal: my-master Dostai in-my-master Yannai from-name-of my-master Meir saying: all the-forgetting thing one from-his-repetition, raising upon-him the-written as-if incurring-liability in-his-soul, as-it-was-said (Deut 4): only be-guarded to-you and-guard your-soul very lest you-forget the-things that saw your-eyes. able even-if it-was-strong upon-him his-repetition, teaching to-say (there): and-lest they-depart from-your-heart all days-of your-life, thus not incurring-liability in-his-soul until that-he-sit and-remove-them from-his-heart.

Grammar:

- בְּרַבִּי is a contraction of 'son of Rabbi' (bar-rabbi); בֶּן is not used. The chain is Dostai, son of Rabbi Yannai, in the name of Rabbi Meir.
- The saying has a statement, a proof text, a challenge introduced by יָכוֹל ('one might think') and an answer introduced by תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ('the teaching says'); the final הָא ('so') draws the conclusion.
- The first verse is Deuteronomy 4:9 and the second continues the same verse: שָׁם marks 'in the same place'. The subject of the plural verb רָאוּ is 'eyes', as in the verse.
- שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר is the Nifal of אמר with שֶׁ: 'as it was said'. The citation in brackets (דברים ד) is a note in the printed text, not part of the saying.
- הַשּׁוֹכֵחַ, מִתְחַיֵּב and the like are participles; כָּל הַשּׁוֹכֵחַ is 'every one who forgets', a topic that is resumed by מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו.
- וִיסִירֵם is a Hifil imperfect with a 3rd masculine plural suffix, 'and he removes them'; the subject is the student who sits and does it on purpose.

Note: 'Learning' translates מִשְׁנָה in its general sense of what has been repeated and learned, not the book 'Mishnah'. 'Forfeiting his life' renders מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, literally 'liable in his soul'. 'Too hard for him' is Bartenura's reading of תָּקְפָה עָלָיו: it was hard for him and he forgot it because of the difficulty. The two readings of why forgetting counts against him are recorded under the Bartenura anchor. The printed citations (דברים ד) and (שם) are not translated.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: because he did not review it, it is counted against him as if he were liable with his life: through forgetting he may come to permit what is forbidden, so that a stumbling results and his error becomes deliberate; or: that mishnah was his safeguard and now that he has forgotten it, it no longer guards him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'it was strong for him' means it was hard for him and because of its difficulty he forgot it.

Apparatus:

- Quotation: Deuteronomy 4:9, רַק הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ וּשְׁמֹר נַפְשְׁךָ מְאֹד פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ, and (continued) וּפֶן יָסוּרוּ מִלְּבָבְךָ כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ; the verse continues with 'and you shall make them known to your children'.
- Spelling: Vilna reads כאילו, מתחייב (twice), ושמור and אפילו where the base text has כְּאִלּוּ, מִתְחַיֵּב, וּשְׁמֹר and אֲפִלּוּ.
- Citation: the base text has (דברים ד); Vilna adds the verse number ט (9).
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)
- מִתְחַיֵּב: Vilna reads מתחייב (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads ט (word)
- וּשְׁמֹר: Vilna reads ושמור (spelling)
- אֲפִלּוּ: Vilna reads אפילו (spelling)
- מִתְחַיֵּב: Vilna reads מתחייב (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:9

> רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶן דּוֹסָא אוֹמֵר, כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ, חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּמֶת. וְכָל שֶׁחָכְמָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְיִרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ, אֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּמֶת. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרֻבִּין מֵחָכְמָתוֹ, חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּמֶת. וְכָל שֶׁחָכְמָתוֹ מְרֻבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו, אֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּמֶת:

**Rabbi Hanina son of Dosa says: Anyone whose fear of sin comes before his wisdom, his wisdom endures. But anyone whose wisdom comes before his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure. He used to say: Anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom endures. But anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom does not endure.**

Literal: my-master Hanina son-of Dosa saying: all that-fear-of his-sin preceding to-his-wisdom, his-wisdom enduring. and-all that-his-wisdom preceding to-fear-of his-sin, not his-wisdom enduring. he was saying: all that-his-deeds more-numerous than-his-wisdom, his-wisdom enduring. and-all that-his-wisdom more-numerous than-his-deeds, not his-wisdom enduring.

| מִתְקַיֶּמֶת | endures — as in 3:9.12: Hitpael participle of קום; the lexicon entry offered (קָם 'adversary') is a different word | קָם | קום | verb (hitpael, participle active, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- The saying is built on two matched pairs, each with an affirmative and a negative half. כָּל שֶׁ... 'anyone who/whose' opens each half and is resumed by the main clause (a casus pendens: 'anyone whose fear of sin precedes, his wisdom endures').
- קוֹדֶמֶת and מִתְקַיֶּמֶת are feminine participles agreeing with יִרְאַת and חָכְמָה; מְרֻבִּין is masculine plural (the deeds), מְרֻבָּה feminine singular (the wisdom).
- מִן in מֵחָכְמָתוֹ and מִמַּעֲשָׂיו is comparative: 'more than'. The contrast is between יִרְאַת חֵטְא (fear of sin) and wisdom, and then between deeds and wisdom.
- הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, 'He used to say': the same rabbi continues, with a second saying; the formula is the Avot formula for a second saying.
- אֵין with a participle negates a predicate: אֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּמֶת, 'his wisdom is not enduring'.

Note: מִתְקַיֶּמֶת 'endures' is the Hitpael participle of קום 'stand', 'is established, lasts'. Bartenura explains it as the wisdom bringing him to what his heart desires, so that he takes pleasure in it. For 'deeds exceed wisdom' Bartenura says the case is one who is diligent in positive commandments, the earlier clause being about negative ones; the English keeps the plain 'deeds'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he puts fear of sin first in his thought, thinking 'I shall learn so that I will be one who fears sin'; this is the principle that the beginning of thought is the end of action.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: his wisdom endures because wisdom brings him to what his heart desires, and he takes pleasure in it.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he does not learn in order to act, since his heart is not turned to being one who fears sin.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since wisdom prevents him from following the stubbornness of his heart, he comes to loathe it, reject it and leave it.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: here the mishnah speaks of one who is diligent in positive commandments, while the earlier clause about fear of sin spoke of one who is careful with negative commandments.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the philosophers also agree that when the habit of the virtues comes first and becomes a firm possession, and only afterward he learns wisdom, which spurs him on to those good things, it adds joy and love of wisdom; but when (other) traits of character (קניני הדעות) are acquired first and only then he learns, so that wisdom restrains him from what he has grown used to craving, wisdom grows heavy for him and he abandons it.

Apparatus:

- Spelling: Vilna reads מתקיימת, מרובין and מרובה where the base text has מִתְקַיֶּמֶת, מְרֻבִּין and מְרֻבָּה.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads the first pair as about intention: one who strives to know wisdom in order to guard himself from sin keeps it. On 'deeds exceed wisdom' he asks how deeds can exceed knowledge, and answers that one who undertakes beforehand to do whatever the sages will teach him is credited as if he had done it, citing 'we will do and we will hear' (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 22).
- מִתְקַיֶּמֶת: Vilna reads מתקיימת (spelling)
- מִתְקַיֶּמֶת: Vilna reads מתקיימת (spelling)
- מְרֻבִּין: Vilna reads מרובין (spelling)
- מִתְקַיֶּמֶת: Vilna reads מתקיימת (spelling)
- מְרֻבָּה: Vilna reads מרובה (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:10

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, כָּל שֶׁרוּחַ הַבְּרִיּוֹת נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ, רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ. וְכָל שֶׁאֵין רוּחַ הַבְּרִיּוֹת נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ, אֵין רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ. רַבִּי דוֹסָא בֶן הַרְכִּינַס אוֹמֵר, שֵׁנָה שֶׁל שַׁחֲרִית, וְיַיִן שֶׁל צָהֳרַיִם, וְשִׂיחַת הַיְלָדִים, וִישִׁיבַת בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת שֶׁל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ, מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:

**He used to say: Anyone with whom the spirit of people is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. And anyone with whom the spirit of people is not pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him. Rabbi Dosa son of Harkinas says: Morning sleep, midday wine, the chatter of children, and sitting in the synagogues of the unlearned remove a person from the world.**

Literal: he was saying: all that-spirit-of the-creatures pleased from-him, spirit-of the-Place pleased from-him. and-all that-not spirit-of the-creatures pleased from-him, not spirit-of the-Place pleased from-him. my-master Dosa son-of Harkinas saying: sleep of morning, and-wine of noon, and-talk-of the-children, and-sitting-of houses-of assemblies of people-of the-land, removing the-man from the-world.

Grammar:

- הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר 'He used to say' continues Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's sayings from 3:9. The pair of sayings is built on כָּל שֶׁ... 'anyone whose/with whom'.
- נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ: נוֹחָה is a feminine participle (agreeing with רוּחַ, which is here feminine); הֵימֶנּוּ is the Mishnaic form of מִמֶּנּוּ, 'from him'. The idiom is 'the spirit is at ease with him'.
- The two halves are parallel. Bartenura reads the first as a sign, not a cause: whoever is loved below is known (בְּיָדוּעַ) to be loved above. אֵין negates each half.
- Rabbi Dosa's list has four items joined by וְ: two use the genitive particle שֶׁל (שֵׁנָה שֶׁל שַׁחֲרִית 'sleep of morning', יַיִן שֶׁל צָהֳרַיִם 'wine of noon') and two are construct chains (שִׂיחַת הַיְלָדִים, יְשִׁיבַת בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת); the plural participle מוֹצִיאִין has the whole list as subject.
- עַם הָאָרֶץ is literally 'people of the land'; in the Mishnah it means an unlearned person, a person ignorant of Torah. הַמָּקוֹם is literally 'the Place', a name of God.

Note: הַמָּקוֹם is rendered 'the Omnipresent' (literally 'the Place') as in the work's decisions. עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ is 'the unlearned' (literally 'people of the land'). 'Synagogues' renders בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת, 'houses of assembly'. Bartenura says the last item is wrong because people gather there and talk of idle things. 'Spirit ... is pleased' renders רוּחַ ... נוֹחָה, 'the spirit is at ease'; Bartenura glosses it as love: whoever is loved below is loved above.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: whoever is beloved below is known to be beloved above.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: sleeping late in the morning until the time for reciting the Shema has passed.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: wine draws a person's heart, as it is written 'to draw my flesh with wine' (Ecclesiastes 2:3), and brings him to drunkenness.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the chatter of children keeps their fathers from engaging in Torah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they gather there and speak idle things.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: he says that these things prevent and cancel a person's excellence until he goes out of the world and is lost.

Apparatus:

- Spelling: Vilna reads שינה for שֵׁנָה and ילדים for הַיְלָדִים.
- Ecclesiastes 2:3 (לִמְשׁוֹךְ בַּיַּיִן אֶת בְּשָׂרִי) is quoted by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.
- שֵׁנָה: Vilna reads שינה (spelling)
- הַיְלָדִים: Vilna reads ילדים (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:11

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הַמּוֹדָעִי אוֹמֵר, הַמְחַלֵּל אֶת הַקָּדָשִׁים, וְהַמְבַזֶּה אֶת הַמּוֹעֲדוֹת, וְהַמַּלְבִּין פְּנֵי חֲבֵרוֹ בָרַבִּים, וְהַמֵּפֵר בְּרִיתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, וְהַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֲלָכָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ תוֹרָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים, אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

**Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in says: One who profanes the sacred things, and one who despises the festivals, and one who shames his fellow in public, and one who breaks the covenant of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, and one who brazenly flouts the Torah, contrary to the halakha: even though he has Torah and good deeds, he has no share in the world to come.**

Literal: my-master Elazar the-Modi'ite saying: the-profaning the-holy-things, and-the-despising the-festivals, and-the-whitening face-of his-fellow among-the-many, and-the-breaking his-covenant of Abraham our-father upon-him the-peace, and-the-uncovering face in-the-Torah that-not as-halakha, even upon mouth-of that-there-is in-his-hand Torah and-deeds good, there-is-not to-him share to-the-world the-coming.

Grammar:

- Each of the five offences is a participle with the article (הַמְחַלֵּל, הַמְבַזֶּה, הַמַּלְבִּין, הַמֵּפֵר, הַמְגַלֶּה) and all form the long subject; the main clause is only at the end: אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק.
- הַמַּלְבִּין פְּנֵי חֲבֵרוֹ is literally 'the one who whitens his fellow's face': a person shamed first reddens, then goes pale. The phrase is a fixed idiom for public shaming.
- אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ is a concessive conjunction: 'even though'. יֵשׁ בְּיָדוֹ is the possessive construction 'there is in his hand', that is, 'he has'.
- אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק is the negative possessive: 'there is not to him a share'. הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא (the world to come) is a participle used adjectivally.
- The stem גלה in the Piel with פָּנִים means 'to uncover a face'; with בַּתּוֹרָה the idiom is 'to bare one's face (shamelessly) against the Torah'.
- עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם 'peace upon him' is a formula said after the name of a righteous person; it is not a statement of the mishnah.

Note: 'Brazenly flouts the Torah' renders הַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֲלָכָה. Rambam, Rabbeinu Yonah and Bartenura's second explanation take the idiom as acting shamelessly, in the open, against the Torah. Bartenura's first explanation, one who 'shows faces' (explanations) in the Torah that are not according to halakha, is recorded under the Bartenura anchor. 'The sacred things' renders הַקָּדָשִׁים: Bartenura includes both the offerings of the altar and property consecrated to the Temple's upkeep. 'The covenant of Abraham' is circumcision; Bartenura takes the offence as one who was not circumcised, or who was circumcised and draws the foreskin forward to hide it; Rabbeinu Yonah names only the second. 'The festivals' is Bartenura's reading, the intermediate days (חוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד).

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who brings the offerings of the altar to a state of piggul, nothar or impurity, or who misappropriates and has benefit from the sanctified things, whether of the altar or of the upkeep of the Temple.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the intermediate days of a festival: he does work on them, or treats them as weekdays in eating and drinking.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a person who is shamed first reddens and then pales, because the soul has two movements, outward and inward; when he cannot find an answer he is anxious within and the spirit moves to his face and it goes pale.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who was not circumcised, or who was circumcised and draws his foreskin forward to cover the circumcision so that it is not seen that he is circumcised.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura gives two explanations. The first: he 'shows faces' and explanations in the Torah that are not according to halakha, for example one who translates 'you shall not give of your seed to pass to Molech' as 'to pass to the Aramean'; this includes one who expounds disgraceful expositions. The second: he brazenly breaks the words of the Torah in public, with a high hand and no shame. The English adopts the second, which is Rambam's and Rabbeinu Yonah's reading, and records the first here.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: this is one who did not repent of any of these transgressions; even if suffering came upon him and he died in suffering, he has no share in the world to come. But if he repented before his death, nothing stands before repentance.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: one who shames his fellow.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: one who bares his face in the Torah is one who transgresses a commandment of the Torah publicly, the height of heresy, as it says 'and the soul that does with a high hand'; the phrase means 'bares a face and acts impudently', a term of heresy, as the Yerushalmi (Peah) explains it: one who transgresses words of Torah publicly, like Jehoiakim son of Josiah.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'one who breaks the covenant' is as it sounds. He adds that, for all the offences the sages said bar one from the world to come, this applies when the person did not repent and died in suffering: these sins are graver than others, since suffering together with death does not atone for them.

Apparatus:

- Bartenura's first reading of הַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים (one who shows or reveals interpretations in the Torah contrary to the halakha) is not adopted in the English; see the commentary.
- The mishnah's 'the sacred things' and 'the festivals' are linked by Rabbeinu Yonah because both are called 'holy' in Scripture.
- Numbers 15:30 (בְּיָד רָמָה) is quoted by Rambam, not by the mishnah.
- Alternative to the English 'festivals': 'appointed times'.

#### Pirkei Avot 3:12

> רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי קַל לְרֹאשׁ, וְנוֹחַ לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת, וֶהֱוֵי מְקַבֵּל אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם בְּשִׂמְחָה:

**Rabbi Yishmael says: Be yielding to a superior, and composed with the young, and receive every person with joy.**

Literal: my-master Yishmael saying: be light to-head, and-easy to-youth, and-be receiving the-all the-man with-joy.

| רַבִּי | Rabbi | רַב | רבב | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 1st person, singular) | 2 |
| יִשְׁמָעֵאל | Yishmael | יִשְׁמָעֵאל |  | noun (proper name, person, masculine) | 1 |
| אוֹמֵר | says | אָמַר | אמר | verb (qal, participle active, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.1 |

| קַל | yielding — קַל: 'light'; Rambam and Bartenura: quick to serve, yielding | קַל | קלל | adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

| לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת | with the young — לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת: 'to a young person' (from שחר, 'black', the black hair of youth) | ל: to, for + תִּשְׁחֹרֶת | שחר | preposition + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וֶהֱוֵי | and be — וֶהֱוֵי | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |

| אֶת | - — object marker | אֶת |  | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| כָּל | every | כֹּל | כלל | adjective (quantifier, all, construct) | 1.2 |
| הָאָדָם | person — הָאָדָם: 'the man', the human being | ה: the + אָדָם | אדם | article (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| בְּשִׂמְחָה | with joy | ב: in, with, by + שִׂמְחָה | שמח | preposition + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1.1 |

Grammar:

- הֱוֵי is the Mishnaic imperative of הָיָה ('be'); וֶהֱוֵי is the same with the conjunction, the vowel pattern of the conjunction before a guttural.
- הֱוֵי קַל לְרֹאשׁ: the predicate adjective with ל. קַל is 'light'; Rambam says its sense is known, 'lightness'; the figure is of a person who does not weigh on a superior, who is quick to serve.
- נוֹחַ is used as an adjective, 'easy, at rest, composed' (Rambam: הַיִּשּׁוּב וְהַהֲנָחָה); תִּשְׁחֹרֶת is a rare noun from the root שחר 'black', for 'youth', the time of black hair (Bartenura, Rambam). Rabbeinu Yonah derives it differently: from שחוור, a lord or official, or from the Targum's שחרית 'forced service' (Num 16:15).
- מְקַבֵּל is the Piel participle of קבל, 'to receive'. With הֱוֵי it forms a periphrastic imperative, 'be one who receives'.
- The sentence is three clauses of the pattern 'be + adjective/participle'. The last sets the general rule for every person (אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם), after two specific cases of an older and a younger person.

Note: 'Yielding to a superior' renders קַל לְרֹאשׁ. Bartenura and Rambam both read it as being quick to serve a person of standing; the English keeps the idiom without expanding it. 'Composed with the young' renders נוֹחַ לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת; Bartenura and Rambam: do not make yourself light with the young but stand before them calmly and with dignity, and yet receive everyone cheerfully. 'Receive' is the plain sense of מְקַבֵּל; Bartenura also derives it from the Aramaic קֳבֵל 'facing', so 'meet'. Bartenura's alternative reading (youth and old age with the Creator) is recorded under his anchor.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: before a great old man who sits at the head of the academy, be quick to do his service and to attend him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: toward a young man with black hair you need not make yourself so light; stand before him calmly and with composure.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: toward every person, whether an elder or a youth, stand with joy; מְקַבֵּל is like מַקְבִּיל, from the Aramaic קֳבֵל 'opposite'. He adds another explanation, applying the maxim to God: in your youth be quick to do your Maker's will and in old age, when your face has darkened, be at ease with Him. This second explanation is recorded and not adopted.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the meaning of 'lightness' is known.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: נוֹחַ is settledness and rest; before a person of great standing make yourself light, serve him, and stand as he wishes; with a young person do not do so but honour yourself with him, and do not jest or play; but do not take the warning about young people as license to receive them with anger: receive every person, small and great, free and slave, with joy, more than what Shammai said ('with a pleasant face').

Apparatus:

- Spelling: Vilna reads לתשחורת for לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת.
- Bartenura's alternative explanation (the first two clauses are about one's own youth and old age toward the Creator) is recorded under his anchor and not adopted.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads קַל לְרֹאשׁ as making oneself light before a chief or lord; he does not take תִּשְׁחֹרֶת as 'youth' but as an official (from שחוור, 'lord'), to whom one should be pleasant in speech, or, from the Targum's שחרית in Num 16:15, as service: be easy in serving a great man and doing his will.
- לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת: Vilna reads לתשחורת (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:13

> רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר, שְׂחוֹק וְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ, מַרְגִּילִין לְעֶרְוָה. מָסֹרֶת, סְיָג לַתּוֹרָה. מַעַשְׂרוֹת, סְיָג לָעשֶׁר. נְדָרִים, סְיָג לַפְּרִישׁוּת. סְיָג לַחָכְמָה, שְׁתִיקָה:

**Rabbi Akiva says: Laughter and levity accustom a person to lewdness. The Masoretic tradition is a fence for the Torah; tithes are a fence for wealth; vows are a fence for abstinence; a fence for wisdom is silence.**

Literal: Rabbi Akiva says laughter and-lightness-of head accustom to-lewdness. Tradition fence to-the-Torah. Tithes fence to-wealth. Vows fence to-abstinence. Fence to-wisdom silence.

Grammar:

- The saying is built of four short nominal clauses of the form 'X, a fence for Y', with no verb; the English supplies 'is/are'. The last clause reverses the order (the fence first, then its identity), which puts silence at the end.
- מַרְגִּילִין is a Hifil participle, plural masculine, agreeing with the two subjects שְׂחוֹק and קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ.
- The tradition (מָסֹרֶת) is listed with tithes, vows and silence: each is a protective fence (סְיָג) around something valuable.
- The first sentence is a warning, the next four are the positive fences; the saying is one continuous teaching of Rabbi Akiva.

Note: מָסֹרֶת is rendered 'Masoretic tradition' because Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah both say it means the received tradition of plene and defective spellings of the Torah text; the Hebrew word alone could also mean 'tradition' in general. The Jastrow lemma on לָעשֶׁר is a verb entry (עָשַׂר); I keep the data but read the noun 'wealth'. Rambam reads נְדָרִים as a means of acquiring the habit of restraint. For סְיָג לַחָכְמָה שְׁתִיקָה, Bartenura limits the silence to optional talk between people; the English keeps the Hebrew's unlimited wording.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the tradition the sages handed down about the defective and plene spellings of the Torah is a fence and support for the written Torah, since from it we learn how to perform commandments (for example, the defective and plene spelling of בסכות shows that a sukkah may have three walls).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'for it is written עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר, tithe in order that you become rich' (Ta'anit 9). Tithing is thus a fence for wealth.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: when a person begins abstinence and fears he may transgress, he takes it upon himself in the form of a vow not to do such and such, and by this he subdues his inclination.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the silence is not silence from Torah or from forbidden speech (those are commanded or forbidden anyway) but silence from permitted talk between people, which one should limit as far as possible.
- Rambam (records): Rambam: when a person vows and keeps his vows, he acquires the habit of holding back from what he wants to avoid, and separation (פְּרִישׁוּת) becomes easy for him; he takes פְּרִישׁוּת as guarding oneself from ritual impurity, as in 'the garments of an unlearned person are midras-impure for Perushim' (Hagigah 18b).

Apparatus:

- Vilna spells מסורת, סייג (four times) and לעושר where the base text reads מָסֹרֶת, סְיָג and לָעשֶׁר; these are spelling variants only.
- Bartenura quotes Ta'anit 9a for 'tithe in order that you become rich'; the underlying verse is Deuteronomy 14:22 (עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר).

#### Pirkei Avot 3:14

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, חָבִיב אָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְצֶלֶם. חִבָּה יְתֵרָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְצֶלֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (בראשית ט) כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם. חֲבִיבִין יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ בָנִים לַמָּקוֹם. חִבָּה יְתֵרָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ בָנִים לַמָּקוֹם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים יד) בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם. חֲבִיבִין יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּתַּן לָהֶם כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה. חִבָּה יְתֵרָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּתַּן לָהֶם כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (משלי ד) כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם, תּוֹרָתִי אַל תַּעֲזֹבוּ:

**He used to say: Beloved is a human being, for he was created in the image. Extra love was made known to him, that he was created in the image, as it is said (Genesis 9): 'For in the image of God He made the human being.' Beloved are Israel, for they were called children of the Omnipresent. Extra love was made known to them, that they were called children of the Omnipresent, as it is said (Deuteronomy 14): 'You are children of the LORD your God.' Beloved are Israel, for a desirable vessel was given to them. Extra love was made known to them, that a desirable vessel was given to them, by which the world was created, as it is said (Proverbs 4): 'For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake my Torah.'**

Literal: He was saying: beloved human that-was-created in-image. Love extra is-made-known to-him that-was-created in-image, that-it-was-said (Genesis 9): for in-image-of God He-made [object-marker] the-human. Beloved Israel that-they-were-called children to-the-Place. Love extra is-made-known to-them that-they-were-called children to-the-Place, that-it-was-said (Deuteronomy 14): children you to-YHWH your-God. Beloved Israel that-was-given to-them vessel-of desire. Love extra is-made-known to-them that-was-given to-them vessel-of desire that-in-it was-created the-world, that-it-was-said (Proverbs 4): for teaching good I-have-given to-you my-Torah do-not forsake.

Grammar:

- The saying has three parallel units, each of the same shape: (1) 'Beloved is X, for ...'; (2) 'Extra love was made known to X, that ...'; (3) a proof text introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר. The repetition is deliberate, and the English keeps it.
- חִבָּה יְתֵרָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ: the verb is a Nifal participle of יָדַע, 'is made known'. The point (Rambam, Bartenura) is that God's telling the human being of the gift is itself a further proof of love.
- שֶׁנִּבְרָא, שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ, שֶׁנִּתַּן are Nifal perfect forms with the relative particle שֶׁ ('that/for'). Three Nifal verbs (was created, were called, was given) carry the argument; the passive leaves God unnamed as the agent until the proof text.
- The three proof texts come from Genesis 9:6, Deuteronomy 14:1 and Proverbs 4:2. In the third (Proverbs 4:2) the speaker is God (or wisdom's teacher) addressing Israel about the Torah.
- אֱלֹהֵיכֶם is plural construct with a 2nd person plural suffix ('your God'); תּוֹרָתִי is construct with the 1st person singular suffix; the object marker אֶת has no English counterpart.

Note: חִבָּה יְתֵרָה: 'extra love' (Jastrow: 'love'; יָתֵר 'surplus'). I keep 'extra' rather than 'special' to preserve the idea of a second, additional love beyond the first. נוֹדַעַת is read 'is made known' (Nifal of יָדַע) following Rambam as quoted by Bartenura: God informs the creature of the gift. The pack's BDB keys for טוֹב and אָדָם are proper names (Tob, Adam); the pack also lists jastrow:טוֹב II and jastrow:אָדָם, which give 'good' and 'man'. כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה is rendered 'a desirable vessel' to keep the biblical wording of חֶמְדָּה; the vessel is the Torah, by which the world was created. In Proverbs 4:2 תּוֹרָתִי can mean 'my teaching'; the English reads 'my Torah', as the mishnah applies the verse to the Torah.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura, citing Rambam: the Holy One showed the human being extra love by informing him that he was created in the image, for one who does a kindness and tells his friend of it shows more love than one who does it without telling. Another reading: נוֹדַעַת means a love that is revealed and public: not only a hidden love of the Omnipresent for the human being, but a love open and known to all.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: everything in the work of creation of which it is said 'and God saw that it was good' was created only for the sake of the Torah, which is called לֶקַח, 'teaching', as in יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי. The English 'teaching' follows this.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: letting someone know the measure of the benefit done to him is itself another benefit, for a person sometimes does a kindness out of pity and does not tell the recipient its extent because the recipient seems lowly to him. This is why the Hebrew says extra love is 'made known'.

Apparatus:

- Genesis 9:6 (כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם).
- Deuteronomy 14:1 (בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם).
- Proverbs 4:2 (כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם תּוֹרָתִי אַל תַּעֲזֹבוּ).
- Vilna reads יתירה, שניתן and תעזובו (spelling only) and ו for כִּי at 3:14.17; it also adds א and ב in the citations of Deuteronomy 14 and Proverbs 4. These are the verse numbers (Deuteronomy 14:1, Proverbs 4:2), not words of the text; the ו at 3:14.17 may likewise be the verse number of Genesis 9:6, aligned against כִּי.
- יְתֵרָה: Vilna reads יתירה (spelling)
- כִּי: Vilna reads ו (word)
- יְתֵרָה: Vilna reads יתירה (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads א (word)
- שֶׁנִּתַּן: Vilna reads שניתן (spelling)
- יְתֵרָה: Vilna reads יתירה (spelling)
- שֶׁנִּתַּן: Vilna reads שניתן (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads ב (word)
- תַּעֲזֹבוּ: Vilna reads תעזובו (spelling)

| הַמַּעֲשֶׂה | the deed | ה: the + מַעֲשֶׂה | עשה | article + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.1 |

Grammar:

- Four short clauses, each a noun and a passive participle or verb: הַכֹּל צָפוּי, הָרְשׁוּת נְתוּנָה, הָעוֹלָם נִדּוֹן, הַכֹּל לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. The first two clauses state an apparent tension (foreknowledge and choice) without resolving it.
- צָפוּי and נְתוּנָה are passive participles (Qal) used predicatively; the passive leaves the agent, God, unstated.
- בְּטוֹב is 'in goodness' (with the preposition בְּ): the world is judged 'with goodness' (by mercy), and the final clause qualifies this: each person receives it in proportion to deeds.
- הַכֹּל occurs twice, in the first and the last clause, and carries a different sense each time: 'everything' that happens is foreseen; 'everyone' (or 'all') is judged according to deeds.

Note: Rambam's reading of the last clause as 'but not according to the deed' (אֲבָל לֹא עַל פִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה) is a variant; I translate the text of the pack, which reads לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. הָרְשׁוּת is translated 'freedom of choice' because both normative commentators say it means the power in the hand of a person to do good or evil; the plain sense of the word is 'permission, authority'. For רֹב I keep 'abundance' and give Bartenura's alternative 'majority' in the apparatus.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: everything a person does in the innermost chambers is revealed before Him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: it is in a person's own hand to do good or evil, as it is written (Deut. 30:15) 'See, I have set before you today life...'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the world is judged with the measure of mercy; and yet not all are equal in this, since everything is according to the abundance of deeds: whoever has many good deeds receives much mercy. He adds another reading: a person is judged by the majority of his deeds (a majority of merits, innocent; of sins, guilty).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: according to how much a person repeats and persists in doing good, so his reward is great (a hundred coins given to charity in a hundred separate acts is not like giving them at once). He also records that Rambam's text reads 'but not according to the deed'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'everything is foreseen': all that is in the world is known to God; but foreknowledge does not compel, for 'the choice is given' to every person (his eighth chapter). God judges people with grace and goodness, not by the strict judgment due them. Virtues come according to the number (רֹב) of good deeds, not the size of one deed: a thousand coins given one at a time build generosity more than a thousand given at once.

Apparatus:

- Bartenura 3:15:4 records Rambam's reading of the last clause: וְהַכֹּל לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, אֲבָל לֹא עַל פִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה ('but not according to the deed').
- Bartenura 3:15:3 gives a second reading of רֹב: 'by the majority of his deeds'.
- Deuteronomy 30:15 (רְאֵה נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַיּוֹם אֶת הַחַיִּים) is cited by Bartenura for the freedom of choice.
- Vilna spells רוב for רֹב.
- רֹב: Vilna reads רוב (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:16

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, הַכֹּל נָתוּן בְּעֵרָבוֹן, וּמְצוּדָה פְרוּסָה עַל כָּל הַחַיִּים. הַחֲנוּת פְּתוּחָה, וְהַחֶנְוָנִי מֵקִיף, וְהַפִּנְקָס פָּתוּחַ, וְהַיָּד כּוֹתֶבֶת, וְכָל הָרוֹצֶה לִלְווֹת יָבֹא וְיִלְוֶה, וְהַגַּבָּאִים מַחֲזִירִים תָּדִיר בְּכָל יוֹם, וְנִפְרָעִין מִן הָאָדָם מִדַּעְתּוֹ וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ, וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם עַל מַה שֶּׁיִּסְמֹכוּ, וְהַדִּין דִּין אֱמֶת, וְהַכֹּל מְתֻקָּן לַסְּעוּדָה:

**He used to say: Everything is given as a pledge, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, the shopkeeper extends credit, the ledger is open, and the hand writes; and whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow. The collectors make their rounds constantly, every day, and exact payment from a person with his knowledge and without his knowledge. They have what to rely on, and the judgment is a judgment of truth. And everything is prepared for the banquet.**

Literal: He was saying: the-all given in-pledge, and-net spread over all-of the-living. The-shop open, and-the-shopkeeper extends-credit, and-the-ledger open, and-the-hand writing, and-all the-wishing to-borrow will-come and-will-borrow, and-the-collectors go-around constantly in-every day, and-they-collect-payment from the-person from-his-knowledge and-that-not from-his-knowledge, and-there-is to-them on what that-they-rely, and-the-judgment judgment-of truth, and-the-all prepared to-the-meal.

Grammar:

- The saying is a single extended metaphor: a shop that gives credit. The clauses are strung with 'and' and almost all use participles (נָתוּן, פְּרוּסָה, פְּתוּחָה, מֵקִיף, כּוֹתֶבֶת, מַחֲזִירִים, נִפְרָעִין, מְתֻקָּן), giving the sense of an ongoing, present process.
- הַכֹּל נָתוּן בְּעֵרָבוֹן, 'everything is given as a pledge', and the following clause וּמְצוּדָה פְרוּסָה עַל כָּל הַחַיִּים, 'a net is spread over all the living', open the images of security for a debt and of capture.
- The pairs מִדַּעְתּוֹ / וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ ('with his knowledge' / 'without his knowledge') contrast the debtor who remembers his debt and the one who has forgotten it.
- וְכָל הָרוֹצֶה לִלְווֹת יָבֹא וְיִלְוֶה uses a jussive-like imperfect ('let him come and borrow'): the borrower acts freely, linking to the freedom of choice in the previous mishnah.
- The last clause וְהַכֹּל מְתֻקָּן לַסְּעוּדָה resolves the metaphor: the collection ends in a meal. Rambam and Bartenura read the meal as the world to come.

Note: The shop metaphor is read as the commentators read it: the shopkeeper is God, the ledger is the record of deeds, the collectors are sufferings and death (Bartenura, Rambam), and the banquet is the world to come. The English keeps the images and puts the application in the commentary, as the saying itself does. מֵקִיף is rendered 'extends credit' (from הַקָּפָה); the pack's lemma is the root קוף. מַחֲזִירִים, 'make their rounds', follows Jastrow's 'to go around (searching)'. The Jastrow entries for בָּא I and לָוָה in the pack give only cross-references or a different meaning, so I give no sense for those verbs; the data are kept. Bartenura's explanations of לְדַעְתּוֹ and שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעְתּוֹ are attached to the whole verse in the pack.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura (citing Sukkah 53a): a person's feet are his guarantors; they lead him to the place where he is wanted. Everything is given as a pledge.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the net is suffering and death.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: people enter the shop and take goods on credit.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the shopkeeper trusts everyone who comes to take; so people sin every day and the Holy One, blessed be He, waits for them until their time comes.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the ledger is open to write in the credits so that they are not forgotten.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: lest one say that the shopkeeper is sometimes busy and does not write everything, the mishnah adds 'and the hand writes'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: this is the same as 'the choice is given' above: no one is forced to borrow against his will.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the collectors are sufferings and bad occurrences.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on מִדַּעְתּוֹ: sometimes he remembers his debt and says 'You have judged me well'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ: sometimes he has forgotten and protests against the judgment of the Omnipresent.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they rely on the ledger and on the shopkeeper, who is believed about his ledger; so the sufferings rely on a person's deeds recorded before the Omnipresent, even though the person has forgotten them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal with His creatures by unfair, tyrannical claims (אֵינוֹ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא, Avodah Zarah 3a); the judgment is just.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: righteous and wicked alike have a share in the world to come after the debt has been collected from them.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'the shopkeeper extends credit' means that one's debt may lengthen without being demanded at once; 'whoever wishes to borrow may come' supports the earlier point that there is no compulsion; 'the collectors' is a figure for death and other punishments that come upon a person.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the final aim of all this is the life of the world to come.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: a long note, attached in the pack to the word הָרוֹצֶה in 3:16.21 but about knowledge and understanding (דַּעַת and בִּינָה) of 3:17: each of the two is useful for the existence of the other and completes it. It does not bear on the plain sense of 3:16.

Apparatus:

- Vilna spells ללות for לִלְווֹת, שיסמוכו for שֶּׁיִּסְמֹכוּ and מתוקן for מְתֻקָּן.
- Bartenura 3:16:1 cites Sukkah 53a: רַגְלוֹהִי דְּבַר נַשׁ אִינוּן עֲרֵבִין בֵּיהּ (a person's feet are guarantors for him).
- Bartenura 3:16:12 cites Avodah Zarah 3a for 'the Holy One does not come with a complaint against His creatures'.
- Rambam's note on דעת and בינה (rambam:3:17:1), which concerns 3:17, is anchored in the pack to the word הָרוֹצֶה in 3:16.21.
- לִלְווֹת: Vilna reads ללות (spelling)
- שֶּׁיִּסְמֹכוּ: Vilna reads שיסמוכו (spelling)
- מְתֻקָּן: Vilna reads מתוקן (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:17

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹמֵר, אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה, אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ. אִם אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, אֵין תּוֹרָה. אִם אֵין חָכְמָה, אֵין יִרְאָה. אִם אֵין יִרְאָה, אֵין חָכְמָה. אִם אֵין בִּינָה, אֵין דַּעַת. אִם אֵין דַּעַת, אֵין בִּינָה. אִם אֵין קֶמַח, אֵין תּוֹרָה. אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה, אֵין קֶמַח. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, כָּל שֶׁחָכְמָתוֹ מְרֻבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו, לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאִילָן שֶׁעֲנָפָיו מְרֻבִּין וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מֻעָטִין, וְהָרוּחַ בָּאָה וְעוֹקַרְתּוֹ וְהוֹפַכְתּוֹ עַל פָּנָיו, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (ירמיה יז) וְהָיָה כְּעַרְעָר בָּעֲרָבָה וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבוֹא טוֹב וְשָׁכַן חֲרֵרִים בַּמִּדְבָּר אֶרֶץ מְלֵחָה וְלֹא תֵשֵׁב. אֲבָל כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרֻבִּין מֵחָכְמָתוֹ, לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאִילָן שֶׁעֲנָפָיו מֻעָטִין וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מְרֻבִּין, שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ כָל הָרוּחוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם בָּאוֹת וְנוֹשְׁבוֹת בּוֹ אֵין מְזִיזִין אוֹתוֹ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם) וְהָיָה כְּעֵץ שָׁתוּל עַל מַיִם וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבֹא חֹם, וְהָיָה עָלֵהוּ רַעֲנָן, וּבִשְׁנַת בַּצֹּרֶת לֹא יִדְאָג, וְלֹא יָמִישׁ מֵעֲשׂוֹת פֶּרִי:

**Rabbi Elazar son of Azariah says: If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He used to say: Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are many and whose roots are few; and the wind comes and uproots it and overturns it on its face, as it is said (Jeremiah 17): 'He shall be like a bare shrub in the desert plain, and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, a salt land, uninhabited.' But anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are few and whose roots are many, so that even if all the winds in the world come and blow against it, they do not move it from its place, as it is said (ibid.): 'He shall be like a tree planted by water, and by a stream it sends out its roots, and it shall not see when heat comes; its leaf shall be fresh, and in a year of drought it shall not worry, and it shall not cease from yielding fruit.'**

Literal: Rabbi Elazar son-of Azariah says: if not Torah, not way-of land; if not way-of land, not Torah. If not wisdom, not fear; if not fear, not wisdom. If not understanding, not knowledge; if not knowledge, not understanding. If not flour, not Torah; if not Torah, not flour. He was saying: all-that his-wisdom is-increased more-than-his-deeds, to-what is-he similar, to-a-tree that-its-branches many and-its-roots few, and-the-wind comes and-uproots-it and-overturns-it on its-face, that-it-was-said (Jeremiah 17): and-he-will-be like-a-shrub in-the-desert-plain and-not will-see when will-come good, and-will-dwell parched-places in-the-wilderness land salt and-not will-be-inhabited. But all-that his-deeds are-many more-than-his-wisdom, to-what is-he similar, to-a-tree that-its-branches few and-its-roots many, that-even all-of the-winds that-in-the-world coming and-blowing in-it not move it from-its-place, that-it-was-said (ibid.): and-he-will-be like-a-tree planted on water and-on stream sends-out its-roots and-not will-see when will-come heat, and-will-be its-leaf fresh, and-in-year-of drought not will-worry, and-not will-cease from-doing fruit.

Grammar:

- The first part is four mirror-image pairs of conditionals אִם אֵין X, אֵין Y / אִם אֵין Y, אֵין X: each of Torah and proper conduct, wisdom and fear, understanding and knowledge, flour and Torah depends on the other. The English keeps the repetition, because the symmetry is the argument.
- אֵין is the negative existential particle, not a verb: 'there is not'. In a conditional with אִם: 'if there is no X, there is no Y'.
- The second saying is introduced by הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר and has two parallel images (tree with many branches and few roots; tree with few branches and many roots), each with the same structure: כָּל שֶׁ... לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאִילָן שֶׁ..., then a proof text. The English keeps the repeated question.
- מְרֻבָּה, מְרֻבִּין, מֻעָטִין are Pual participles ('are increased, are decreased'), used as predicate adjectives; the passive implies natural growth.
- וְהָרוּחַ בָּאָה וְעוֹקַרְתּוֹ וְהוֹפַכְתּוֹ עַל פָּנָיו: three feminine participles (בָּאָה, then two Qal participles with object suffixes) in a series; the image is told in the present, 'the wind comes and uproots it and overturns it'. In the second image the verbs are participles too: בָּאוֹת וְנוֹשְׁבוֹת, 'coming and blowing'.
- Both proof texts are from Jeremiah 17: the first (verse 6) is about 'the one who trusts in man'; the second (verse 8) about 'the one who trusts in the LORD'. The mishnah quotes only the images.

Note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ: rendered 'proper conduct' because Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah both read it as decent behaviour toward people and good character traits in the first pair; in the pair about flour (קֶמַח) the same phrase could be read as 'worldly occupation', and I note that rather than change the word. The mishnah's יִרְאָה is 'fear', without 'of God', as in the Hebrew. For the pair דַּעַת / בִּינָה I follow Bartenura's distinction (דַּעַת 'finds the reason of a thing'; בִּינָה 'derives one thing from another'); the English uses the ordinary words 'knowledge' and 'understanding'. Rabbeinu Yonah describes the two differently (knowledge as what one grasps of oneself, understanding as inferring one thing from another). The pack's default lexicon keys for טוֹב, בָּא, דָּמָה, יוּבַל and צֹרֶת point to different words (a place, 'father', 'to cease', a proper name, a proper name); where the pack also lists the right entry (jastrow:טוֹב II, jastrow:דָּמָה ²) it is used, otherwise no sense is given and the correct word is read. Rambam's comment on דעת and בינה is anchored in the pack to 3:16.21 and is ruled on under 3:16.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if there is no Torah, a person's dealings with people are not good (his conduct is not proper).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if there is no proper conduct, in the end his Torah is forgotten by him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: דַּעַת is finding the reason for a thing; בִּינָה is understanding one thing from another without being able to show its reason (אֵינוֹ מַרְאֶה לוֹ טַעַם). Without knowledge to give the reason there is no understanding, for not knowing the reason is like not knowing the thing; yet understanding comes first, so without understanding there is no knowledge.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who has nothing to eat, how can he occupy himself with Torah?
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: what use is the flour in his hand if it has no Torah in it? Better for him that he had no flour and died of hunger.

Apparatus:

- Jeremiah 17:6 (וְהָיָה כְּעַרְעָר בָּעֲרָבָה וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבוֹא טוֹב וְשָׁכַן חֲרֵרִים בַּמִּדְבָּר אֶרֶץ מְלֵחָה וְלֹא תֵשֵׁב).
- Jeremiah 17:8 (וְהָיָה כְּעֵץ שָׁתוּל עַל מַיִם וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבֹא חֹם וְהָיָה עָלֵהוּ רַעֲנָן וּבִשְׁנַת בַּצֹּרֶת לֹא יִדְאָג וְלֹא יָמִישׁ מֵעֲשׂוֹת פֶּרִי).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (3:17:5, 3:17:6) places knowledge before understanding; Bartenura says understanding comes first (אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת).
- Vilna spells מרובה, מרובין, מועטין, יבא, שאפילו, חום and בצורת for מְרֻבָּה, מְרֻבִּין, מֻעָטִין, יָבוֹא, שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ, חֹם and בַּצֹּרֶת; in the citations it adds the verse number ו (Jeremiah 17:6) and reads ירמיה יז ח (Jeremiah 17:8) for שם.
- מְרֻבָּה: Vilna reads מרובה (spelling)
- מְרֻבִּין: Vilna reads מרובין (spelling)
- מֻעָטִין: Vilna reads מועטין (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads ו (word)
- יָבוֹא: Vilna reads יבא (spelling)
- מְרֻבִּין: Vilna reads מרובין (spelling)
- מֻעָטִין: Vilna reads מועטין (spelling)
- מְרֻבִּין: Vilna reads מרובין (spelling)
- שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ: Vilna reads שאפילו (spelling)
- שם: Vilna reads ירמיה יז ח (word)
- חֹם: Vilna reads חום (spelling)
- בַּצֹּרֶת: Vilna reads בצורת (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 3:18

> רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן חִסְמָא אוֹמֵר, קִנִּין וּפִתְחֵי נִדָּה, הֵן הֵן גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת. תְּקוּפוֹת וְגִימַטְרִיאוֹת, פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת לַחָכְמָה:

**Rabbi Eliezer son of Hisma says: Bird offerings and the openings of the menstruant, these very things are the essentials of the laws. Astronomical cycles and gematria are the desserts of wisdom.**

Literal: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Hisma says: nests and-openings-of menstruant, they they bodies-of laws. Cycles and-gematriot, desserts to-the-wisdom.

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |

| אֱלִיעֶזֶר | Eliezer | אֱלִיעֶזֶר |  | noun (proper name, person, masculine) |  |
| בֶּן | son of | בֵּן | בנה | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| חִסְמָא | Hisma | חִסְמָא |  | noun (proper name, person, masculine) |  |
| אוֹמֵר | says | אָמַר | אמר | verb (qal, participle active, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.1 |
| קִנִּין | nests (bird offerings) — קִנִּין, literally 'nests': the bird offerings (turtledoves and pigeons) of the Temple, from קֵן 'nest' (Bartenura). | קֵן | קנן | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| וּפִתְחֵי | and openings of — פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה: 'openings of the menstruant': the laws of a woman who has lost track of her cycle and must keep watch until she returns to her opening (Bartenura). Rabbeinu Yonah also mentions three places (a house, an upper room, a hall) and the many appearances of blood. | ו: and + פֶּתַח | פתח | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) | 1 |
| נִדָּה | menstruant | נִדָּה | נדה | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1.1.2 |

| הֵן | they | הֵן |  | pronoun (personal pronoun, 3rd person, common, plural) |  |

| הֲלָכוֹת | laws | הֲלָכָה | הלך | noun (common, feminine, plural, absolute) | 4 |
| תְּקוּפוֹת | cycles — תְּקוּפוֹת: 'cycles, turnings', i.e. astronomical cycles, the course of the constellations (Bartenura). | תְּקוּפָה | קוף | noun (common, feminine, plural, absolute) | 1 |
| וְגִימַטְרִיאוֹת | and gematria — גִּימַטְרִיָּה: gematria, the counting of the numerical values of letters (a Greek loanword). | ו: and + גִּימַטְרִיָּה |  | conjunction + noun (common, feminine, plural, absolute) |  |
| פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת | desserts — פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת: 'dessert', the sweets eaten at the end of a meal (Bartenura; Greek loanword). | פַּרְפְּרָה | פרפר | noun (common, feminine, plural, absolute) |  |
| לַחָכְמָה | to wisdom — The preposition ל here means 'for, of': 'the desserts (belonging) to wisdom'. | ל: to, for + חָכְמָה | חכם | preposition + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- Two sentences, each of two coordinated nouns followed by a predicate. The first has a doubled pronoun, הֵן הֵן, which marks emphasis: 'these, indeed these'. The second has no pronoun at all; the predicate is the single noun פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת.
- קִנִּין is the plural of קֵן ('nest') used as a technical term for bird offerings. פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה is a construct chain, 'openings of the menstruant'.
- גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת is a construct chain: 'bodies of laws', meaning the core or essentials.
- גִּימַטְרִיאוֹת and פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת are Greek loan words that the mishnah uses as technical terms; תְּקוּפוֹת is Hebrew, from the root קוף/נקף 'to go around' (Jastrow: 'turn, cycle'). The contrast of גּוּף ('body') with פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת ('after-dishes') is the point of the saying: the essential versus the ornamental.

Note: Two choices to record. פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה: the English keeps the literal 'the openings of the menstruant' because the sense of 'openings' is not simple (Bartenura: her opening or onset; Rabbeinu Yonah: three places in the house, and many appearances of blood). קִנִּין is rendered 'bird offerings' following Bartenura, with the literal 'nests' in the gloss. פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת is 'desserts' following Bartenura's image of the sweets eaten at the end of a meal, which continues the meal metaphor of the previous mishnah. The default Jastrow entry גּוּף I is the verb 'to squeeze'; the noun is jastrow:גּוּף II, sense 2 'essence'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the bird offerings are called קִנִּין, from 'a bird's nest' (קַן צִפּוֹר); they contain weighty laws, for example when an obligatory offering is mixed with a freewill one, or a burnt offering (whose rites are above) with a sin offering (whose rites are below).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the laws of a menstruant woman who has lost her regular time and must keep watch until she returns to her 'opening'; sometimes she must immerse ninety-five times, according to the view that immersion at its proper time is a commandment.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: these are the core of the Oral Torah, for which one receives reward.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: תְּקוּפוֹת concerns the course of the constellations.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: גִּימַטְרִיאוֹת is the counting of letters.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: as the dessert eaten at the end of a meal for the sake of cleansing the palate and enjoyment, so these branches of wisdom bring honor to those who know them in the eyes of people.

Apparatus:

- Vilna spells קינין for קִנִּין and וגמטריאות for וְגִימַטְרִיאוֹת.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (3:18:1) gives the name as רבי אלעזר חסמא (Rabbi Elazar Hisma), against the base text רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן חִסְמָא, and glosses קִנִּים as the nests of doves of women who have given birth.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (3:18:3) cites Bava Metzia 84b: sixty colors of blood were brought before him and he ruled all of them pure blood.
- קִנִּין: Vilna reads קינין (spelling)
- וְגִימַטְרִיאוֹת: Vilna reads וגמטריאות (spelling)

## Chapter 4 — פֶּרֶק ד (Pirkei Avot 4:1–4:22)

### Reading text

<sup>4:1</sup> Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? One who learns from every person, as it is said: "From all my teachers I have gained insight, for Your testimonies are my meditation." Who is mighty? One who subdues his impulse, as it is said: "Better is one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city." Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion, as it is said: "When you eat the toil of your hands, happy are you, and it is well with you." "Happy are you": in this world. "And it is well with you": in the world to come. Who is honored? One who honors people, as it is said: "For those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be lightly esteemed."

<sup>4:2</sup> Ben Azzai says: Run to a light commandment as to a weighty one, and flee from transgression. For a commandment draws a commandment, and a transgression draws a transgression. For the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression.

<sup>4:3</sup> He used to say: Do not be contemptuous of any person, and do not dismiss any thing as remote; for there is no person who has no hour, and no thing that has no place.

<sup>4:4</sup> Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says: Be very, very humble of spirit, for the hope of man is the worm. Rabbi Yohanan son of Beroka says: Whoever profanes the name of Heaven in secret, payment is exacted from him in the open. Whether unwitting or willful, in profaning the Name.

<sup>4:5</sup> Rabbi Ishmael, his son, says: One who learns Torah in order to teach, they enable him to learn and to teach. And one who learns in order to do, they enable him to learn and to teach, to keep and to do. Rabbi Zadok says: Do not make them a crown to exalt yourself with, nor a spade to dig with. And thus Hillel used to say: "And he who makes use of the crown passes away." Hence you have learned: whoever derives benefit from the words of Torah takes his life from the world.

<sup>4:6</sup> Rabbi Yose says: Whoever honors the Torah, his body is honored by people. And whoever profanes the Torah, his body is profaned by people.

<sup>4:7</sup> Rabbi Ishmael his son says: One who holds himself back from judging removes from himself enmity, robbery, and a vain oath. But one who is overbold of heart in giving rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit.

<sup>4:8</sup> He used to say: Do not judge alone, for none judges alone but One. And do not say, "Accept my opinion," for they are permitted, and you are not.

<sup>4:9</sup> Rabbi Jonathan says: Whoever fulfills the Torah from poverty will in the end fulfill it from wealth. And whoever neglects the Torah from wealth will in the end neglect it from poverty.

<sup>4:10</sup> Rabbi Meir says: Limit your business, and engage in the Torah. And be humble of spirit before every person. And if you neglect the Torah, you have many idle ones against you. And if you toil in the Torah, He has much reward to give you.

<sup>4:11</sup> Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says: One who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate. And one who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser. Repentance and good deeds are like a shield before punishment. Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker says: Every assembly that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure.

<sup>4:12</sup> Rabbi Eleazar son of Shammua says: Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, and the honor of your colleague like the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher like the reverence for Heaven.

<sup>4:13</sup> Rabbi Yehuda says: Be careful in study, for an error in study counts as deliberate sin. Rabbi Shimon says: There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of kingship; but the crown of a good name rises above them.

<sup>4:14</sup> Rabbi Nehorai says: Go into exile to a place of Torah, and do not say that it will come after you, that your colleagues will establish it in your hand. And do not lean on your own understanding.

<sup>4:15</sup> Rabbi Yannai says: It is not in our hands: not the tranquility of the wicked, nor yet the suffering of the righteous. Rabbi Matya son of Harash says: Be first to greet every person, and be a tail to lions, and do not be a head to foxes.

<sup>4:16</sup> Rabbi Yaakov says: This world is like a vestibule before the world to come. Prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the great hall.

<sup>4:17</sup> He used to say: Better is one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world than all the life of the world to come. And better is one hour of spiritual contentment in the world to come than all the life of this world.

<sup>4:18</sup> Rabbi Shimon son of Elazar says: Do not appease your fellow at the time of his anger, and do not comfort him at the time when his dead lies before him, and do not question him at the time of his vow, and do not strive to see him at the time of his disgrace.

<sup>4:19</sup> Samuel the Small says: When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, let your heart not be glad, lest the Lord see it, and it displease Him, and He turn His anger away from him.

<sup>4:20</sup> Elisha son of Avuyah says: One who learns as a child, to what is he compared? To ink written on new paper. And one who learns as an old man, to what is he compared? To ink written on erased paper. Rabbi Yose son of Yehudah, a man of Kefar HaBavli, says: One who learns from the young, to what is he compared? To one who eats unripe grapes and drinks wine from its winepress. And one who learns from the old, to what is he compared? To one who eats ripe grapes and drinks aged wine. Rabbi says: Do not look at the jar, but at what is in it. There is a new jar full of old wine, and an old one in which there is not even new.

<sup>4:21</sup> Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: Envy, desire, and honor take a person out of the world.

<sup>4:22</sup> He used to say: Those who are born are to die, and the dead are to be revived, and the living are to be judged; to know, to make known, and to come to know that He is God, He is the Former, He is the Creator, He is the Discerner, He is the Judge, He is the Witness, He is the Plaintiff, and He is destined to judge. Blessed is He, before whom there is no injustice, no forgetfulness, no partiality, and no taking of bribes, for everything is His. And know that everything is according to the reckoning. And do not let your impulse assure you that Sheol is a place of refuge for you, for against your will you were formed, and against your will you were born, and against your will you live, and against your will you die, and against your will you are destined to give judgment and account before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

### Chapter 4 by mishnah

#### Pirkei Avot 4:1

> בֶּן זוֹמָא אוֹמֵר, אֵיזֶהוּ חָכָם, הַלּוֹמֵד מִכָּל אָדָם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים קיט) מִכָּל מְלַמְּדַי הִשְׂכַּלְתִּי כִּי עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שִׂיחָה לִּי. אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר, הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (משלי טז) טוֹב אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם מִגִּבּוֹר וּמשֵׁל בְּרוּחוֹ מִלֹּכֵד עִיר. אֵיזֶהוּ עָשִׁיר, הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים קכח) יְגִיעַ כַּפֶּיךָ כִּי תֹאכֵל אַשְׁרֶיךָ וְטוֹב לָךְ. אַשְׁרֶיךָ, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה. וְטוֹב לָךְ, לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא. אֵיזֶהוּ מְכֻבָּד, הַמְכַבֵּד אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמואל א ב) כִּי מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ:

**Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? One who learns from every person, as it is said: "From all my teachers I have gained insight, for Your testimonies are my meditation." Who is mighty? One who subdues his impulse, as it is said: "Better is one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city." Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion, as it is said: "When you eat the toil of your hands, happy are you, and it is well with you." "Happy are you": in this world. "And it is well with you": in the world to come. Who is honored? One who honors people, as it is said: "For those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be lightly esteemed."**

Grammar:

- The saying has four parallel questions, each introduced by אֵיזֶהוּ ('who is it that...?') and answered by a participle with the article (הַלּוֹמֵד, הַכּוֹבֵשׁ, הַשָּׂמֵחַ, הַמְכַבֵּד): 'the one who learns', 'the one who subdues'. The participle with the article serves as a relative clause.
- Each answer is closed by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ('as it is said') and a verse from the Bible; the verses are quoted in their biblical form, so Psalm 119 and 128 address God and the hearer directly, with biblical forms (עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ; לָךְ, the pausal form of the masculine לְךָ) that are not mishnaic Hebrew.
- Proverbs 16:32 is built on מִ of comparison, doubled: טוֹב אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם מִגִּבּוֹר וּמֹשֵׁל בְּרוּחוֹ מִלֹּכֵד עִיר, 'better the slow-of-anger than the hero, and the ruler over his spirit than the taker of a city'.
- Psalm 128:2: אַשְׁרֶיךָ is a plural construct noun used as an exclamation ('happy are you'). The mishnah splits the verse in two and gives a time to each half: 'in this world' for אַשְׁרֶיךָ and 'in the world to come' for טוֹב לָךְ.
- 1 Samuel 2:30 pairs a Piel participle (מְכַבְּדַי) with the matching Piel imperfect (אֲכַבֵּד); the verb root כבד has the sense 'be heavy' and the Piel 'give weight to, honor'. The same root underlies מְכֻבָּד (Pual), 'honored'. יֵקָלּוּ 'will be light' is the opposite of 'heavy'.

Note: The four questions are answered with the verb in a participle; I kept the form 'One who...' so that each answer stays as brief as the Hebrew. 'Impulse' for יֵצֶר: the inclination of a person's mind and desires, neither good nor evil by the word alone. 'Honored' (מְכֻבָּד) is passive: honored by others, not 'honorable'. Bartenura's reading of מִלֹּכֵד עִיר (see commentary entry 4:1:5) takes the min as 'coming from', and I record it. The Psalm's 'happy are you' and 'well with you' have no verb in Hebrew, and the English likewise has none for 'it is well'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since he did not live long and was not ordained to be called 'Rabbi', they called him by his father's name, as with Ben Azzai; both were named Shimon. The English keeps Ben Zoma as a name.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'so he says: who is wise, such that it is fitting for him to be praised for his wisdom?' The question asks who deserves the title, not who has knowledge; the English keeps the plain question.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'even if he is smaller than he'; since he does not spare his honor and learns from the young, it is clear that his wisdom is for the sake of Heaven and not to be proud. 'Every person' therefore includes those lesser than oneself.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the end of the verse, כִּי עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שִׂיחָה לִי, means 'I learned Torah from all my teachers, even the younger ones, without regard for my honor, because my whole intention was for Heaven alone'; similarly the one who is fit to boast of his heroism is the one who subdues his impulse.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: the verse means 'better is the patience that comes from the heroism of conquering the impulse, not from a soft nature'; and 'one who rules his spirit' when 'he comes from capturing a city', the king who has taken the city and the men who rebelled are in his hand, yet rules his spirit and does not kill them. This reads the min as 'coming from', not as comparison; the English keeps the comparison of the verse.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the one for whom it is fitting to boast of his wealth is the one who rejoices in his portion.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: the three good things named so far, wisdom, might and wealth, make the one who has them honored in the eyes of God and man by himself; so the tanna joins this: he who has these traits and is honored in himself, what shall he do to be honored by others? Let him honor people. It explains why the fourth saying follows; it does not change the words.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: an a fortiori argument: if the Holy One, who is the King of Glory and created all things only for His glory, honors those who honor Him, how much more flesh and blood.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: we learn the humility of the Holy One; He does not say 'those who despise Me I will curse' but 'they will be lightly esteemed' of themselves (the passive); and He is more strict over the honor of the righteous, as in Gen 12:3 וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: 'this is clear, and we already mentioned its matter in the preceding chapters'. The comment is on the whole mishnah (its DH is the word זה 'this' of his own sentence), not on הַזֶּה; it adds nothing to the English.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not-applicable): Rabbeinu Yonah: an 'erekh appayim' is one who holds back his anger and does not want to take revenge at once, but waits for a time and a place to take it; the hot-tempered man who avenges himself at once spoils his deeds and acts without understanding. A moral gloss, not a reading of the words.

Apparatus:

- Prov 16:32 (Vilna adds לב): טוֹב אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם מִגִּבּוֹר וּמֹשֵׁל בְּרוּחוֹ מִלֹּכֵד עִיר.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:2

> בֶּן עַזַּאי אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי רָץ לְמִצְוָה קַלָּה כְבַחֲמוּרָה, וּבוֹרֵחַ מִן הָעֲבֵרָה. שֶׁמִּצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה, וַעֲבֵרָה גוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵרָה. שֶׁשְּׂכַר מִצְוָה, מִצְוָה. וּשְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה, עֲבֵרָה:

**Ben Azzai says: Run to a light commandment as to a weighty one, and flee from transgression. For a commandment draws a commandment, and a transgression draws a transgression. For the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression.**

Grammar:

- הֱוֵי is an imperative of 'be' (an Aramaic-style form common in the sayings); with the participle רָץ it means 'be running', i.e. 'run'. The two commands are parallel: 'run to...' and 'flee from...' (בּוֹרֵחַ is also a participle).
- קַלָּה and חֲמוּרָה are feminine adjectives agreeing with מִצְוָה; the second is used alone with כְּ + בְּ: 'as to a weighty one'.
- The reasons come in two clauses with שֶׁ ('for'), each a pair of short sentences: 'a commandment draws a commandment, and a transgression draws a transgression'; 'the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression'. The second pair has no verb 'is': the two nouns are placed side by side.
- גּוֹרֶרֶת is a feminine participle of גרר, literally 'drag' (Jastrow 3), here 'draw along, bring after it'.

Note: שְׂכַר is 'reward' (wages), and the saying is left as brief as the Hebrew: the reward of a commandment is a commandment. The ambiguity is kept: either the result is another commandment given to the doer (Bartenura's first reading) or the pleasure taken in the act is counted as a commandment (his second). I did not choose between them in the English.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: it is the way of the world that one who has done one commandment finds it easy to do others, and one who starts on transgressions finds it hard to leave them; also, Heaven helps and arranges that he who has done one commandment does another, in order to give him reward for both. Another explanation: whatever pleasure a man takes in doing a commandment is counted as a commandment of its own, and he takes reward for the commandment and for the pleasure he enjoyed in doing it.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: the gain and enjoyment that come to a man in doing the transgression is counted as a transgression in itself; he is punished for the transgression and for the profit and enjoyment he received. This is the second explanation of the two sayings on reward; the English keeps the plain saying, which can be read either way.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam refers to his explanation in Sanhedrin ch. 10 and gives the example of Moses, who set apart three cities across the Jordan though they did not yet take effect: 'since a commandment came to my hand, I will do it'. An illustration of the first clause, not a reading of the words.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:3

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, אַל תְּהִי בָז לְכָל אָדָם, וְאַל תְּהִי מַפְלִיג לְכָל דָּבָר, שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שָׁעָה וְאֵין לְךָ דָבָר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מָקוֹם:

- Two parallel prohibitions with אַל and the jussive תְּהִי + a predicate (בָז; מַפְלִיג, a Hiphil participle). Both are followed by לְכָל, 'of any'.
- The reason has the idiom שֶׁאֵין לְךָ X שֶׁאֵין לוֹ Y, 'there is no X that has no Y': the 'to you' (לְךָ) is not translated; literally 'for you have no person who has not his hour'.
- The word מָקוֹם 'place' is a different word from the divine name הַמָּקוֹם in the decisions; here it means 'a place, a role'.

Note: מַפְלִיג has several senses in Jastrow (put off, go too far, speak indefinitely, reject). Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah gloss it as 'regards as distant, far-fetched': 'it is far off that it will happen, no need to worry', so I chose 'dismiss as remote'. Another reading, 'speak too lightly of anything', would also fit the Hebrew, and I did not use it. שָׁעָה 'hour' is a short time, the moment when a person (or thing) counts, as the commentators say: a time when he can harm or help.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'to say, what can so-and-so do to harm me?' Contempt for a person is the belief that he can do no harm.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: מַפְלִיג is 'keeps at a distance' (מַרְחִיק) regarding every matter about which one should be careful: do not say 'it is far off that it will be, and there is nothing to worry about'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: it is impossible that there is not for every person a time when he can harm or benefit, even in a small thing.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'that he can harm or benefit, a little or a lot': the hour is a time of power to do either.

Apparatus:

- No biblical quotation in this mishnah.
- No variants are noted in the pack for this mishnah.
