Grammar:

- רַבִּי is 'my master' with the pronominal suffix frozen into the title; אִישׁ יַבְנֶה is 'man of Yavneh', here 'of Yavneh'. The Latin name לְוִיטָס is Levitas.
- מְאֹד מְאֹד הֱוֵי שְׁפַל רוּחַ: the repeated adverb stands before the imperative. שְׁפַל רוּחַ is a construct chain with an adjective, 'low of spirit'. The reason שֶׁתִּקְוַת אֱנוֹשׁ רִמָּה has no verb: 'the hope of man (is) the worm'.
- כָּל הַמְחַלֵּל ... נִפְרָעִין מִמֶּנּוּ: a casus pendens. The subject is stated first ('whoever profanes...') and then picked up by the pronoun on מִמֶּנּוּ. נִפְרָעִין is an impersonal Nifal participle plural, 'they exact payment' in the passive.
- אֶחָד שׁוֹגֵג וְאֶחָד מֵזִיד: the pattern 'one X and one Y' means 'X and Y alike', with the predicate unspoken. בְּחִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם gives the context, 'in the case of profaning the Name'.

Note: תִּקְוַת אֱנוֹשׁ: 'the hope of man' can mean 'what man hopes for in the end' (the worm) or 'the expectation of man is for the worm'; Rabbeinu Yonah reads the end of man as the worm, which is the sense kept. For אֶחָד שׁוֹגֵג וְאֶחָד מֵזִיד I kept the ellipsis; Rambam (4:4:2) explains that in both cases payment is exacted openly, each for its own kind of offense, so the pair is 'alike' as to the open exaction, not as to the amount. 'The Name' is the divine name, as in 'profaning the Name'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: although in other traits the middle way is praised, pride is different; one should lean to the extreme of humility, because pride is most detestable and most people stumble in it; so make an extra distance from it. This is why the doubled מְאֹד.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: humility is a middle trait between pride and lowness of spirit, but for pride alone the pious went to the opposite extreme; hence the sage said 'very, very be low of spirit', 'because the end of the body is the worm'. The English keeps the extreme.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the unwitting has sin, so it needs atonement by a sacrifice, but is not like the willful; the meaning of the mishnah is that for profaning the Name, whether unwitting or willful, payment is exacted in the open: the punishment of the willful for the willful, of the unwitting for the unwitting, but both punishments are open.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: not that they exact payment for the unwitting as for the willful, but even for the unwitting they exact payment openly, each according to his sin.

Apparatus:

- No biblical quotation in this mishnah.
- No variants are noted in the pack for this mishnah. Rabbeinu Yonah (4:4:4-5) reads 'in secret' as profaning the Name by an act that is itself a profanation, such as a false oath.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:5

> רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ אוֹמֵר, הַלּוֹמֵד תּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לְלַמֵּד, מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לִלְמֹד וּלְלַמֵּד. וְהַלּוֹמֵד עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת, מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לִלְמֹד וּלְלַמֵּד לִשְׁמֹר וְלַעֲשׂוֹת. רַבִּי צָדוֹק אוֹמֵר, אַל תַּעֲשֵׂם עֲטָרָה לְהִתְגַּדֵּל בָּהֶם, וְלֹא קַרְדֹּם לַחְפֹּר בָּהֶם. וְכָךְ הָיָה הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר, וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּתָגָא, חָלָף. הָא לָמַדְתָּ, כָּל הַנֶּהֱנֶה מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם:

**Rabbi Ishmael, his son, says: One who learns Torah in order to teach, they enable him to learn and to teach. And one who learns in order to do, they enable him to learn and to teach, to keep and to do. Rabbi Zadok says: Do not make them a crown to exalt yourself with, nor a spade to dig with. And thus Hillel used to say: "And he who makes use of the crown passes away." Hence you have learned: whoever derives benefit from the words of Torah takes his life from the world.**

Literal: my-master Ishmael son-of-him says the-one-learning Torah upon portion-of to-teach they-supply in-hand-of-him to-learn and-to-teach and-the-one-learning upon portion-of to-do they-supply in-hand-of-him to-learn and-to-teach to-keep and-to-do my-master Zadok says not you-make-them crown to-make-oneself-great in-them and-not spade to-dig in-them and-thus was Hillel saying and-who-used in-crown passed-away behold you-learned all-of the-one-deriving-benefit from-words-of Torah taking lives-of-him from the-world

Grammar:

- The first two sayings are in parallel: הַלּוֹמֵד עַל מְנָת לְ... מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ ...; the subject is a participle with the article, the verb is an impersonal plural participle (מַסְפִּיקִין, 'they enable'), and the aims are infinitives with לְ. The second saying adds 'to keep and to do'.
- אַל תַּעֲשֵׂם ... וְלֹא קַרְדֹּם: a prohibition with אַל and the imperfect; the second clause, with וְלֹא, takes its verb from the first ('nor (make them) a spade'). The suffix -ם 'them' stands for the words of the Torah, to which the prior saying referred.
- Hillel's saying וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּתָגָא חָלָף is in Aramaic: the relative דְּ, the Ithpaal perfect אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, תָּגָא 'crown' with the Aramaic ending -ā, and the verb at the end. Rabbeinu Yonah notes 'tagā means crown, as in the Targum'.
- הָא לָמַדְתָּ ('behold, you have learned') introduces the conclusion drawn by the editor from Hillel's saying; כָּל הַנֶּהֱנֶה is again 'whoever + participle'. נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם is a participle, the present of a general rule: 'takes his life out of the world'.
- The word חַיָּיו is plural in form (חַיִּים 'life') and has a singular sense; מִן הָעוֹלָם 'from the world' needs the world to come in the Rambam's reading.

Note: עַל מְנָת: 'in order to, with the intention of' (literally 'on the portion of'). The mishnah's first two sayings are about intent: in each case the aim of the learning decides what he is enabled to do. The reading 'they enable' is Bartenura's majority text; he records another text, 'one who learns in order to teach, they do not enable him to learn and to teach', for those who take 'to teach' as 'in order to be called Rabbi'; I follow the majority text. קַרְדֹּם is 'spade' (the tool named with לַחְפֹּר 'to dig'); Rabbeinu Yonah's variant 'to cut' (לַחְתֹּךְ) would make it an axe. נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם: Rambam says 'his life from the world', i.e. from the life of the world to come; I kept the literal words and give the gloss here.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'we read': one who learns in order always to be occupied with Torah, with no intention to do acts of kindness, they enable his intention to be done, to learn and to teach; one who learns in order to do, wanting to be occupied with Torah and also to do kindness, they enable him to complete his intention and he merits to learn, teach, keep and do. Some explain 'to teach' as 'to be called Rabbi' and read 'they do not enable him'; but in most books he found the first reading, which is the main one.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'so that you do not say, I will learn so that I be called Rabbi and they seat me at the head, but learn from love, and in the end honor will come.'
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not learn Torah to make from it a trade by which to live, like a spade to dig with; whoever does so misuses the holiness of the Torah and is liable to death at the hands of Heaven, like one who benefits from the Temple's consecrated property. Teachers of children take only the wages of watching the children and of teaching the cantillation, not for teaching itself.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'do not make the Torah a spade to dig with' means do not regard it as an instrument to live by; he who benefits in this world from the honor of the Torah 'takes his life from the world', that is, from the life of the world to come. He devotes a long defense of sages who lived by a trade, not by the community's money, and tells the story of R. Tarfon.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'tagā is a word for a crown, as its Targum.'

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah's own text (4:5:1) reads 'Rabbi Shimon his son'; the editor's bracket in it notes that our text reads 'Rabbi Ishmael'. The base text here has Rabbi Ishmael.
- Vilna spelling variants: ללמוד (4:5.12, 4:5.20), לשמור (4:5.22), קרדום (4:5.33), לחפור (4:5.34), ודישתמש (4:5.40, for the base וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ); the pack also shows that Vilna has no word at 4:5.6 where the base has תּוֹרָה.
- Bartenura's variant text: 'one who learns in order to teach: they do not enable him to learn and to teach' (taking לְלַמֵּד as 'in order to be called Rabbi'); he follows the reading in most books.
- תּוֹרָה: Vilna reads — (word)
- לִלְמֹד: Vilna reads ללמוד (spelling)
- לִלְמֹד: Vilna reads ללמוד (spelling)
- לִשְׁמֹר: Vilna reads לשמור (spelling)
- קַרְדֹּם: Vilna reads קרדום (spelling)
- לַחְפֹּר: Vilna reads לחפור (spelling)
- וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ: Vilna reads ודישתמש (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:6

> רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, כָּל הַמְכַבֵּד אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, גּוּפוֹ מְכֻבָּד עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת. וְכָל הַמְחַלֵּל אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, גּוּפוֹ מְחֻלָּל עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת:

**Rabbi Yose says: Whoever honors the Torah, his body is honored by people. And whoever profanes the Torah, his body is profaned by people.**

Grammar:

- Two antithetical sayings, one with מְכַבֵּד / מְכֻבָּד (root כבד, Piel / Pual) and one with מְחַלֵּל / מְחֻלָּל (root חלל, Piel / Pual). In each, the Piel participle with the article after כָּל is the subject, and the Pual participle is the predicate of the main clause (a casus pendens: 'whoever honors..., his body is honored').
- The two verbs are opposites: כבד 'give weight to', חלל 'treat as common, make profane'. The second saying keeps the same word order to make the contrast plain.
- עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת, literally 'upon the creatures', stands for the agent: 'honored by people', 'in the eyes of people'. The word גּוּף 'body' with the suffix is a way to say 'he himself, his person'.
- The verb חִלֵּל is the same as in 4:4 (חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם): to profane the Name and to profane the Torah are both 'make common'.

Note: גּוּפוֹ is 'his body' in the Hebrew, and I kept it, though it can be read as 'he himself'; Rabbeinu Yonah explains that Heaven helps people to honor him (or to despise him), i.e. 'body' is the person in the eyes of others. 'By people' for עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת: literally 'upon the creatures', the persons in whose eyes the honor is held.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who expounds the extra and missing letters of the Torah and shows a reason for every point, saying nothing in it is superfluous, no greater honor to the Torah; or one who honors a Torah scroll and those who learn and engage in it; all these are 'one who honors the Torah'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the honor of the Torah is shown by zeal in doing it, and by honoring the sages who uphold it and the books they wrote on it; and the profaning of the Torah is the opposite.

Apparatus:

- No biblical quotation in this mishnah.
- Vilna spelling variants: מכובד (4:6.9), מחולל (4:6.17), for the base's מְכֻבָּד and מְחֻלָּל.
- מְכֻבָּד: Vilna reads מכובד (spelling)
- מְחֻלָּל: Vilna reads מחולל (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:7

**Rabbi Ishmael his son says: One who holds himself back from judging removes from himself enmity, robbery, and a vain oath. But one who is overbold of heart in giving rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit.**

Grammar:

- הַחוֹשֵׂךְ and הַגַּס are articular participle and adjective used as subjects: 'the one who holds back', 'the one who is coarse'.
- The first sentence gives a cause and its three results, enmity, robbery and a vain oath; the second sets the opposite case, with three damning terms.
- גַּס לִבּוֹ is a subject-predicate phrase: 'coarse of heart'; גַּס רוּחַ is a construct chain: 'coarse of spirit'.
- Rabbi Ishmael is called 'his son': the son of Rabbi Yose in 4:6.

Note: Rabbi Ishmael 'his son' is, by Rabbeinu Yonah's heading, the son of Rabbi Yose in 4:6. Bartenura and Rambam give the sense of גַּס לִבּוֹ בַהוֹרָאָה as giving rulings without study or fear, and the English 'overbold' follows that; the literal sense is 'coarse of heart'. שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא is 'a vain oath', which keeps both of Bartenura's readings. גַּס is Jastrow's גַּס III ('bulky, coarse') and עַצְמוֹ Jastrow's עֶצֶם ('self').

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one holds back where there is a greater person present, or tells the litigants to compromise.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: whoever leaves the court as the losing party hates the judge, saying in his heart that the judge did not turn the case in his favor.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the judge might hold the innocent party liable, so that a robbery comes about through him.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the judge might impose an oath on one not liable to it and so bring about a false oath; or the tanna calls a lying oath 'an oath of falsehood'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he rules 'without examination and without waiting', which gives 'overbold' for גַּס לִבּוֹ.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'his heart is coarse in rulings, emboldened to give rulings without awe and fear'.

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma reads 'Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose'; the pack's base text has only 'his son'.
- Rabbeinu Yonah cites Deut 16:18-20 and the duty to judge, answered by 'where there are no other judges'.

- שֶׁאֵין דָּן יְחִידִי אֶלָּא אֶחָד: 'there is none judging alone except One'; the play is on יְחִידִי and אֶחָד.
- שֶׁהֵן רַשָּׁאִין: the word רַשַּׁאי is the Mishnaic adjective 'authorized'.

Note: 'None judges alone but One': Bartenura reads אֶחָד as the Holy One; the English keeps 'One' with a capital so the ambiguity of 'one man' is not lost. דָּן is the participle of דין (Jastrow דִּין I), not the name Dan.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even an expert who may judge alone should not, as a way of piety, unless the parties have accepted him; then he may.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'One' is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is alone in His world.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'do not say' to your colleagues who disagree with you.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'accept my opinion' means 'I am an expert and could have judged without your joining'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since you joined them with you, the ruling should be decided by the majority.

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah brings a second explanation of 'except One': the expert (mumhe) alone may judge, but others should not count themselves experts.
- Rambam on this mishnah (anchored at 4:9 in the pack): the Torah lets an expert judge alone; the warning is moral counsel, not a prohibition; colleagues who disagree may not be forced to accept your view, for it is not in your power to compel them.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:9

> רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר, כָּל הַמְקַיֵּם אֶת הַתּוֹרָה מֵעֹנִי, סוֹפוֹ לְקַיְּמָהּ מֵעשֶׁר. וְכָל הַמְבַטֵּל אֶת הַתּוֹרָה מֵעשֶׁר, סוֹפוֹ לְבַטְּלָהּ מֵעֹנִי:

**Rabbi Jonathan says: Whoever fulfills the Torah from poverty will in the end fulfill it from wealth. And whoever neglects the Torah from wealth will in the end neglect it from poverty.**

Literal: Rabbi Jonathan saying: every the-fulfilling the-Torah from-poverty, his-end to-fulfill-it from-wealth. And-every the-neglecting the-Torah from-wealth, his-end to-neglect-it from-poverty.

Grammar:

- The two halves are in chiastic parallel: fulfilling from poverty leads to fulfilling from wealth; neglecting from wealth leads to neglecting from poverty.
- מֵעֹנִי and מֵעשֶׁר: the מִן is of the circumstance, 'out of'.
- The suffix הָ on לְקַיְּמָהּ refers to the Torah, which is feminine.
- סוֹפוֹ לְ + infinitive means 'his end is to ...', 'he will end by ...'.

Note: 'Fulfills' and 'neglects' are chosen from Bartenura and Rambam: studying Torah under the pressure of need, as against leaving it for the preoccupation of wealth. The pack's lexicon entries for קְיָם ('decree') and עָשַׂר (tithing verb) do not fit קִיֵּם and עֹשֶׁר.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: from poverty means he is pressed for food and leaves his work to engage in Torah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: from wealth means that for the abundance of money he must turn his heart one way and another and has no leisure for Torah.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam (filed at 4:8): the Torah allowed an expert to judge alone; the mishnah warns only as a moral counsel; colleagues who disagree cannot be forced. It bears on 4:8, not on the words of 4:9.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: one who studies Torah in poverty will in the end study it in wealth, free of distraction; one who neglects it for the sake of abundance will become poor, and his trouble to find bread will cause his neglect.

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads המקיים, מעוני, לקיימה, מעושר (twice) and מעוני; the base text has the short spellings. No difference of meaning.
- Rabbeinu Yonah cites Prov 30:8, 'give me neither poverty nor riches'.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:10

> רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי מְמַעֵט בְּעֵסֶק, וַעֲסֹק בַּתּוֹרָה. וֶהֱוֵי שְׁפַל רוּחַ בִּפְנֵי כָל אָדָם. וְאִם בָּטַלְתָּ מִן הַתּוֹרָה, יֶשׁ לְךָ בְטֵלִים הַרְבֵּה כְנֶגְדָּךְ. וְאִם עָמַלְתָּ בַתּוֹרָה, יֶשׁ לוֹ שָׂכָר הַרְבֵּה לִתֶּן לָךְ:

- בְטֵלִים הַרְבֵּה is 'many idle ones'; הַרְבֵּה is a Hifil infinitive absolute used as an adverb or adjective.
- יֶשׁ לוֹ ... לִתֶּן is 'he has ... to give': a possessive idiom with an infinitive.

Note: בְטֵלִים is kept as 'idle ones': Bartenura offers two readings, those who help make you idle, and the wicked and beasts who are idle, by whom the Holy One brings punishment. Rabbeinu Yonah has the second. The English keeps the plain word. 'He has' keeps the Hebrew shift to the third person; Bartenura reads God as the subject.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: reduce your trade and work, and let your main occupation be Torah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: be humble in order to learn even from one lesser than you in wisdom. Rambam reads it more widely, humble even with the great and the small.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura gives two readings: those who help to make you idle, or the idle wicked and beasts through whom the Holy One brings punishment. The English keeps the plain 'idle ones'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: He Himself pays your reward, not through a messenger; thus the measure of good exceeds the measure of punishment.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: reduce trade and persist in the Torah; be humble before every person, not only the great, speaking with anyone as if he were greater than you, to flee from pride. 'Many idle ones against you' means many things that cause idleness and demand attention: if you do not engage in the Torah, time will occupy you with one of them.

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads ועסוק and ליתן; base וַעֲסֹק, לִתֶּן.
- Bartenura's second reading of בְטֵלִים, and Rabbeinu Yonah's 'bears and lions idle from work', both rest on the sense 'those who are idle'.
- Rambam reads בְטֵלִים הַרְבֵּה as 'many things that make idle': affairs that demand attention and, if you leave the Torah, will occupy you.
- Bartenura's lemma reads וְאִם עָסַקְתָּ בַתּוֹרָה, 'if you engaged in the Torah', for the base עָמַלְתָּ; Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma has עמלת. Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma also reads הרבה בטלין, with the word order reversed.
- וַעֲסֹק: Vilna reads ועסוק (spelling)
- לִתֶּן: Vilna reads ליתן (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:11

> רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר, הָעוֹשֶׂה מִצְוָה אַחַת, קוֹנֶה לוֹ פְרַקְלִיט אֶחָד. וְהָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵרָה אַחַת, קוֹנֶה לוֹ קַטֵּגוֹר אֶחָד. תְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים, כִּתְרִיס בִּפְנֵי הַפֻּרְעָנוּת. רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הַסַּנְדְּלָר אוֹמֵר, כָּל כְּנֵסִיָּה שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם. וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, אֵין סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם:

**Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says: One who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate. And one who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser. Repentance and good deeds are like a shield before punishment. Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker says: Every assembly that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure.**

Literal: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Jacob saying: the-doing commandment one, acquiring for-him advocate one. And-the-passing transgression one, acquiring for-him accuser one. Repentance and-deeds good, like-shield before-the-retribution. Rabbi Johanan the-sandal-maker saying: every assembly that-it for-name-of Heaven, its-end to-be-established. And-that-not-it for-name-of Heaven, not its-end to-be-established.

Grammar:

- הָעוֹשֶׂה and הָעוֹבֵר are participles with the article used as subjects; קוֹנֶה לוֹ is the predicate.
- פְרַקְלִיט and קַטֵּגוֹר are Greek loanwords (paraklētos, katēgoros); one speaks for, the other against.
- תְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים is a short sentence without a verb: a nominal predicate with כ-.
- With Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker the saying changes: the two halves differ by לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם and its negation.

Note: פְרַקְלִיט and קַטֵּגוֹר are rendered 'advocate' and 'accuser', following Bartenura's 'good intercessor' and 'evil intercessor' and Rambam's court setting before the ruler. פֻּרְעָנוּת is 'punishment'; Rambam says blows and diseases. טוֹב is Jastrow's טוֹב II and שֵׁם Jastrow's שֵׁם II; for קָנָה Jastrow only gives a cross-reference.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: פְרַקְלִיט is an angel who intercedes for good.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: קַטֵּגוֹר is an intercessor for evil; the word comes from 'calling a quarrel', and its opposite סַנֵּגוֹר means 'hating a quarrel'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the פרקליט is the man who speaks well of a person to the ruler; the קטיגור is the opposite, who informs against him to the king and seeks his death. Repentance after evil deeds, or good deeds from the start, each of the two keeps blows and diseases from coming upon a man.

Apparatus:

- Variants: Vilna reads עבירה, קטיגור, הפורענות and להתקיים (twice); base spellings are the short forms.
- Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma 4:13:4 is anchored here in error; it belongs to 4:13.
- עֲבֵרָה: Vilna reads עבירה (spelling)
- קַטֵּגוֹר: Vilna reads קטיגור (spelling)
- הַפֻּרְעָנוּת: Vilna reads הפורענות (spelling)
- לְהִתְקַיֵּם: Vilna reads להתקיים (spelling)
- לְהִתְקַיֵּם: Vilna reads להתקיים (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:12

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן שַׁמּוּעַ אוֹמֵר, יְהִי כְבוֹד תַּלְמִידְךָ חָבִיב עָלֶיךָ כְּשֶׁלְּךָ, וּכְבוֹד חֲבֵרְךָ כְּמוֹרָא רַבְּךָ, וּמוֹרָא רַבְּךָ כְּמוֹרָא שָׁמָיִם:

**Rabbi Eleazar son of Shammua says: Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, and the honor of your colleague like the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher like the reverence for Heaven.**

Grammar:

- יְהִי is the jussive of הָיָה: 'let ... be'.
- The last two clauses form a chain: the 'reverence of your teacher' that ends the second clause begins the third; each clause sets one duty beside a higher one.
- כְּשֶׁלְּךָ uses the Mishnaic particle שֶׁל: 'like that of yours'.
- שָׁמָיִם, with qamets, is the pausal form of שָׁמַיִם at the end of the saying; the noun, plural in form, stands for God.

Note: The three comparisons increase in rank: student, colleague, teacher, Heaven. The decision on שָׁמַיִם, of God, is 'Heaven'. The commentators (Bartenura) bring a verse for each clause; see the apparatus.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Moses made Joshua his student equal to himself, saying 'choose us men'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Aaron said to Moses 'Oh my lord', though Moses was his younger brother, and called him lord.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'my lord Moses, destroy them': whoever rebels against your teacher rebels as if against the Holy One and deserves destruction.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads חבירך for חֲבֵרְךָ.
- Bartenura's verses: Exod 17:9 (Moses to Joshua, 'choose us men'); Num 12:11 (Aaron to Moses, 'Oh my lord'); Num 11:28 (Joshua, 'my lord Moses, destroy them').
- חֲבֵרְךָ: Vilna reads חבירך (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:13

> רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי זָהִיר בַּתַּלְמוּד, שֶׁשִּׁגְגַת תַּלְמוּד עוֹלָה זָדוֹן. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר, שְׁלשָׁה כְתָרִים הֵם, כֶּתֶר תּוֹרָה וְכֶתֶר כְּהֻנָּה וְכֶתֶר מַלְכוּת, וְכֶתֶר שֵׁם טוֹב עוֹלֶה עַל גַּבֵּיהֶן:

**Rabbi Yehuda says: Be careful in study, for an error in study counts as deliberate sin. Rabbi Shimon says: There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of kingship; but the crown of a good name rises above them.**

Literal: Rabbi Yehuda says: be careful in-the-study, for-error-of study rises (to) deliberate-sin. Rabbi Shimon says: three crowns they: crown-of Torah, and-crown-of priesthood, and-crown-of kingship; and-crown-of name good rises over their-backs.

Grammar:

- Two sayings joined in one mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda on care in study, Rabbi Shimon on the three crowns.
- שִׁגְגַת תַּלְמוּד עוֹלָה זָדוֹן: a wordplay of opposites, שְׁגָגָה (inadvertent error) and זָדוֹן (deliberate sin). עוֹלָה is 'rises to the level of, counts as'.
- עוֹלָה / עוֹלֶה: the same verb used twice, first for an error that 'rises' to deliberate sin, then for the good name that 'rises' above the crowns.
- כֶּתֶר is in the construct state throughout: 'crown of Torah', 'crown of priesthood', 'crown of kingship', 'crown of a good name'.
- גַּבֵּיהֶן: the plural of גַּב with the suffix -הֶן, referring to the three crowns. כְּתָרִים is masculine (see שְׁלשָׁה); the Mishnah often writes -ן for the 3rd masculine plural ending.

Note: תַּלְמוּד is rendered 'study' (Bartenura: one's learning done with precision and according to halakha), not the later Talmud. The pack lexicon gives the Jastrow entry for תַּלְמוּד and for זָהִיר. For וְכֶתֶר שֵׁם טוֹב the vav is rendered 'but' because the good name is set against the three crowns above it.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'be careful in study' means that your study should be precise and in accord with halakha.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if you err in a ruling because you were not precise in your study and you permit what is forbidden, the Holy One, blessed be He, counts it against you as if you had acted deliberately.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the three crowns are those written in the Torah, for which the Torah obliges us to show honour.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: of the crown of Torah it is written 'you shall honour the face of an elder' (Lev 19:32); this is one who has acquired wisdom.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: of the crown of priesthood it is written 'you shall sanctify him, he shall be holy to you' (Lev 21:8).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: of the crown of kingship it is written 'you shall surely set a king over yourself' (Deut 17:15), so that his awe is upon you.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the one whose deeds are good and whose reputation is good on their account has no crown in the Torah that obliges honour, yet it rises above all three, because all three need it: a disciple of the sages of ill repute may be disgraced; of a high priest the Gemara (Yoma 71b) says the children of the nations who do Aaron's deeds may come in peace, but not the sons of Aaron who do not; and the king is protected from cursing (Ex 22:27) only when he acts as one of 'your people'.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: one must review one's learning and not rely on a first impression; since error is common in Torah matters, one who does not take care is a negligent sinner rather than an inadvertent one.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not-applicable): Rabbeinu Yonah: priesthood was given to the house of Aaron, kingship to the house of David, while the crown of Torah lies before all who come into the world.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: all the crowns need the crown of a good name, which itself depends on the crown of Torah; he cites 'a good name is better than good oil' (Eccl 7:1).

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads כהונה for כְּהֻנָּה (4:13.20); the sense is the same.
- Lev 19:32; 21:8; Deut 17:15; Eccl 7:1 are cited by the commentators, not by the mishnah.
- כְּהֻנָּה: Vilna reads כהונה (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:14

> רַבִּי נְהוֹרַאי אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי גוֹלֶה לִמְקוֹם תּוֹרָה, וְאַל תֹּאמַר שֶׁהִיא תָבֹא אַחֲרֶיךָ, שֶׁחֲבֵרֶיךָ יְקַיְּמוּהָ בְיָדֶךָ. וְאֶל בִּינָתְךָ אַל תִּשָּׁעֵן (משלי ג):

**Rabbi Nehorai says: Go into exile to a place of Torah, and do not say that it will come after you, that your colleagues will establish it in your hand. And do not lean on your own understanding.**

Literal: Rabbi Nehorai says: be going-into-exile to-place-of Torah, and-not you-say that-she will-come after-you, that-your-colleagues will-establish-her in-your-hand. And-unto your-understanding not you-lean (Proverbs 3).

Grammar:

- The verse quoted at the end, Prov 3:5, is cited in the mishnah by name: משלי ג.
- גּוֹלֶה is a participle after הֱוֵי: 'be one who goes into exile'.
- יְקַיְּמוּהָ: Piel imperfect 3rd masculine plural of קום (Mishnaic קִיֵּם 'make endure, secure'), built with a consonantal yod on the Aramaic pattern, with the 3rd feminine singular suffix -הָ referring to the Torah.
- אַל תֹּאמַר and אַל תִּשָּׁעֵן: negative commands use אַל with the jussive-form imperfect.
- The Hebrew sets the two clauses by position: the move to a place of Torah is paired with the refusal to rely on colleagues, then on one's own insight.

Note: Bartenura (first reading) and Rabbeinu Yonah take the clause שֶׁחֲבֵרֶיךָ יְקַיְּמוּהָ בְיָדֶךָ as what one must not rely on: colleagues who return from the teacher will not secure the Torah for you. Rambam and Bartenura's second reading take it as the reason for going into exile: only with colleagues does learning endure. The English keeps the bare 'that', which follows the first reading most naturally; the second is recorded. In 4:14.16 the corpus links וְאֶל to BDB אַל 'not'; the token is the preposition אֶל (BDB אֵל), set by a lex override. The words משלי ג at the end are a source marker and are not translated into the saying.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: go into exile 'if there are no disciples of the sages in your place'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not say that the disciples of the sages will come here.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not rely on your colleagues, when they come from the master's house, to establish the Torah in your hand by teaching you what they learned; go yourself to the master, for hearing from a disciple is unlike hearing from the master. A second reading: I tell you to go into exile because your colleagues will establish it in your hand, for however sharp you are, the Torah endures in you only through the give and take of colleagues; hence 'do not lean on your own understanding'.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam (anchored on 4:14.18 but on 4:13): the three good qualities, priesthood, kingship and Torah, were given to Israel at the giving of the Torah; Aaron won priesthood and David kingship, but the crown of Torah lies ready for anyone who wants it, and it is greater than the other two ('by me kings reign', Prov 8:15). The crown of a good name comes from the Torah, from knowing it and doing it.
- Rambam (records): Rambam: seek a place of reading and study, for study endures only with others; do not lean on your own understanding and say you need no colleagues and pupils to rouse you.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: live in a place with much Torah and many sages.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not rely on colleagues who have gone to study to come and teach you; you yourself must go into exile with them and pursue the Torah.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: even when you have studied and gone into exile to a place of Torah and become wise, do not rely on yourself.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not rely on your own reasoning, but do every act on the counsel of the sages.

Apparatus:

- The last clause quotes Prov 3:5: 'Do not lean on your own understanding'.
- Vilna reads תבוא, שחביריך and יקיימוה (4:14.11, 13, 14), spelling variants only; Vilna omits משלי ג (4:14.20-21).
- תָבֹא: Vilna reads תבוא (spelling)
- שֶׁחֲבֵרֶיךָ: Vilna reads שחביריך (spelling)
- יְקַיְּמוּהָ: Vilna reads יקיימוה (spelling)
- משלי ג: Vilna reads — (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:15

> רַבִּי יַנַּאי אוֹמֵר, אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ לֹא מִשַּׁלְוַת הָרְשָׁעִים וְאַף לֹא מִיִּסּוּרֵי הַצַּדִּיקִים. רַבִּי מַתְיָא בֶן חָרָשׁ אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי מַקְדִּים בִּשְׁלוֹם כָּל אָדָם. וֶהֱוֵי זָנָב לָאֲרָיוֹת, וְאַל תְּהִי רֹאשׁ לַשּׁוּעָלִים:

**Rabbi Yannai says: It is not in our hands: not the tranquility of the wicked, nor yet the suffering of the righteous. Rabbi Matya son of Harash says: Be first to greet every person, and be a tail to lions, and do not be a head to foxes.**

Grammar:

- Two sayings: Rabbi Yannai on the unanswerable question of the wicked and the righteous; Rabbi Matya on greeting and on where to stand.
- אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ לֹא מִ... וְאַף לֹא מִ...: 'it is not in our hands, neither from ... nor even from ...'. The מִ governs each object: neither the tranquility nor the suffering is within our grasp.
- מַקְדִּים בִּשְׁלוֹם: a Hiphil participle after הֱוֵי: 'be one who is first in greeting'.
- וֶהֱוֵי with the vav pointed with segol before the guttural-initial imperative; it is the same imperative as הֱוֵי.
- זָנָב לָאֲרָיוֹת and רֹאשׁ לַשּׁוּעָלִים form a chiastic pair of opposites: tail/head, lions/foxes; לְ marks the group one is tail or head of.

Note: אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ is kept in its literal, ambiguous form. Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah take it as 'we cannot grasp (why the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer)'; Bartenura's second reading, 'in exile we have neither the ease of the wicked nor the sufferings of the righteous', is given in the commentary entry. In 4:15.23 וֶהֱוֵי has the same lemma as הֱוֵי. The BDB entries the corpus gives for אֵין, אַף, אָדָם, רֹאשׁ and שׁוּעָל are wrong homographs (where?, nose, Adam, Rosh, Shual); lex overrides point to the Jastrow entries.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'like לֹא הֲוָה בְיָדֵיהּ': the matter is not known to us, why the way of the wicked prospers and why the righteous are afflicted. A second explanation: in exile we have neither the ease God usually gives the wicked to drive them from the world to come, nor the sufferings reserved for the righteous.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: greet first 'even a non-Jew in the market'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a tail to lions means to those greater than you.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the head of foxes means of those smaller than you.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: it is better and more fitting to be a student of a greater sage than a teacher of a lesser one, for the first adds and the second diminishes; he compares the rule that one raises but does not lower in holy matters.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: the righteous do not have the quiet, security and wealth that the wicked have.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: the sufferings of love that the righteous have, which do not stop them from learning Torah.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: although the wicked fare well and the righteous badly, we cannot grasp the reason (Jer 12:1: 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?').
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not-applicable): Rabbeinu Yonah: greeting everyone is a matter of musar, moral conduct.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: serve disciples of the sages and cling to their company.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: it is better to be a disciple of one wiser than oneself, adding daily, than a teacher of one less wise, who diminishes.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah, another explanation: do not be head and ruler over the wicked, citing Prov 13:20: 'he who walks with the wise becomes wise'.

Apparatus:

- Jer 12:1 and Prov 13:20 are cited by Rabbeinu Yonah, not by the mishnah. אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ is compared by Bartenura to Yevamot 105a.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:16

> רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר, הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דּוֹמֶה לִפְרוֹזְדוֹר בִּפְנֵי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא. הַתְקֵן עַצְמְךָ בַפְּרוֹזְדוֹר, כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּכָּנֵס לַטְּרַקְלִין:

**Rabbi Yaakov says: This world is like a vestibule before the world to come. Prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the great hall.**

Literal: Rabbi Yaakov says: the-world the-this is-like to-vestibule before the-world the-coming. Prepare yourself in-the-vestibule, so-that you-will-enter to-the-hall.

- The saying is a simile (דּוֹמֶה לְ) followed by an imperative drawing the practical consequence.
- בִּפְנֵי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא: 'before the world to come', in front of it as an entrance hall is in front of the hall.
- הַתְקֵן is a Hiphil imperative of תקן: 'make ready, put in order'; the object is the reflexive עַצְמְךָ.
- פְּרוֹזְדוֹר and טְרַקְלִין are Greek loanwords; טְרַקְלִין is triklinion, a dining hall. The first is the entrance room, the second the inner hall.
- הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא is the standard term for the world to come; הַבָּא is a participle used as an adjective.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: פְּרוֹזְדוֹר is a gatehouse; the Targum renders the biblical אוּלָם (porch) by פְּרוֹזְדוֹרָא.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: טְרַקְלִין is the place where the king sits; so prepare yourself in this world to merit the world to come.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: טְרַקְלִין is the palace hall and פְּרוֹזְדוֹר the gatehouse; in this world one acquires the virtues that bring merit in the next, for this world is a road and a passage to the next.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: טְרַקְלִין is the palace; this world exists only to earn the world to come.

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah's text of the saying lacks the name; the pack matches it on the sentence.

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, יָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, מִכָּל חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא. וְיָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת שֶׁל קוֹרַת רוּחַ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, מִכָּל חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:

Grammar:

- The saying has two balanced halves, each pairing one hour in one world against all the life of the other.
- הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: 'He used to say', a habitual past formed with הָיָה plus a participle.
- יָפָה שָׁעָה is a predicate adjective before its subject: 'better is an hour'.
- קוֹרַת רוּחַ: the idiom means contentment; literally 'coolness of spirit' (Jastrow's קוֹרָה II) rather than 'beam of spirit'.
- מִכָּל after יָפָה is the comparative מִ: 'than all'.

Note: The corpus links קוֹרָה to BDB 'rafter, beam', which does not fit; a lex override points to Jastrow's קוֹרָה II 'cold, cooling' (קוֹרַת רוּחַ, satisfaction). 'Spiritual contentment' renders the idiom; the literal sense is in the phrase note. The subject of הוּא is Rabbi Yaakov of 4:16 per the plain sequence.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'for the sake of repentance and good deeds'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: repentance and good deeds give no benefit in the world to come, which exists only to receive reward for what one did in this world.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: as explained in Sanhedrin chapter 10, after death there is neither perfection nor increase; a person perfects himself and adds merit in this world, as Solomon hints (Eccl 9:10), so one must strive in this short time.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam (anchored on הַזֶּה of 4:17.11 but filed at 4:18): this is clear; these are moral teachings on the proper ordering of human society, putting each thing in its useful place.

Apparatus:

- Eccl 9:10 is cited by Rambam, not by the mishnah.

#### Pirkei Avot 4:18

> רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר, אַל תְּרַצֶּה אֶת חֲבֵרְךָ בִשְׁעַת כַּעֲסוֹ, וְאַל תְּנַחֲמֶנּוּ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁמֵּתוֹ מֻטָּל לְפָנָיו, וְאַל תִּשְׁאַל לוֹ בִשְׁעַת נִדְרוֹ, וְאַל תִּשְׁתַּדֵּל לִרְאוֹתוֹ בִשְׁעַת קַלְקָלָתוֹ:

Grammar:

- Four prohibitions, each with the same shape: אַל + verb + the person + בִשְׁעַת (at the time of) + his state.
- אַל תְּרַצֶּה אֶת חֲבֵרְךָ: the Piel of רצה governs the direct object marked by אֶת.
- תְּנַחֲמֶנּוּ: Piel imperfect 2nd masculine singular with the 3rd masculine singular suffix joined by an energic nun (-ֶנּוּ), as often on the imperfect.
- מֵתוֹ מֻטָּל לְפָנָיו: מֻטָּל is the Hofal participle of נטל ('cast, lay'), the nun assimilated into the doubled ט: his dead 'lies before him', the time between death and burial.
- תִּשְׁאַל לוֹ בִשְׁעַת נִדְרוֹ: 'question him'; the commentators explain it as probing for openings (פְּתָחִים) to release the vow while he is still angry.
- The repeated בִשְׁעַת / בְּשָׁעָה gives the saying its rhythm: the right time matters as much as the act.

Note: שָׁעָה is 'hour, moment', rendered 'at the time of'. תִּשְׁאַל לוֹ is to question the vower: Bartenura (seek openings to release his vow, for he will answer each that he vowed with it in mind) and Rabbeinu Yonah (do not ask of him the openings) agree. מֻטָּל is the Hofal participle of נטל; the corpus links it to טָלַל, the wrong root. תִּשְׁתַּדֵּל is the Hitpael of שׁדל, 'make an effort, strive'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: as it is written 'My face shall go and I will give you rest' (Ex 33:14): the Holy One told Moses to wait until the face of wrath passed (Berakhot 7a).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: at the destruction God, so to speak, was mourning, and the ministering angels sought to comfort Him, but the holy spirit answered 'do not press to comfort me' (Isa 22:4).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not seek openings to release his vow, because he will reply to each opening that he vowed with that in mind, and you will not find one; he cites God's oath to Moses.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'at the time of his disgrace' means when he has fallen into sin; he is ashamed before everyone, as with Adam, to whom God did not appear until they made loincloths (Gen 3).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: you will lead him to say unseemly words, for you add anger to his anger.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: in the hour of grief consolation adds anger and he says bad words.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not ask him for openings to release, as he is angry and vowing and will state every question to be bound into the vow so that no release can be found; you cause him harm.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (follows): Rabbeinu Yonah: do not see and shame him in the hour of his misfortune or sin, when he is already ashamed of himself.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads חבירך and מוטל (4:18.9, 4:18.16), spelling variants only.
- Ex 33:14; Isa 22:4; Gen 3:7 are cited by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.
- חֲבֵרְךָ: Vilna reads חבירך (spelling)
- מֻטָּל: Vilna reads מוטל (spelling)

Grammar:

- Samuel the Small quotes Proverbs 24:17-18 word for word; the mishnah's own words are only the introduction.
- בִּנְפֹל and בִּכָּשְׁלוֹ are infinitives construct with ב: temporal clauses ('when he falls', 'when he stumbles').
- אַל with the imperfect (תִּשְׂמָח, יָגֵל) is a prohibition; the second is in the third person, 'let your heart not exult'.
- פֶּן ('lest') introduces the feared result, three verbs in a chain: He sees, it is evil in His eyes, He turns away.
- הֵשִׁיב is Hiphil of שׁוב ('cause to return, turn back'), not the Qal שָׁב: Bartenura draws a lesson from this.

Note: The quoted verse is kept in the order of the Hebrew. 'Turn His anger away from him' is the plain sense; Bartenura reads the Hiphil as: He removes it from your enemy and brings it back onto you. Both readings take the anger as turned away from the enemy. Rambam's remark on אַפּוֹ (not 'his burning anger') is recorded.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: this is a verse in Proverbs, but Samuel the Small was accustomed to admonish people with this saying.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'lest the Lord see' (and it be evil in His eyes) because you made Him, in your heart, as though He were your agent to fulfil your wish. The English keeps the text's sense that it is evil in His eyes.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since the verse says 'turn' (וְהֵשִׁיב) and not 'return' (וְשָׁב), it means He will remove the anger from your enemy and bring it onto you. The English 'turn His anger away from him' agrees that the anger leaves the enemy; the transfer to the reader is Bartenura's reading of the Hiphil.
- Rambam (records): Rambam: the verse does not say 'his burning anger' but 'his anger', which teaches that all his sins are forgiven; Solomon said this as a precept but this sage used to admonish with it against this transgression. The forgiveness reading is recorded, not added to the English.

Apparatus:

- Source verse: Proverbs 24:17-18, quoted from בִּנְפֹל to אַפּוֹ.
- Variant: Vilna reads יז for the chapter number in the citation (Prov. 24 here; the reference is a gloss).
- Variant: Vilna spells בנפול.
- —: Vilna reads יז (word)
- בִּנְפֹל: Vilna reads בנפול (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:20

> אֱלִישָׁע בֶּן אֲבוּיָה אוֹמֵר, הַלּוֹמֵד יֶלֶד לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לִדְיוֹ כְתוּבָה עַל נְיָר חָדָשׁ. וְהַלּוֹמֵד זָקֵן לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לִדְיוֹ כְתוּבָה עַל נְיָר מָחוּק. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַר יְהוּדָה אִישׁ כְּפַר הַבַּבְלִי אוֹמֵר, הַלּוֹמֵד מִן הַקְּטַנִּים לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאֹכֵל עֲנָבִים קֵהוֹת וְשׁוֹתֶה יַיִן מִגִּתּוֹ. וְהַלּוֹמֵד מִן הַזְּקֵנִים לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאֹכֵל עֲנָבִים בְּשֵׁלוֹת וְשׁוֹתֶה יַיִן יָשָׁן. רַבִּי אוֹמֵר, אַל תִּסְתַּכֵּל בַּקַּנְקַן, אֶלָּא בְמַה שֶּׁיֶּשׁ בּוֹ. יֵשׁ קַנְקַן חָדָשׁ מָלֵא יָשָׁן, וְיָשָׁן שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ חָדָשׁ אֵין בּוֹ:

**Elisha son of Avuyah says: One who learns as a child, to what is he compared? To ink written on new paper. And one who learns as an old man, to what is he compared? To ink written on erased paper. Rabbi Yose son of Yehudah, a man of Kefar HaBavli, says: One who learns from the young, to what is he compared? To one who eats unripe grapes and drinks wine from its winepress. And one who learns from the old, to what is he compared? To one who eats ripe grapes and drinks aged wine. Rabbi says: Do not look at the jar, but at what is in it. There is a new jar full of old wine, and an old one in which there is not even new.**

Grammar:

- The three sayings share the formula לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה ('to what is he like'), which opens a mashal (comparison).
- The pairs run in parallel: child and old man (ink on new or erased paper); the young and the old (unripe and ripe grapes, wine fresh from the press and aged wine).
- רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַר יְהוּדָה: בַר is Aramaic for 'son of'; the Vilna text reads 'son of Rabbi'.
- Rabbi answers with a different image: אַל תִּסְתַּכֵּל with בְּ takes the jar as the object looked at, and אֶלָּא בְמַה שֶּׁיֶּשׁ בּוֹ gives what to look at instead.
- The last sentence is elliptical: 'a new jar full of old' means old wine, and 'an old one that has not even new in it' means an old jar with not even new wine.

Note: The Hebrew of the first saying leaves the child as the learner ('learns a child'); the English reads 'learns as a child', as the commentators do. אִישׁ כְּפַר הַבַּבְלִי: 'a man of Kefar HaBavli', a place name; the literal 'village of the Babylonian' is given in the token glosses. דְּיוֹ, ink, is spelled לִדְיוֹ in the base text.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: writing on new paper endures; so what one learns in childhood (גִּרְסַת הַיַּלְדוּת) is not forgotten.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: unripe grapes have not ripened fully and set the teeth on edge (קֵהוֹת); so the wisdom of a child has not settled and his words are not accepted or settled in the heart.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: wine from its winepress still has its lees mixed in it; so the wisdom of a child is a mixture of doubts.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Rabbi disagrees with Rabbi Yose son of Yehudah: there is a new jar full of old wine, and so there is a child whose taste is the taste of the old, and there are old men who fall short of the young in wisdom.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: learning in childhood endures and is not easily forgotten; the reverse for old age. Rabbi Yose says the wisdom of the young has questions and doubts not yet refined; Rabbi says 'do not judge the wine by its jar', for there is a new jar with old wine and an old jar that is empty.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads נייר (spelling) in both places.
- Variant: Vilna reads ברבי ('son of Rabbi') for בַר, and לאוכל, בשולות, שאפילו for the base spellings.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the old man's learning is lost quickly; he adds a comparison from Mivchar HaPeninim: engraving on stone against engraving on sand.
- Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma reads הלמד תורה לילד ... הלמד תורה לזקן ('who learns Torah as a child ... as an old man') for הַלּוֹמֵד יֶלֶד ... הַלּוֹמֵד זָקֵן, and בן יהודה for בַר יְהוּדָה; he too takes it of the learner's own childhood (תורה שבילדותו).
- נְיָר: Vilna reads נייר (spelling)
- נְיָר: Vilna reads נייר (spelling)
- בַר: Vilna reads ברבי (word)
- לְאֹכֵל: Vilna reads לאוכל (spelling)
- לְאֹכֵל: Vilna reads לאוכל (spelling)
- בְּשֵׁלוֹת: Vilna reads בשולות (spelling)
- שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ: Vilna reads שאפילו (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:21

> רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הַקַּפָּר אוֹמֵר, הַקִּנְאָה וְהַתַּאֲוָה וְהַכָּבוֹד, מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:

**Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: Envy, desire, and honor take a person out of the world.**

Grammar:

- The three nouns, each with the article, form the subject; the plural participle מוֹצִיאִין agrees with all three. The ending ־ין is the Mishnaic plural.
- אֶת הָאָדָם is a definite object ('the person'): a person in general.
- מִן הָעוֹלָם: 'out of the world'; the Hebrew does not say which world. Rambam explains that these traits destroy a man's faith in the Torah and keep from him the perfections of intellect and character; Rabbeinu Yonah's second explanation is early death (this world).
- The saying is a short triad with no explanation, and the English leaves it so.

Note: 'Honor' stands for the pursuit of honor (Rambam: אהבת הכבוד; Bartenura: that people honor him). 'Desire' is Bartenura's appetite for food, drink and sex; 'envy' is קִנְאָה, as in the commentary. The ambiguity of 'out of the world' is kept.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: תַּאֲוָה is one who seeks to fulfil his desire in eating, drinking, sexual relations and the like. The English 'desire' is kept general.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: כָּבוֹד is that people should honor him, that is, the wish to be honored. The English 'honor' keeps this.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: envy, desire and the love of honor: by these traits or any one of them a man loses faith in the Torah, and neither intellectual nor moral excellence reaches him. The English keeps the plain 'take out of the world'.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads אליעזר for אֶלְעָזָר.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) cites Prov. 14:30 (envy), 21:25 (desire) and the death of Joseph (honor, Berakhot 55a) for how each takes a person out of the world.
- אֶלְעָזָר: Vilna reads אליעזר (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 4:22

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, הַיִּלּוֹדִים לָמוּת, וְהַמֵּתִים לְהֵחָיוֹת, וְהַחַיִּים לִדּוֹן. לֵידַע לְהוֹדִיעַ וּלְהִוָּדַע שֶׁהוּא אֵל, הוּא הַיּוֹצֵר, הוּא הַבּוֹרֵא, הוּא הַמֵּבִין, הוּא הַדַּיָּן, הוּא עֵד, הוּא בַעַל דִּין, וְהוּא עָתִיד לָדוּן. בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁאֵין לְפָנָיו לֹא עַוְלָה, וְלֹא שִׁכְחָה, וְלֹא מַשּׂוֹא פָנִים, וְלֹא מִקַּח שֹׁחַד, שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ. וְדַע שֶׁהַכֹּל לְפִי הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן. וְאַל יַבְטִיחֲךָ יִצְרְךָ שֶׁהַשְּׁאוֹל בֵּית מָנוֹס לְךָ, שֶׁעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה נוֹצָר, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה נוֹלָד, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה חַי, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה מֵת, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה עָתִיד לִתֵּן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:

**He used to say: Those who are born are to die, and the dead are to be revived, and the living are to be judged; to know, to make known, and to come to know that He is God, He is the Former, He is the Creator, He is the Discerner, He is the Judge, He is the Witness, He is the Plaintiff, and He is destined to judge. Blessed is He, before whom there is no injustice, no forgetfulness, no partiality, and no taking of bribes, for everything is His. And know that everything is according to the reckoning. And do not let your impulse assure you that Sheol is a place of refuge for you, for against your will you were formed, and against your will you were born, and against your will you live, and against your will you die, and against your will you are destined to give judgment and account before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.**

Grammar:

- The first line is a threefold sequence with לְ + infinitive (or participle): born to die, dead to be revived, living to be judged.
- לֵידַע לְהוֹדִיעַ וּלְהִוָּדַע is a series of three infinitives (Qal, Hiphil, Niphal) of ידע, and the three cases, Bartenura says, are from others, to others, and of oneself.
- A string of הוּא clauses names God in seven roles; הוּא before each noun is a pronoun used as a copula ('He is ...').
- Five times the same phrase עַל כָּרְחֲךָ ('against your will') opens a clause; each time אַתָּה with a passive or stative form follows.
- מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים ('king of the kings of kings'): the construct chain heaps up the superlative; the Vilna text has the same.
- וְדַע שֶׁהַכֹּל לְפִי הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן is a bare imperative and a short sentence: the Hebrew does not say who reckons.

Note: The Hebrew leaves open who 'knows', 'makes known' and 'comes to know'; the English keeps the three infinitives bare, and Bartenura's glosses (from others, to others, from oneself) are given in the commentary entries. אֵל is read as 'God', following Bartenura's silence and Rabbeinu Yonah's gloss 'strong, mighty' recorded in the apparatus; the pack lexicon links token 14 to אַל ('not'), which is not the word, and its sense is removed. עָתִיד לָדוּן is 'is destined to judge' (Bartenura: in the world to come), the same word as עָתִיד לִתֵּן below. שֶׁהַכֹּל לְפִי הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן: 'according to the reckoning'; Bartenura gives the sum of small coins, which the English does not add. In the line on the impulse, שְׁאוֹל is Sheol; the pack lemma (Saul) is wrong, and its sense is removed.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who has been born is already destined to die.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the dead are destined to live and to stand on the Day of Judgment, some to eternal life, some to shame and eternal contempt (Dan. 12:2). The English keeps the plain 'to be revived'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the living are standing to be judged on the Day of Judgment.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on לֵידַע: from others. The English 'to know' keeps the bare infinitive.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura (on 'וּלְהוֹדִיעַ'): to others. The English 'to make known' renders the Hiphil.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on וּלְהִוָּדַע: to understand of oneself. The English 'to come to know' renders the Niphal.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the whole world is in His hand like clay in the potter's hand, and the reason is that He is the Creator, who made the whole world from nothing; therefore He can do with it as He wishes. The English follows the potter image of 'the Former'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since He has understood all their deeds, He brings them to judgment before Him. This is why the Discerner is followed by the Judge.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'plaintiff' means that He claims against sinners. The English 'Plaintiff' follows.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on 'He is about to judge': in the world to come.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: He does not show partiality even to a perfect righteous man, to spare him punishment for a light transgression that came his way, and He does not take a bribe, a commandment's reward set against a transgression, but gives reward for the commandment and punishment for the transgression.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: coin by coin is added to a great sum; so light transgressions, when many, add up to a great reckoning. The English keeps 'the reckoning' without the coin image.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the soul does not wish to leave the curtain (the pure place where souls are kept) and enter a woman's womb, an impure place; an angel comes and brings it out against its will. The English keeps the bare 'against your will'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: at the time of birth he does not want to come out, and an angel brings him out against his will.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: there is a man crushed by suffering who wants to die and cannot.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'to know, to make known and to be known' refers to those to be born, those born now who will die, and those who will live after death; from these three classes one learns that He is the Former and the Creator. 'The Judge' is His judging now, in life and death; 'destined to judge' is the judgment, with reward and punishment, of those who live in the world to come. 'No taking of bribes' does not mean a bribe to pervert judgment, which is absurd of God, but that He does not let many good deeds buy off one transgression: He punishes the one and rewards the others; 'no partiality' means even the great are punished for a small sin (Moses). 'Against your will' lists only natural events without choice; it does not say 'against your will you sin'.

Apparatus:

- Variant: Vilna reads לידון (4:22.9), הדיין (4:22.22), שוחד (4:22.44), ליתן (4:22.78) for the base spellings.
- Rambam (normative): מִקַּח שֹׁחַד does not mean a bribe to pervert judgment, but that a man's thousand good deeds do not buy off one transgression; מַשּׂוֹא פָנִים, that the great are punished for a small matter. He cites the Torah's לֹא יִשָּׂא פָנִים וְלֹא יִקַּח שֹׁחַד (Deut. 10:17).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): אֵל from the sense 'mighty' (as in 2 Kings 24:15, 'the mighty of the land').
- Rabbeinu Yonah: 'Former' is the start of the work and 'Creator' its completion.
- Rabbeinu Yonah on 'let your impulse assure you': do not say that Sheol is a place of refuge, as the heretics say, 'in the world to come there is neither judgment nor judge'.
- לִדּוֹן: Vilna reads לידון (spelling)
- הַדַּיָּן: Vilna reads הדיין (spelling)
- שֹׁחַד: Vilna reads שוחד (spelling)
- לִתֵּן: Vilna reads ליתן (spelling)

## Chapter 5 — פֶּרֶק ה (Pirkei Avot 5:1–5:23)

### Reading text

<sup>5:1</sup> By ten utterances the world was created. What does the text teach in saying so? Could it not have been created by a single utterance? Rather, it was to exact punishment from the wicked, who destroy the world that was created by ten utterances, and to give good reward to the righteous, who sustain the world that was created by ten utterances.

<sup>5:2</sup> Ten generations from Adam to Noah, to make known how patient He is, for all the generations kept on provoking Him until He brought upon them the waters of the Flood. Ten generations from Noah to Abraham, to make known how patient He is, for all the generations kept on provoking Him until Abraham came and received upon himself the reward of them all.

<sup>5:3</sup> Abraham our father, peace be upon him, was tested with ten trials and stood firm in all of them, to make known how great was the love of Abraham our father, peace be upon him.

<sup>5:4</sup> Ten miracles were done for our fathers in Egypt, and ten at the sea. Ten plagues the Holy One, blessed be He, brought upon the Egyptians in Egypt, and ten at the sea. With ten trials our fathers tested the Omnipresent, blessed be He, in the wilderness, as it is said (Numbers 14): "They have tested me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice."

<sup>5:5</sup> Ten miracles were done for our fathers in the Temple. No woman miscarried from the smell of the holy flesh; and the holy flesh never turned putrid; and no fly was seen in the slaughterhouse; and no emission befell the high priest on the Day of Atonement; and the rains did not extinguish the fire of the wood-pile; and the wind did not overcome the column of smoke; and no disqualification was found in the omer, the two loaves, or the showbread; they stood pressed together and bowed with room to spare; and no serpent or scorpion ever harmed anyone in Jerusalem; and no man said to his fellow, "The place is too narrow for me to lodge in Jerusalem."

<sup>5:6</sup> Ten things were created on the eve of the Sabbath at twilight, and these are they: the mouth of the earth, the mouth of the well, the mouth of the donkey, the rainbow, the manna, the staff, the shamir, the script, the inscription, and the tablets. And some say: also the demons, and the burial place of Moses, and the ram of Abraham our father. And some say: also tongs made with tongs.

<sup>5:7</sup> Seven things are in the unformed person, and seven in the wise person. The wise person does not speak in the presence of one who is greater than he in wisdom and in number; does not break into his fellow's words; is not hasty to answer; asks to the point and answers according to the law; speaks to the first point first and to the last point last; says of what he has not heard, "I have not heard"; and admits the truth. And their opposites are in the unformed person.

<sup>5:8</sup> Seven kinds of calamity come to the world for seven principal transgressions. When some of them tithe and some do not tithe, a famine of drought comes: some go hungry and some are sated. When they have resolved not to tithe, a famine of tumult and of drought comes. And for not taking the dough-offering, a famine of annihilation comes. Pestilence comes to the world for the death penalties stated in the Torah that were not delivered to the court, and for the produce of the seventh year. Sword comes to the world for the delaying of justice, for the perverting of justice, and for those who teach the Torah not according to the law.

<sup>5:9</sup> A wild beast comes to the world for a vain oath and for the profanation of the Name. Exile comes to the world for those who worship idols, for forbidden sexual relations, for the shedding of blood, and for violating the release of the land. At four times pestilence increases: in the fourth year, in the seventh, at the close of the seventh year, and at the close of the festival in every single year. In the fourth, because of the poor man's tithe of the third. In the seventh, because of the poor man's tithe of the sixth. At the close of the seventh year, because of the produce of the seventh year. And at the close of the festival in every single year, because of the robbery of the gifts to the poor.

<sup>5:10</sup> There are four dispositions among people. One who says, "What is mine is mine, and what is yours is yours": this is a middling disposition; and some say, this is the disposition of Sodom. "What is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine": an unlearned person. "What is mine is yours, and what is yours is yours": a pious person. "What is mine is mine, and what is yours is mine": a wicked person.

<sup>5:11</sup> There are four dispositions in temperaments. Easy to anger and easy to appease: his gain is outweighed by his loss. Hard to anger and hard to appease: his loss is outweighed by his gain. Hard to anger and easy to appease: a pious person. Easy to anger and hard to appease: a wicked person.

<sup>5:12</sup> There are four dispositions in disciples. Quick to hear and quick to forget: his gain is outweighed by his loss. Hard to hear and hard to forget: his loss is outweighed by his gain. Quick to hear and hard to forget: a wise person. Hard to hear and quick to forget: this is a bad lot.

<sup>5:13</sup> There are four types in giving charity. One who wants to give but wants others not to give has an evil eye toward what belongs to others. One who wants others to give but himself not to give has an evil eye toward his own. One who wants to give and wants others to give is pious. One who wants neither himself nor others to give is wicked.

<sup>5:14</sup> There are four types in going to the house of study. One who goes but does not do: the reward of going is in his hand. One who does but does not go: the reward of doing is in his hand. One who goes and does is pious. One who neither goes nor does is wicked.

<sup>5:15</sup> There are four types among those who sit before the sages: a sponge, a funnel, a strainer, and a sieve. A sponge, because it absorbs everything. A funnel, because it takes in through this and lets out through that. A strainer, because it lets the wine out and retains the dregs. And a sieve, because it lets out the fine meal and retains the choice flour.

<sup>5:16</sup> Any love that depends on a thing: when the thing ceases, the love ceases. And that which does not depend on a thing never ceases. Which is the love that depends on a thing? This is the love of Amnon and Tamar. And that which does not depend on a thing? This is the love of David and Jonathan.

<sup>5:17</sup> Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure. Which is a dispute that is for the sake of Heaven? This is the dispute of Hillel and Shammai. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven? This is the dispute of Korah and all his company.

<sup>5:18</sup> Whoever makes the many meritorious, no sin comes through him. And whoever causes the many to sin, they do not give him the means to repent. Moses was meritorious and made the many meritorious; the merit of the many rests on him, as it is said, Deuteronomy 33: "He performed the righteousness of the LORD, and His judgments with Israel." Jeroboam sinned and caused the many to sin; the sin of the many rests on him, as it is said, 1 Kings 15: "For the sins of Jeroboam (son of Nebat), which he sinned and which he caused Israel to sin."

<sup>5:19</sup> Whoever has these three things is of the disciples of Abraham our father; and three other things, of the disciples of Balaam the wicked. A good eye, a humble spirit, and a modest soul: of the disciples of Abraham our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit, and a broad soul: of the disciples of Balaam the wicked. What is the difference between the disciples of Abraham our father and the disciples of Balaam the wicked? The disciples of Abraham our father eat in this world and inherit in the world to come, as it is said: "To bequeath to those who love me substance, and I will fill their treasuries." But the disciples of Balaam the wicked inherit Gehinnom and go down to the pit of destruction, as it is said: "And You, God, will bring them down to the pit of destruction; men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in You."

<sup>5:20</sup> Judah son of Tema says: Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and strong as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven. He used to say: The bold-faced to Gehinnom, and the shamefaced to the Garden of Eden. May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You rebuild Your city speedily in our days, and give us our portion in Your Torah.

<sup>5:21</sup> He used to say: At five years old, for Scripture; at ten, for Mishnah; at thirteen, for the commandments; at fifteen, for Talmud; at eighteen, for the wedding canopy; at twenty, for pursuit; at thirty, for strength; at forty, for understanding; at fifty, for counsel; at sixty, for old age; at seventy, for gray hair; at eighty, for might; at ninety, for stooping; at a hundred, it is as if he had died and passed away and ceased from the world.

<sup>5:22</sup> Ben Bag Bag says: Turn it and turn it, for everything is in it; and in it you will see, and grow old and worn in it, and do not move from it, for you have no quality better than it.

<sup>5:23</sup> Ben He He says: According to the toil is the reward.

Grammar:

- The saying has the form of a question and answer: 'what is the teaching... could it not...? but...'. וַהֲלֹא introduces a rhetorical question expecting 'yes'.
- שֶׁמְּאַבְּדִין and שֶׁמְּקַיְּמִין are Piel participles with the mishnaic plural ending -ין; they describe habitual action ('who destroy', 'who sustain').
- Two parallel clauses, each ending with the same refrain שֶׁנִּבְרָא בַעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת: the wicked destroy, the righteous sustain, the same world.
- לְהִפָּרַע (Nifal) is passive in form but means 'to exact payment'; compare לִתֵּן שָׂכָר, 'to give reward', its counterpart.

Note: The Hebrew leaves the subject of 'What does the text teach' unstated; 'the text' (Genesis 1) is supplied because the question asks why Scripture says ten utterances. מַאֲמָרוֹת is rendered 'utterances' (the nine 'And God said' of Genesis 1 plus the opening word, per Bartenura and Rambam).

Commentary:

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura counts nine times 'and He said' plus Bereshit itself, which is also an utterance, citing Psalm 33:6 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made'. This identifies the ten but does not change the English.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura first gives the reading 'whoever destroys one soul destroys a whole world', then prefers his own: the wicked destroy the world literally, by tipping the whole world toward guilt, so that it is lost on their account. The English keeps 'destroy the world'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who destroys a work made in one day is not like one who destroys a work made over many days; so the world's being made by ten utterances makes the wicked's destruction of it graver. The English keeps the refrain 'that was created by ten utterances' in both clauses.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: nine times 'and He said' plus Bereshit make ten; one utterance could have sufficed, but the separate utterances show the greatness of existence and the goodness of its order, so that whoever ruins it ruins something great, namely his own soul, which he can perfect or destroy. The English follows the plain sense that one utterance would have been possible.

Apparatus:

- Variant spellings: 5:1.23 Vilna וליתן for וְלִתֵּן; 5:1.27 Vilna שמקיימין for שֶׁמְּקַיְּמִין.
- Cross-reference: Psalm 33:6, cited by Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah to show that Bereshit is also an utterance.
- וְלִתֵּן: Vilna reads וליתן (spelling)
- שֶׁמְּקַיְּמִין: Vilna reads שמקיימין (spelling)

Grammar:

- The mishnah is built on two parallel halves, each beginning with the number ten and each ending with a figure who changes the course: the Flood in the first, Abraham in the second.
- מַכְעִיסִין וּבָאִין is a pair of participles: 'provoking and coming (on)', that is, they went on provoking.
- אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם is the biblical idiom for patience (Exodus 34:6, 'slow to anger'); לְפָנָיו marks it as God's patience.
- שֶׁהֵבִיא is a Hifil with the relative שֶׁ, 'that He brought'; עַד שֶׁ- 'until that' introduces the end of the long forbearance.
- וְקִבֵּל עָלָיו: Piel of קבל; 'to receive upon oneself' means to take on as one's own, hence 'received the reward of them all'.

Note: The Hebrew שְׂכַר כֻּלָּם is 'the reward of all of them'. Bartenura explains it as the reward Abraham earned by doing good in the measure the whole generations should have done; the English leaves the compressed wording, and the explanation is in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not be surprised that He has been patient with the nations of the world through all the years they enslave His children, since He was more patient with the generations from Adam to Noah, and afterwards they were flooded. The English keeps 'how patient He is'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Abraham did good deeds in the measure that all should have done, so all were saved by his merit; as he took the yoke of commandments in this world against them all, so he received in the world to come a reward against them all, for each person has two portions, in Eden and in Gehinnom (Chagigah 15b). The English follows 'received the reward of them all'.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: these generations are the Torah's genealogies, so-and-so begot so-and-so in order. This list and those after it are mentioned because the ten utterances were mentioned; they hold moral instruction for a person, to rouse him and to perfect his soul in the moral and intellectual virtues, which is the aim of this tractate.

Apparatus:

- Variants: 5:2.4 and 5:2.25 Vilna עד for וְעַד; 5:2.43 Vilna כולם for כֻּלָּם.
- Cross-reference: Genesis 5 (Adam to Noah) and Genesis 11 (Noah to Abraham) give the ten generations; Exodus 34:6 for אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם.
- וְעַד: Vilna reads עד (word)
- וְעַד: Vilna reads עד (word)
- כֻּלָּם: Vilna reads כולם (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:3

> עֲשָׂרָה נִסְיוֹנוֹת נִתְנַסָּה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְעָמַד בְּכֻלָּם, לְהוֹדִיעַ כַּמָּה חִבָּתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם:

**Abraham our father, peace be upon him, was tested with ten trials and stood firm in all of them, to make known how great was the love of Abraham our father, peace be upon him.**

Grammar:

- נִסְיוֹנוֹת נִתְנַסָּה: the verb and its noun share a root (נסה): 'was tried with trials'.
- עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם is a formula of respect, 'peace be upon him', added after the name of Abraham in both halves of the mishnah.
- חִבָּתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם: the possessive is doubled, 'his love of Abraham', a mishnaic construction with שֶׁל instead of the construct state.
- The Hebrew infinitive לְהוֹדִיעַ, 'to make known', has no stated subject; it is the purpose of the ten trials and of Abraham's standing firm.

Note: חִבָּה: 'love, affection'. Rabbeinu Yonah reads the trials as revealing to people that Abraham feared God and was whole in all his traits, so the 'love' shown is Abraham's own devotion; the English keeps the construction 'the love of Abraham', which allows both readings.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura lists the ten trials: Ur of the Chaldees (thrown by Nimrod into the fiery furnace), 'Go forth from your land', the famine, Sarah taken to Pharaoh's house, the war of the kings, the covenant between the pieces, circumcision, Abimelech taking Sarah, the expulsion of Hagar and her son, and the binding of Isaac. This identifies the trials without bearing on the wording.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam gives a different list of ten: the emigration, the famine, the seizure of Sarah by Pharaoh, the war with the four kings, taking Hagar as a wife, circumcision, the seizure of Sarah by the king of Gerar, the expulsion of Hagar, the distancing of Ishmael, and the binding of Isaac. The lists differ in places; neither alters the English.

Apparatus:

- Variant: 5:3.9 Vilna בכולם for בְּכֻלָּם.
- Cross-reference: Genesis 12–22 for the trials; the number and contents of the ten differ between Bartenura and Rambam.
- בְּכֻלָּם: Vilna reads בכולם (spelling)

Grammar:

- The mishnah has three parallel statements of ten: miracles in Egypt and at the sea, plagues in Egypt and at the sea, trials in the wilderness. The second sentence explains the first.
- נִסִּים (miracles, from נסס) and נִסְיוֹנוֹת (trials, from נסה) come from different roots but sound alike; the mishnah plays on the likeness: God's miracles, the people's testing.
- In the first two sentences the second 'ten' is elliptical: וַעֲשָׂרָה עַל הַיָּם, 'and ten at the sea', the noun is understood from the first half.
- הֵבִיא ... עַל is the idiom 'to bring upon' (a plague); הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא is the subject, separated from the verb.
- The proof text is Numbers 14:22, וַיְנַסּוּ אֹתִי זֶה עֶשֶׂר פְּעָמִים, introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר 'as it is said'. The parenthesized (במדבר יד) is the printed edition's reference, not the mishnah's; Vilna adds the verse number כב.

Note: הַמָּקוֹם, of God, is rendered 'the Omnipresent', with the literal sense 'the Place' here recorded. The verse is quoted from the Hebrew of the mishnah, not from any translation. 'Plagues' renders מַכּוֹת, 'blows'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'miracles' means they were saved from the ten plagues, and all the plagues were upon the Egyptians and not upon Israel. The English follows by saying the miracles were done 'for our fathers in Egypt'.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura lists ten miracles at the sea (the waters split, the sea became like a tent, the sea floor became dry, and so on). This is an enumeration that does not bear on the wording.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura gives the mnemonic for the ten plagues (the first letters of the three groups: Detzakh Adash Be'achav). It is an aid to memory, not a reading.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: the ten at the sea correspond to the ten 'fallings' in the Song at the Sea ('He has thrown into the sea', 'sank in the Red Sea', and so on). It is an enumeration.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura lists the ten wilderness trials: two at the sea, 'Were there no graves in Egypt', Marah, Rephidim, two over the manna, two over the quail, the calf, the complainers, and the spies, 'the tenth', where Numbers 14:22 is said. An enumeration.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the miracles in Egypt are their being saved from the ten plagues, each one reaching only Egypt and not Israel, which is unquestionably miraculous; for the lice the Torah does not say it, but the sages explain so. The ten at the sea are tradition. The English follows 'miracles done for our fathers in Egypt'.

Apparatus:

- Quotation: Numbers 14:22, וַיְנַסּוּ אֹתִי זֶה עֶשֶׂר פְּעָמִים וְלֹא שָׁמְעוּ בְּקוֹלִי, from the Hebrew of the mishnah.
- Variants: 5:4.18 Vilna ועשרה for וְעֶשֶׂר; 5:4.21 Vilna עשר for עֲשָׂרָה; 5:4.34 Vilna אותי for אֹתִי.
- Editorial reference: (במדבר יד) after שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר is the edition's, not the mishnah's text; Vilna reads (במדבר יד, כב), adding the verse.
- וְעֶשֶׂר: Vilna reads ועשרה (word)
- עֲשָׂרָה: Vilna reads עשר (word)
- —: Vilna reads כב (word)
- אֹתִי: Vilna reads אותי (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:5

> עֲשָׂרָה נִסִּים נַעֲשׂוּ לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ. לֹא הִפִּילָה אִשָּׁה מֵרֵיחַ בְּשַׂר הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְלֹא הִסְרִיחַ בְּשַׂר הַקֹּדֶשׁ מֵעוֹלָם, וְלֹא נִרְאָה זְבוּב בְּבֵית הַמִּטְבָּחַיִם, וְלֹא אֵרַע קֶרִי לְכֹהֵן גָּדוֹל בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, וְלֹא כִבּוּ גְשָׁמִים אֵשׁ שֶׁל עֲצֵי הַמַּעֲרָכָה, וְלֹא נָצְחָה הָרוּחַ אֶת עַמּוּד הֶעָשָׁן, וְלֹא נִמְצָא פְסוּל בָּעֹמֶר וּבִשְׁתֵּי הַלֶּחֶם וּבְלֶחֶם הַפָּנִים, עוֹמְדִים צְפוּפִים וּמִשְׁתַּחֲוִים רְוָחִים, וְלֹא הִזִּיק נָחָשׁ וְעַקְרָב בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם מֵעוֹלָם, וְלֹא אָמַר אָדָם לַחֲבֵרוֹ צַר לִי הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאָלִין בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם:

**Ten miracles were done for our fathers in the Temple. No woman miscarried from the smell of the holy flesh; and the holy flesh never turned putrid; and no fly was seen in the slaughterhouse; and no emission befell the high priest on the Day of Atonement; and the rains did not extinguish the fire of the wood-pile; and the wind did not overcome the column of smoke; and no disqualification was found in the omer, the two loaves, or the showbread; they stood pressed together and bowed with room to spare; and no serpent or scorpion ever harmed anyone in Jerusalem; and no man said to his fellow, "The place is too narrow for me to lodge in Jerusalem."**

Literal: ten miracles were-done for-our-fathers in-house-of the-sanctuary. not caused-to-fall woman from-smell-of flesh-of the-holy; and-not made-putrid flesh-of the-holy from-ever; and-not was-seen fly in-house-of the-slaughtering-places; and-not befell emission to-priest great on-day-of the-Atonements; and-not extinguished rains fire of wood-of the-arrangement; and-not overcame the-wind [object-marker] column-of the-smoke; and-not was-found disqualification in-the-omer and-in-two-of the-bread and-in-bread-of the-faces; standing crowded and-bowing roomy; and-not harmed serpent and-scorpion in-Jerusalem from-ever; and-not said man to-his-fellow narrow to-me the-place that-I-lodge in-Jerusalem
