Grammar:

- The mishnah opens with the heading 'ten miracles' and lists ten items. The first begins with לֹא, the others with וְלֹא, 'and not', except the eighth (standing pressed together and bowing with room), which is stated positively, one miracle in two halves.
- הִפִּילָה (Hifil of נפל) is literally 'caused to fall'; with אִשָּׁה as the subject the sense is miscarriage. The verb is feminine singular because the subject is.
- קֶרִי is the legal term for a seminal emission; the high priest on the Day of Atonement could not be unclean.
- עוֹמְדִים צְפוּפִים וּמִשְׁתַּחֲוִים רְוָחִים is a contrast of two participles with adverbial adjectives: the miracle is that they were crowded when standing and spacious when bowing.
- The last item quotes direct speech: צַר לִי הַמָּקוֹם, 'the place is too narrow for me', an echo of Isaiah 49:20, where הַמָּקוֹם is not God but the physical place; here the same word is 'the place'.
- שֶׁאָלִין is the relative שֶׁ with the Qal imperfect 1st person singular of לין, 'to spend the night, lodge': 'that I should lodge'. Bartenura notes the variant כְּשֶׁאָלִין, 'when I lodge'.

Note: צְפוּפִים: the plain sense is 'crowded, pressed together' (Rambam: each stood beside his fellow). Bartenura derives it from צף 'floating' and says the crowd was so dense their feet were lifted from the ground; the English keeps the plain sense and records Bartenura's. רְוָחִים: Bartenura says each worshipper had four cubits of room, so as not to hear his fellow confessing; Rambam says they did not press upon each other at the prostration. The English says 'with room to spare', which agrees with both. The Hebrew of the last item has no object for הִזִּיק; 'anyone' is supplied. The subject of 'they stood pressed together' is the people in the Temple court.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: because a seminal emission comes out of the high priest's own body, it would have been more shameful and repulsive than other kinds of uncleanness. The English renders קֶרִי as 'emission'.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura: even though the altar stood in an open place. This tells why the miracle was remarkable and does not alter the words.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the smoke did not fail to rise straight up. The English keeps 'overcome', with the sense that the wind did not bend the column.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura explains why a disqualification would have been serious: the omer is reaped at night, the two loaves are baked on the eve of the festival, and the showbread on the eve of the Sabbath, so no replacement was possible. It explains the point of the miracle, not the wording.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: 'צְפוּפִים' is from the root of 'floating on the water': from the great crowd they pressed on one another until their feet were lifted from the ground and they stood in the air. The English takes the plain sense 'pressed together' and records this derivation.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: at the time of prostration a miracle was done, and each bowed with room, four cubits from his fellow, so that he should not hear his fellow confessing and mentioning his sins. The English follows 'with room to spare'; the four cubits is a further detail.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'we read שֶׁאָלִין' (that I lodge), because the Place provided their livelihood and none of them had to leave and say his livelihood was straitened and he could not live in Jerusalem. Some books read כְּשֶׁאָלִין and it is said of the pilgrims, who were not cramped when they lodged in Jerusalem; compare Isaiah 49:20. The English follows 'that I lodge'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the altar was in the middle of the court and open to the sky, yet the rains did not put out the altar fire nor did the wind scatter the smoke column from the offerings; at the offering the air was clear, they stood in the court side by side, and at the prostration they did not press each other, because of their awe and settled calm in that place. The English follows this.

Apparatus:

- Variants: 5:5.24 Vilna אירע for אֵרַע; 5:5.46 Vilna בעומר for בָּעֹמֶר; 5:5.54 Vilna רווחים for רְוָחִים.
- Cross-reference: Isaiah 49:20, צַר לִי הַמָּקוֹם גְּשָׁה לִּי וְאֵשֵׁבָה, cited by Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah for the idiom.
- Bartenura notes the variant reading כְּשֶׁאָלִין ('when I lodge') for שֶׁאָלִין in the last item.
- אֵרַע: Vilna reads אירע (spelling)
- בָּעֹמֶר: Vilna reads בעומר (spelling)
- רְוָחִים: Vilna reads רווחים (spelling)

> עֲשָׂרָה דְבָרִים נִבְרְאוּ בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת, וְאֵלּוּ הֵן, פִּי הָאָרֶץ, וּפִי הַבְּאֵר, וּפִי הָאָתוֹן, וְהַקֶּשֶׁת, וְהַמָּן, וְהַמַּטֶּה, וְהַשָּׁמִיר, וְהַכְּתָב, וְהַמִּכְתָּב, וְהַלּוּחוֹת. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, אַף הַמַּזִּיקִין, וּקְבוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל משֶׁה, וְאֵילוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, אַף צְבָת בִּצְבָת עֲשׂוּיָה:

And some say: also the demons, and the burial place of Moses, and the ram of Abraham our father. And some say: also tongs made with tongs.**

Grammar:

- The mishnah lists ten created things in an elliptical series of nouns after the heading 'and these are they'; each after the first is joined with וְ-. No verb is repeated.
- בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת, literally 'between the suns', is the idiom for twilight; the mishnah means twilight of the first Friday evening, at the close of creation.
- וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, 'and there are those who say', is the mishnaic form for an anonymous alternative opinion; here it adds three further items, then another.
- The Hebrew uses שֶׁל ('of') for possession in קְבוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה and אֵילוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם: the suffix on the noun is doubled by the phrase with שֶׁל.
- צְבָת בִּצְבָת עֲשׂוּיָה gives the reason of those who say it: tongs are made with tongs, so the first tongs must have been made by Heaven. Bartenura adds that the Gemara (Pesachim 54) answers that the first could have been cast in a mould.

Note: The ten are: the mouth of the earth, the mouth of the well, the mouth of the donkey, the bow, the manna, the staff, the shamir, the script, the inscription, the tablets; the other lists add the demons, the burial of Moses, Abraham's ram, and the tongs. The pack's lexicon links וְהַמָּן to מִן; the manna is meant. הַכְּתָב and הַמִּכְתָּב: Bartenura takes the script as the form of the letters engraved on the tablets and the inscription as the writing readable from all four sides; Rambam reads the script as the Torah written before God and the inscription as the writing on the tablets. The English 'script' and 'inscription' keeps both. הַמַּזִּיקִין is rendered 'the demons' after Bartenura (the Hebrew is literally 'the harmful ones').

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'twilight' is on the eve of the first Sabbath of creation, before creation was completed. The English reads 'between the suns' as twilight.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the mouth of the earth was to swallow Korah and his company. The English keeps 'the mouth of the earth'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Miriam's well, which went with Israel in the wilderness on all their journeys; and some say it opened its mouth and sang, 'Spring up, O well' (Numbers 21:17). The English keeps 'the mouth of the well'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: at twilight it was decreed that the donkey would speak with Balaam. The English keeps 'the mouth of the donkey'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the rainbow is the sign of the covenant that there will not again be a flood. The English renders קֶשֶׁת as 'rainbow'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the manna that came down for Israel for forty years in the wilderness. The English renders הַמָּן as 'the manna'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the staff with which the signs were done, which was of sapphire. The English keeps 'the staff'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the shamir is a kind of worm the size of a barleycorn; when it was shown to stones marked out with ink, they split of themselves, and with it the stones of the ephod and the breastplate were engraved, as is written of them 'in their settings'. The English keeps the name 'shamir'.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: the script is the form of the letters engraved on the tablets. Rambam takes it as the Torah written before God. The English keeps the neutral 'script' and records Rambam's reading.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the inscription could be read from all four sides. The English renders הַמִּכְתָּב as 'the inscription'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the tablets were of sapphire, six handbreadths long, six wide and three thick, split from one block, rolled, and hewn from the sun's disc. The English keeps 'the tablets'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the harmful ones are the demons: after God created Adam and Eve He was busy creating them, and when He created their spirits He had not time to create their bodies before the day was sanctified, so spirits were left without bodies. The English renders הַמַּזִּיקִין as 'the demons'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: it was decreed at twilight that the ram would be caught in the thicket by its horns at the time of the binding. The English keeps 'the ram of Abraham our father'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: tongs can only be made with other tongs, so who made the first; it must have been made by itself, by Heaven, and created at twilight. The Gemara (Pesachim 54) rejects this, since the first tongs could have been cast in a mould. The English keeps the riddle 'tongs made with tongs'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: 'who made the first tongs': he explains that at the beginning of things God set in nature all that would be done, whether as natural events or rare miracles, so on the sixth day He set in nature that the earth should swallow Korah, the water come out, the donkey speak, and so on; the script is the Torah written before Him, the inscription the writing on the tablets. The English follows the riddle; his reading of the script is recorded under 5:6:9.

Apparatus:

- Cross-references: Numbers 16:32 (Korah), Numbers 21:17-18 (the well), Numbers 22:28 (the donkey), Genesis 9:13 (the bow), Exodus 16 (the manna), Exodus 4:17 (the staff), Exodus 32:16 (the tablets and the inscription), Deuteronomy 34:6 (the burial of Moses), Genesis 22:13 (the ram).
- Alternative opinions: the first list is ten; 'some say' adds the demons, Moses' burial place and Abraham's ram; a second 'some say' adds tongs, which are made with tongs.
- Open question: whether the shamir, the script and the inscription are physical objects or the Torah's text is the difference between Bartenura and Rambam.

#### Pirkei Avot 5:7

> שִׁבְעָה דְבָרִים בַּגֹּלֶם וְשִׁבְעָה בֶחָכָם. חָכָם אֵינוֹ מְדַבֵּר בִּפְנֵי מִי שֶׁהוּא גָדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ בְחָכְמָה וּבְמִנְיָן, וְאֵינוֹ נִכְנָס לְתוֹךְ דִּבְרֵי חֲבֵרוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ נִבְהָל לְהָשִׁיב, שׁוֹאֵל כָּעִנְיָן וּמֵשִׁיב כַּהֲלָכָה, וְאוֹמֵר עַל רִאשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן וְעַל אַחֲרוֹן אַחֲרוֹן, וְעַל מַה שֶּׁלֹּא שָׁמַע, אוֹמֵר לֹא שָׁמָעְתִּי, וּמוֹדֶה עַל הָאֱמֶת. וְחִלּוּפֵיהֶן בַּגֹּלֶם:

**Seven things are in the unformed person, and seven in the wise person. The wise person does not speak in the presence of one who is greater than he in wisdom and in number; does not break into his fellow's words; is not hasty to answer; asks to the point and answers according to the law; speaks to the first point first and to the last point last; says of what he has not heard, "I have not heard"; and admits the truth. And their opposites are in the unformed person.**

Literal: seven things in-the-golem and-seven in-the-wise. wise not speaking in-presence-of who he great from-him in-wisdom and-in-number, and-not entering into-midst-of words-of his-fellow, and-not being-hurried to-answer, asking like-the-matter and-answering like-the-law, and-saying on first first and-on last last, and-on what that-not he-heard saying not I-heard, and-admitting on the-truth. and-their-opposites in-the-golem.

Grammar:

- שִׁבְעָה דְבָרִים: the numeral שִׁבְעָה (feminine form) stands with the masculine noun, as is usual for the numbers 3 to 10.
- The seven traits of the wise person are a string of present-tense clauses built on participles (מְדַבֵּר, נִכְנָס, נִבְהָל, שׁוֹאֵל, מֵשִׁיב, אוֹמֵר, מוֹדֶה); the negative is אֵינוֹ + participle.
- The relative שֶׁ appears twice: מִי שֶׁהוּא גָדוֹל ('one who is great') and מַה שֶּׁלֹּא שָׁמַע ('what he did not hear').
- The doubling רִאשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן ... אַחֲרוֹן אַחֲרוֹן is distributive: each item in its own place.
- The mishnah gives a list of seven, then closes with the rule וְחִלּוּפֵיהֶן בַּגֹּלֶם: the opposite of each trait belongs to the golem.

Note: גֹּלֶם is kept as 'the unformed person' with the literal sense (an unfinished vessel) in the token note; it is not 'golem' of later legend. חָכָם is 'the wise person', the type, not תַּלְמִיד חָכָם. הֲלָכָה is 'the law' (the settled rule). מִנְיָן is left as 'number': years, numbers of disciples and numbers of those who study are all possible, and neither Bartenura nor Rambam decides it. The lexicon entry offered for שִׁבְעָה (Shebah) is the wrong homograph; the word is the numeral.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: גֹּלֶם is like גָּלְמֵי כֵּלִים, vessels whose work is not finished; so a person not completed in mind, neither in character nor in wisdom, is called a golem. The English 'unformed person' follows this.
- Bartenura (not-applicable): Bartenura gives an example (Elazar and Itamar did not speak before their father Aaron when Moses was angry). It does not change the plain sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he does not confuse the speaker; cites Num 12 'hear my words' (wait for me until I speak). 'Break into his fellow's words' fits this.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he is not hasty to answer so that his answer will be according to the law; compares Elihu in Job 36.
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: this counts as one thing: the student asks about the very subject being studied, and then the teacher answers according to the law; an off-topic question can lead the teacher to answer wrongly. The English, with the wise person as subject of both 'asks' and 'answers', follows Rambam; Bartenura's division between student and teacher is kept here.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he answers each question in its order, as God answered Moses' first objection (Ex 3:11) and then the second. The English keeps the order sense: first point first, last point last.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: if he rules from his own reasoning he does not say 'so I heard from my teachers'; the people of Haran told Jacob what they knew and sent him to Rachel. He says 'I have not heard' about what he has not heard.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he admits the truth even though he could uphold his words with arguments; Moses admitted 'I heard and forgot' (Lev 10) and was not ashamed.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the opposite of these traits of the wise person belongs to the golem. The English follows this.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam defines the four types (bor, am ha'aretz, golem, wise): the golem has both intellectual and ethical qualities, but incomplete and confused, like a vessel not yet finished. He splits the seven into four of character (not speaking before a greater, not interrupting, not claiming to have heard what he has not, admitting the truth even when he could argue it away) and three of intellect: וְאֵינוֹ נִבְהָל לְהָשִׁיב, which he reads as not being confounded when someone tries to mislead him but quickly seeing the error; asking what belongs to the subject and answering from the side the question asks (כהלכה); and ordering what should come first and last. On נִבְהָל the English follows Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah ('hasty'); Rambam's reading is recorded in the apparatus.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: it does not mean answering the first question first and the last last; rather, if the first question is made clear by the last, he explains the last first and then the first. This is a real alternative reading of the order; the English keeps the plain 'first point first'.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads בגולם (without niqqud) at 5:7.3 and 5:7.46, חבירו at 5:7.20; 5:7.15 וּבְמִנְיָן is absent in Vilna.
- Numbers and nouns: the text is Mishnaic Hebrew; Torat Emet is the base.
- Rambam reads וְאֵינוֹ נִבְהָל לְהָשִׁיב as 'is not confounded in answering': when someone tries to mislead him he is not left in doubt but quickly finds the error. The English 'is not hasty to answer' follows Bartenura (כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ כַּהֲלָכָה) and Rabbeinu Yonah (אינו ממהר להשיב).
- בַּגֹּלֶם: Vilna reads בגולם (spelling)
- וּבְמִנְיָן: Vilna reads — (word)
- חֲבֵרוֹ: Vilna reads חבירו (spelling)
- בַּגֹּלֶם: Vilna reads בגולם (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:8

> שִׁבְעָה מִינֵי פֻרְעָנֻיּוֹת בָּאִין לָעוֹלָם עַל שִׁבְעָה גוּפֵי עֲבֵרָה. מִקְצָתָן מְעַשְּׂרִין וּמִקְצָתָן אֵינָן מְעַשְּׂרִין, רָעָב שֶׁל בַּצֹּרֶת בָּאָה, מִקְצָתָן רְעֵבִים וּמִקְצָתָן שְׂבֵעִים. גָּמְרוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְעַשֵּׂר, רָעָב שֶׁל מְהוּמָה וְשֶׁל בַּצֹּרֶת בָּאָה. וְשֶׁלֹּא לִטֹּל אֶת הַחַלָּה, רָעָב שֶׁל כְּלָיָה בָאָה. דֶּבֶר בָּא לָעוֹלָם עַל מִיתוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא נִמְסְרוּ לְבֵית דִּין, וְעַל פֵּרוֹת שְׁבִיעִית. חֶרֶב בָּאָה לָעוֹלָם עַל עִנּוּי הַדִּין, וְעַל עִוּוּת הַדִּין, וְעַל הַמּוֹרִים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֲלָכָה:

**Seven kinds of calamity come to the world for seven principal transgressions. When some of them tithe and some do not tithe, a famine of drought comes: some go hungry and some are sated. When they have resolved not to tithe, a famine of tumult and of drought comes. And for not taking the dough-offering, a famine of annihilation comes. Pestilence comes to the world for the death penalties stated in the Torah that were not delivered to the court, and for the produce of the seventh year. Sword comes to the world for the delaying of justice, for the perverting of justice, and for those who teach the Torah not according to the law.**

Literal: seven kinds-of calamities coming to-the-world on seven bodies-of transgression. some-of-them tithing and-some-of-them not tithing, famine of drought comes; some-of-them hungry and-some-of-them sated. they-resolved that-not to-tithe, famine of tumult and-of drought comes. and-that-not to-take [obj] the-dough-offering, famine of annihilation comes. pestilence comes to-the-world on deaths the-stated in-the-Torah that-not they-were-delivered to-house-of judgment, and-on fruits-of seventh-year. sword comes to-the-world on delay-of the-judgment, and-on perversion-of the-judgment, and-on the-teaching in-the-Torah that-not like-the-law.

Grammar:

- The mishnah is built on a refrain: 'X comes to the world for Y'. The verb is the participle throughout: בָּאִין (masculine plural), בָּאָה (feminine singular) and בָּא (5:8.41, masculine singular with דֶּבֶר). בָּא has the same letters as the perfect, but the parallel clauses show it is the participle.
- שֶׁל is the genitive particle of Mishnaic Hebrew (רָעָב שֶׁל בַּצֹּרֶת 'a famine of drought'), where biblical Hebrew would use the construct state.
- מִקְצָתָן ... וּמִקְצָתָן: 'some of them ... and some of them', a distributive pair; מִקְצָתָן is מִן + קֶצֶת + suffix.
- The conditions of the first three famines are elliptical: 'some tithe and some do not', 'they resolved not to tithe', 'and not to take the dough-offering' (the verb of the earlier clause is carried over). The English fills in only what the verb requires.
- הַמּוֹרִים is a Hifil participle of ירה, 'teach, direct' (the root of תּוֹרָה); the line plays on the word 'Torah'.

Note: פֻרְעָנוּת is 'calamity'; גּוּפֵי עֲבֵרָה is 'principal transgressions' (literally 'bodies of transgression'). The mishnah's list is elliptical; the English does not spell out a conditional for the dough-offering clause ('And for not taking the dough-offering'). The pack's first lexicon entry for בָּא is Jastrow 'בָּא I' (father), a wrong homograph; the tokens are assigned to Jastrow 'בָּא III' (the participle of בוא, 'coming'). The bdbs entries for בַּיִת (a place name), שִׁבְעָה (Shebah) and תּוֹרָה ('law of man') are likewise wrong; Jastrow's entries are used.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the rains are few, and so the price rises. This fixes 'a famine of drought' as lack of rain.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: because of armies they cannot gather the crop. This gives 'a famine of tumult' its sense (war), which the English keeps in 'tumult'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the heavens like iron and the earth like bronze (Deut 28:23); this is total drought, the 'annihilation' famine.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'not delivered to the court' means that no judgment of the Torah was carried out on them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they trade in the produce of the seventh year and do not treat it with the sanctity of the seventh year.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they know which way the case will fall and delay, and do not rule. The English 'delaying' follows this.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: to acquit the guilty and convict the innocent; hence 'perverting' of justice.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: to forbid what is permitted and permit what is forbidden. This explains 'not according to the law'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: drought famine is little rain, in some places none, and where it falls, little; tumult famine is people occupied in wars and quarrels so that the land lies unsown; annihilation famine is no rain at all, rivers dry up, as in 'your heavens shall be bronze'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: עִנּוּי הַדִּין is delay of judgment and long study of a matter that is clear; עִוּוּת הַדִּין is judging by what is not proper. The English 'delaying' and 'perverting' follow this.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah on the tumult famine: it comes through war and calamities so that people cannot work their land; the measure for the measure of all not tithing. Not a different reading of the words, kept as context.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads פורעניות, עבירה, בצורת (twice), ליטול, פירות (spelling only).
- At 5:8.55 Vilna reads בא for בָּאָה.
- Source verses are not quoted in the mishnah; the commentators cite Deut 28:23 for the annihilation famine.
- פֻרְעָנֻיּוֹת: Vilna reads פורעניות (spelling)
- עֲבֵרָה: Vilna reads עבירה (spelling)
- בַּצֹּרֶת: Vilna reads בצורת (spelling)
- בַּצֹּרֶת: Vilna reads בצורת (spelling)
- לִטֹּל: Vilna reads ליטול (spelling)
- פֵּרוֹת: Vilna reads פירות (spelling)
- בָּאָה: Vilna reads בא (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:9

> חַיָּה רָעָה בָאָה לָעוֹלָם עַל שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא, וְעַל חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם. גָּלוּת בָּאָה לָעוֹלָם עַל עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְעַל גִלּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, וְעַל שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים, וְעַל הַשְׁמָטַת הָאָרֶץ. בְּאַרְבָּעָה פְרָקִים הַדֶּבֶר מִתְרַבֶּה, בָּרְבִיעִית, וּבַשְּׁבִיעִית, וּבְמוֹצָאֵי שְׁבִיעִית, וּבְמוֹצָאֵי הֶחָג שֶׁבְּכָל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה. בָּרְבִיעִית, מִפְּנֵי מַעְשַׂר עָנִי שֶׁבַּשְּׁלִישִׁית. בַּשְּׁבִיעִית, מִפְּנֵי מַעְשַׂר עָנִי שֶׁבַּשִּׁשִּׁית. וּבְמוֹצָאֵי שְׁבִיעִית, מִפְּנֵי פֵרוֹת שְׁבִיעִית. וּבְמוֹצָאֵי הֶחָג שֶׁבְּכָל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה, מִפְּנֵי גֶזֶל מַתְּנוֹת עֲנִיִּים:

**A wild beast comes to the world for a vain oath and for the profanation of the Name. Exile comes to the world for those who worship idols, for forbidden sexual relations, for the shedding of blood, and for violating the release of the land. At four times pestilence increases: in the fourth year, in the seventh, at the close of the seventh year, and at the close of the festival in every single year. In the fourth, because of the poor man's tithe of the third. In the seventh, because of the poor man's tithe of the sixth. At the close of the seventh year, because of the produce of the seventh year. And at the close of the festival in every single year, because of the robbery of the gifts to the poor.**

Literal: beast evil comes to-the-world on oath-of vanity, and-on profanation-of the-Name. exile comes to-the-world on worshippers-of worship foreign, and-on uncovering-of nakednesses, and-on shedding-of bloods, and-on the-release-of the-land. in-four periods the-pestilence increases: in-the-fourth, and-in-the-seventh, and-at-the-going-out-of seventh, and-at-the-going-out-of the-festival that-in-every year and-year. in-the-fourth, because-of tithe-of poor that-in-the-third. in-the-seventh, because-of tithe-of poor that-in-the-sixth. and-at-the-going-out-of seventh, because-of fruits-of seventh. and-at-the-going-out-of the-festival that-in-every year and-year, because-of robbery-of gifts-of poor-people.

Grammar:

- This mishnah has two parts: a second list of calamities (wild beast, exile), then the four times at which pestilence increases, each with its reason.
- חַיָּה רָעָה, 'a wild beast', is a noun with an attributive adjective; the participle בָאָה agrees with the feminine noun.
- עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה: a participle in the construct state, 'worshippers of foreign worship'.
- The four times are given first in a bare list (בָּרְבִיעִית, וּבַשְּׁבִיעִית ...), then each is explained with מִפְּנֵי 'because of' (literally 'from the face of'). The repeated forms have the preposition בְּ + the feminine ordinal as a noun ('in the fourth', 'in the seventh'), with 'year' understood.
- וְשָׁנָה: 'every year and year', a doubling that makes the phrase distributive: every single year.

Note: 'The Name' (הַשֵּׁם) stands for God; no decision on this phrase, so the Hebrew word is kept in English capitalised. עֲרָיוֹת is rendered 'forbidden sexual relations' (literally 'nakednesses'). הַשְׁמָטַת הָאָרֶץ is 'the release of the land'; the English adds 'violating' following Bartenura (they plough and sow in the sabbatical year). The 'fourth' and 'seventh' are years of the seven-year sabbatical cycle, supplied from the explanation that follows (the poor man's tithe falls in the third and sixth years). The bdbs entries for מוֹצָא (Moza, a personal name), מַתָּנָה (Mattanah), שֵׁם (Shem) and שָׁנָה (the verb 'repeat') are wrong homographs; the tokens are assigned to Jastrow's מוֹצָא III, מַתָּנָה and שֵׁם II and to bdbs:שָׁנֶה 'year'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא is an oath 'for nothing', not needed. The English 'vain oath' follows this.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: profanation of the Name is sinning openly, defiantly; or that people see and learn from his deeds. This is kept in the note rather than in the English.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they plough and sow in the seventh year. The English 'violating' reflects this.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: in the third and sixth years the poor man's tithe is set aside in place of the second tithe set aside in the other years of the cycle.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: gifts to the poor are gleanings, the forgotten sheaf, the corner, fallen grapes and single grapes.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: in the third and sixth years one separated the first tithe for the Levite and then the poor man's tithe, in place of the second tithe of other years; the gifts to the poor are gleanings, forgotten sheaf, corner, fallen and single grapes; at the festival the work of the land is finished, so whoever did not give them has robbed.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads בא for בָאָה at 5:9.12; שפיכת for שְׁפִיכוּת at 5:9.22; פירות for פֵרוֹת at 5:9.53.
- Deut 32:24 (teeth of beasts) is cited by Rabbeinu Yonah for the wild beast; Lev 18:25, 26:30, 26:34 for exile.
- בָּאָה: Vilna reads בא (word)
- שְׁפִיכוּת: Vilna reads שפיכת (spelling)
- פֵרוֹת: Vilna reads פירות (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:10

> אַרְבַּע מִדּוֹת בָּאָדָם. הָאוֹמֵר שֶׁלִּי שֶׁלִּי וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלָּךְ, זוֹ מִדָּה בֵינוֹנִית. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, זוֹ מִדַּת סְדוֹם. שֶׁלִּי שֶׁלְּךָ וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלִּי, עַם הָאָרֶץ. שֶׁלִּי שֶׁלְּךָ וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלָּךְ, חָסִיד. שֶׁלִּי שֶׁלִּי וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלִּי, רָשָׁע:

**There are four dispositions among people. One who says, "What is mine is mine, and what is yours is yours": this is a middling disposition; and some say, this is the disposition of Sodom. "What is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine": an unlearned person. "What is mine is yours, and what is yours is yours": a pious person. "What is mine is mine, and what is yours is mine": a wicked person.**

Literal: four dispositions in-the-person. the-saying mine mine and-yours yours, this disposition middling; and-there-are saying, this disposition-of Sodom. mine yours and-yours mine, people-of the-land. mine yours and-yours yours, pious. mine mine and-yours mine, wicked.

Grammar:

- The four dispositions are given as formulas with no verb: שֶׁלִּי שֶׁלִּי 'mine (is) mine'. שֶׁל + suffix (שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלְּךָ) is the Mishnaic possessive 'of me, of you', the equivalent of 'mine, yours'.
- The clauses are nominal sentences: subject 'mine', predicate 'yours' or 'mine'; the English supplies 'What is ... is ...'.
- וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, 'and some say', introduces a dissenting opinion on the first disposition; the three forms of זוֹ (feminine singular demonstrative) agree with מִדָּה.
- The first disposition is a middle one and the other three are the extremes: 'unlearned' (generous in exchange), 'pious' (generous without return), 'wicked' (takes both).

Note: עַם הָאָרֶץ is rendered 'an unlearned person', as decided; the literal sense is 'people of the land'. Bartenura connects the title with the settling of the land: he seeks the land's good order but has no wisdom to distinguish the proper ways. Rambam does not comment on the title here; at 5:7 he defines the am ha'aretz as one who has good conduct but no learning, fit for the settling of the land. מִדָּה is 'disposition', not 'trait', to allow 'a middling disposition' and 'the disposition of Sodom'. The bdbs entries for מִדָּה ('tribute') and אָדָם (the name Adam) are wrong homographs; the tokens are assigned to Jastrow's מִדָּה ('measure') and אָדָם ('man').

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'mine is mine, yours is yours' means: I do not want to benefit you, and I wish you would not benefit me.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: this can easily lead to the disposition of Sodom, since being used to this he will refuse to let another benefit even where he loses nothing; this was Sodom's way, though the land was wide and they lacked nothing. The English keeps the dissenting opinion as a separate view ('some say').
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he benefits and gives equally, which is the settlement of the land, but he does not know the verse 'he who hates gifts shall live' (Prov 15:27); this is the sense of 'am ha'aretz' everywhere: one who wants the land's good order but lacks the wisdom to distinguish the right ways. The English 'unlearned person' follows.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: he gives people benefit from his property and takes no benefit from others.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a pious person acts beyond the line of the law (לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין).
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the pious person is one who leans a little to one extreme, doing more good than needed; the wicked is one with a base soul who wants his money and the other's money as well, out of great desire.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: asks how the first disposition can be called middling when one who refuses to give charity is wholly wicked; answers that the first opinion deals with one who gives from fear of God but is miserly by nature, and the dissenting view takes him as the disposition of Sodom. Kept as the two readings of the first case.

Apparatus:

- Ezek 16:49 ('and the hand of the poor and needy she did not strengthen') is cited by Rabbeinu Yonah for Sodom; Prov 15:27 by Bartenura for the unlearned person.
- Vilna variants for this mishnah are not marked in the pack.

Grammar:

- The adjectives נוֹחַ 'easy' and קָשֶׁה 'hard' take the infinitive with לְ: נוֹחַ לִכְעֹס 'easy to be angry'. The two infinitives are of Qal כעס and רצה.
- יָצָא שְׂכָרוֹ בְהֶפְסֵדוֹ is an accounting idiom: the reward 'goes out' (is set off) against the loss. Bartenura reads it so that in the first case the loss is greater, and in the second the gain is greater.
- The four dispositions are four combinations of two pairs: quick or slow to anger, quick or slow to be appeased. The 'mixed' cases get an evaluation (gain/loss); the other two get titles (pious, wicked).
- The titles חָסִיד and רָשָׁע are in the same position as in 5:10; they are predicate nouns with no verb.

Note: יָצָא שְׂכָרוֹ בְהֶפְסֵדוֹ is rendered 'his gain is outweighed by his loss', following Bartenura's reading of which side is larger: in the first case the loss, in the second the gain. Bartenura notes that some read the opposite order (וְאִית דְּגַרְסֵי אִפְּכָא) and states that he prefers his reading; the English follows him. 'Temperaments' for דֵּעוֹת is chosen from the context: Rambam speaks of the quality of anger. The bdbs entries for דֵּעָה ('knowledge (of God)'), נוֹחַ (Jastrow's noun 'rest'), כַּעַס (the noun 'anger') and שָׂכָר (the name Sacar) are replaced by Jastrow's דֵּעָה, נוֹחַ II 'easy', the verb כָּעַס and שָׂכָר 'wages, reward'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one who is angry quickly at everything, even if he is appeased quickly, has a loss greater than his gain, since most of his deeds are spoiled; one hard to anger, even though hard to appease, has his small loss outweighed by his large gain, and most of his deeds are sound. Some read the reverse; this reading seems to him primary. The English follows this order.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: note that he called the patient one, whose patience is so great that he almost does not feel anger, a ḥasid, and one who has the defect of anger a wicked person. This agrees with the titles at the end of the English.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: the loss is greater than the gain because while he is appeased quickly, anger rests in his heart and he is quick to anger and sins in the moment; no one can mend what was damaged in anger. This supports Bartenura's reading.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads לכעוס for לִכְעֹס at 5:11.5, 5:11.12, 5:11.19 and 5:11.24 (spelling only).
- Bartenura notes a variant reading of the second sentence in which the gain and loss are reversed (וְאִית דְּגַרְסֵי אִפְּכָא); the English follows his primary reading.

- לִכְעֹס: Vilna reads לכעוס (spelling)
- לִכְעֹס: Vilna reads לכעוס (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:12

> אַרְבַּע מִדּוֹת בַּתַּלְמִידִים. מַהֵר לִשְׁמֹעַ וּמַהֵר לְאַבֵּד, יָצָא שְׂכָרוֹ בְהֶפְסֵדוֹ. קָשֶׁה לִשְׁמֹעַ וְקָשֶׁה לְאַבֵּד, יָצָא הֶפְסֵדוֹ בִשְׂכָרוֹ. מַהֵר לִשְׁמֹעַ וְקָשֶׁה לְאַבֵּד, חָכָם. קָשֶׁה לִשְׁמֹעַ וּמַהֵר לְאַבֵּד, זֶה חֵלֶק רָע:

**There are four dispositions in disciples. Quick to hear and quick to forget: his gain is outweighed by his loss. Hard to hear and hard to forget: his loss is outweighed by his gain. Quick to hear and hard to forget: a wise person. Hard to hear and quick to forget: this is a bad lot.**

Grammar:

- The adjectives מַהֵר ('quick') and קָשֶׁה ('hard') take the infinitive with לְ, as in 5:11. The infinitive לְאַבֵּד is Piel of אבד ('make lost'), used for losing what one has learned.
- The wording of the first two cases (יָצָא שְׂכָרוֹ בְהֶפְסֵדוֹ ...) repeats 5:11, as does the pattern of four combinations.
- The last two cases do not give a character label but one a skill word (חָכָם) and one a lot in life (חֵלֶק רָע), because, as Bartenura and Rambam say, these are not matters of choice.
- The demonstrative זֶה is the subject of the last clause, with חֵלֶק רָע as predicate: 'this is a bad lot'.

Note: לְאַבֵּד is rendered 'to forget' (literally 'to lose'), which is the Mishnaic sense of letting something go from memory. חֵלֶק רָע is 'a bad lot' (literally 'an evil portion'): Bartenura and Rambam both say the fault is not within a person's choice. The words חָסִיד and רָשָׁע are not used here for that reason. חָכָם here is 'a wise person', not the compound 'disciple of the sages'; Rambam names it an intellectual virtue. The bdbs entries for חֵלֶק (the name Helek), זֶה ('lamb') and שָׂכָר (the name Sacar) are wrong homographs; Jastrow's entries are used.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since he forgets what he learns, what benefit is there in his being quick to hear? His loss is greater than his gain.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the good quality in him exceeds the spoiled one, since what he hears after difficulty he remembers and does not forget. Practical result: if we have two students and can supply food for only one, we put first the one who is hard to forget before the one quick to hear.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: it was not fitting to say 'pious' or 'wicked' here, since this does not depend on a person's choice, but is a deficiency in him from the very beginning of his creation. The English 'a bad lot' follows.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: note how he did not call the one with good memory 'pious' since it is an intellectual virtue, and called him wise; nor did he call the one slow to understand and prone to forget 'wicked', since this is not in his hands and not among the virtues one can acquire.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: the gain is greater since what comes to him with great effort he does not forget; both should keep to learning Torah, for they have good reward in their toil; and from this we learn to put the one with good memory ahead of the forgetful where there is food for one only.

Grammar:

- מִדּוֹת here means 'types, patterns'; the series 'four types' recurs in 5:14-15 (and 5:10-12).
- The participle הָרוֹצֶה with the relative שֶׁ is a headless relative: 'the one who wants that ...'.
- The imperfects יִתֵּן / יִתְּנוּ after שֶׁ express what is wanted; after the first clause the verb 'wants' is understood.
- עֵינוֹ רָעָה, 'his eye is evil', is the idiom for grudgingness; בְּשֶׁל is the Mishnaic genitive 'in that which is of'.
- The four types are given as bare predicates (חָסִיד, רָשָׁע): the first two have an evil eye, the third is pious, the fourth wicked.

Note: The mishnah gives the first two types no label beyond 'evil eye'; the English keeps this. In the second, third and fourth types the Hebrew has bare imperfects, and הָרוֹצֶה is understood from the first clause. The English supplies 'wants' in all three, as Rambam reads the third (the pious man is not content that he alone shows mercy but wants others to show it too). The pack's BDB entries for אַרְבַּע (Arba, a name), מִדָּה (tribute), עַיִן (Ain, a place) and אַחַר (the adverb 'after') are the wrong words. The tokens are pointed to the Jastrow entries the pack lists, or carry no sense.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'four types in the giving of charity', not literally 'in givers of charity', since one type does not give; likewise the next mishnah means 'in the going to the house of study'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the first has an evil eye because he knows that charity enriches and does not want others enriched. Another explanation: he spares his relatives' money more than his own and does not want them to lose it, like the evil eye 'in his own' below.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: see how he called the merciful one 'pious' - it is not enough for him that he alone has mercy until others too have mercy - and the cruel one 'wicked'.

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads 'wants that he give and not others' as wanting all the good and praise for himself, and the miser as 'kilai'.

| וְלֹא | and not | ו: and + לֹא |  | conjunction + particle (negative particle) | 1 |
| עוֹשֶׂה | doing | עָשָׂה | עשה | verb (qal, participle active, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.1.1.1 |
| רָשָׁע | wicked | רָשָׁע | רשע | adjective (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- Pattern as in 5:13: four types, each defined by a pair of participles (הוֹלֵךְ, עוֹשֶׂה); the participles are subjects ('one who ...').
- וְאֵינוֹ is אֵין with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'and he is not'; it negates the participle that follows.
- הֲלִיכָה (a Mishnaic verbal noun, 'going') is contrasted with מַעֲשֶׂה, 'deed, doing'.
- שְׂכַר ... בְיָדוֹ: 'the reward ... is in his hand', i.e. he holds it, it is his.

Note: The English keeps 'does' because the Hebrew word is עוֹשֶׂה. Bartenura (normative) reads 'does' in the first clause as 'learns, reviews and understands' (the one who goes to hear but does not study) and the second as one who studies at home; Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads it as practising the commandments, the first as one who does not seek them out. The English leaves the word open; the reading is recorded rather than adopted.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: he goes to the house of study to hear but does not review and learn and does not understand ('does' read as studying).
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: he learns and reviews in a house of study that is in his own house ('does' read as studying; 'goes' as going out to the public house of study).
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the going to the house of study has four types; note that he called the one who increases in acquiring virtues pious and the one who is lazy about acquiring them wicked.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam's long digression on intellectual and moral virtues, the mean and the extremes, and the terms 'pious', 'sinner', 'unlearned' and 'wise' does not bear on the plain sense of this mishnah.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah: 'does not do' does not mean he does nothing of what he heard, for then he would be wholly wicked; he does not seek out the commandments and does them only when they come to hand.

#### Pirkei Avot 5:15

> אַרְבַּע מִדּוֹת בְּיוֹשְׁבִים לִפְנֵי חֲכָמִים. סְפוֹג, וּמַשְׁפֵּךְ, מְשַׁמֶּרֶת, וְנָפָה. סְפוֹג, שֶׁהוּא סוֹפֵג אֶת הַכֹּל. מַשְׁפֵּךְ, שֶׁמַּכְנִיס בְּזוֹ וּמוֹצִיא בְזוֹ. מְשַׁמֶּרֶת, שֶׁמּוֹצִיאָה אֶת הַיַּיִן וְקוֹלֶטֶת אֶת הַשְּׁמָרִים. וְנָפָה, שֶׁמּוֹצִיאָה אֶת הַקֶּמַח וְקוֹלֶטֶת אֶת הַסֹּלֶת:

**There are four types among those who sit before the sages: a sponge, a funnel, a strainer, and a sieve. A sponge, because it absorbs everything. Grammar:

- The four types are first listed as nouns (סְפוֹג, מַשְׁפֵּךְ, מְשַׁמֶּרֶת, נָפָה) and then each is explained by a clause with שֶׁ ('because it ...').
- The explanations use participles (סוֹפֵג, מַכְנִיס, מוֹצִיא, קוֹלֶטֶת) to describe a habitual action.
- בְּזוֹ ... בְזוֹ, 'in this ... in that', is the Mishnaic use of זוֹ (feminine) as demonstrative pronoun; the antecedent is the two openings (or ends) of the funnel.
- אֶת marks the definite objects of מוֹצִיאָה and קוֹלֶטֶת; it has no English counterpart.
- מְשַׁמֶּרֶת (filter) and נָפָה (sieve) are fem. nouns, hence the fem. participles מוֹצִיאָה, קוֹלֶטֶת.

Note: The mishnah gives only the utensils; the commentators (Bartenura, Rambam) supply the application to the disciple: the sponge cannot tell truth from falsehood, the funnel forgets, the strainer keeps the worthless, the sieve keeps the valued. The English keeps the images without the application. On קֶמַח and סֹלֶת: for Bartenura and Rambam the קֶמַח that passes through the sieve is the fine powder and the סֹלֶת kept is the coarse, choice part, so the English says 'fine meal' and 'choice flour'. The 'this/that' of the funnel is rendered literally.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: above, the four types of disciples concerned memory and forgetting; now the mishnah concerns sound reasoning and sifting the valid from the invalid.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the sponge absorbs water, cloudy or clear; so one has a wide heart and accepts all he hears and cannot tell truth from falsehood.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a funnel is a vessel set on the mouth of a barrel or skin when filling it with wine or oil.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: one takes in all he learns but as he swallows it so he spits it out.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the strainer lets out all he hears in the house of study and retains the worthless.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the sifted fine meal falls through and the coarse, valued סֹלֶת remains; so one can sort and clarify what he hears, retaining the true and letting go the false.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: the sponge (sea-wool) absorbs everything, true and false; the funnel is one who understands at once and remembers nothing; the strainer remembers the bad and forgets the true; the sieve lets out the fine dust and keeps the choice flour.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads ביושבי for בְּיוֹשְׁבִים (5:15.3) and הסולת for הַסֹּלֶת (5:15.33): spelling/word variants, no change in sense.
- בְּיוֹשְׁבִים: Vilna reads ביושבי (word)
- הַסֹּלֶת: Vilna reads הסולת (spelling)

Grammar:

- The first saying is a conditional without a particle: בָּטֵל דָּבָר, בְּטֵלָה אַהֲבָה, '(when) the thing ceases, the love ceases'. Each predicate stands before its subject.
- בְּטֵלָה is the feminine singular of the stative participle (verbal adjective) בָּטֵל, 'ceasing, void', and agrees with אַהֲבָה. The feminine perfect would be בָּטְלָה. The masculine בָּטֵל agrees with דָּבָר; it can be read as the same participle or as the stative perfect 'has ceased'.
- וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ is 'and that which is not' (ש + אֵין + 3rd fem. sing. suffix): the headless relative stands for 'a love which ...'.
- Question and answer: אֵיזוֹ הִיא ... זוֹ ..., 'which is ...? This is ...'; אֵיזוֹ is the feminine of אֵיזֶה, 'which'.
- אַהֲבַת is the construct of אַהֲבָה: 'love of'.

Note: דָּבָר is kept as 'a thing' because it is general: the commentators explain it as the cause or object on which the love depends (beauty in Amnon's case; a lasting purpose for David and Jonathan). The pack's BDB entry for זֶה ('lamb') is the wrong word, so the demonstratives point to Jastrow's זֶה, 'this'. For בָּטֵל, Jastrow's sense 2 ('to cease to exist') is the right one; Jastrow cites this mishnah there. The BDB entry for תָּמָר has David's daughter at sense 4.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: love that depends on a thing does not last: when the thing that caused the love ceases, so does the love. Love not dependent on a thing that perishes but on a lasting thing, such as love of the righteous and the sages, never ceases.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on Amnon and Tamar: because of her beauty.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura on David and Jonathan: to fulfil the will of their Creator, since Jonathan said to David 'You will be king over Israel and I will be second to you'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: bodily causes pass away and what depends on them passes with them; when the cause of love is divine, namely true knowledge, the love can never cease because its cause is permanent.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the love of Jonathan for David did not cease though he risked losing the kingship; the love of Amnon and Tamar needs no elaboration.

Apparatus:

- Names: Amnon and Tamar: 2 Samuel 13; David and Jonathan: 1 Samuel 18-20, 2 Samuel 1:26.

Grammar:

- סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם: 'its end is to endure/be established'; the infinitive with לְ gives the outcome ('is destined to'), and סוֹף 'end' can mean outcome or goal.
- Negative counterpart: אֵין סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם, 'it is not its end to endure'; אֵין negates the nominal clause.
- לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, 'for the name/sake of Heaven': 'Heaven' is the Mishnaic reverent name for God.
- מַחֲלֹקֶת (Vilna מחלוקת) is a Mishnaic feminine noun, 'dispute', from the root of 'division'; the pack's BDB entry glosses it as 'division, course', the nearest sense.
- Question and answer: אֵיזוֹ הִיא ... זוֹ ...; the second case reuses the headless relative וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ.

Note: סוֹפָהּ is rendered 'in the end' so that the English keeps the ambiguity the commentators discuss: for Bartenura's first reading the disputants endure (Hillel's and Shammai's disciples did not perish, Korah's company did); in his second reading the aim of the dispute, the truth, is what endures. The English 'will in the end endure' allows both. Korah's dispute: Numbers 16.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the disputants themselves endure and do not perish (neither Shammai's nor Hillel's disciples perished, while Korah and his company did). He also reports another reading: 'its end' is the aim sought, to attain the truth, which endures ('truth emerges from the argument'), as the law follows Beit Hillel.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the disputants endure, argue about one thing today and another tomorrow, and the dispute continues all their lives; they are given length of days besides.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the dispute not for the sake of Heaven ends at the first dispute, where the disputants die, like Korah's.

Apparatus:

- Vilna reads מחלוקת, להתקיים, and שהוא for שֶׁהִיא: spelling variants, no change in sense (5:17.2, 7, 13, 16, 17, 21, 28).

#### Pirkei Avot 5:18

> כָּל הַמְזַכֶּה אֶת הָרַבִּים, אֵין חֵטְא בָּא עַל יָדוֹ. וְכָל הַמַּחֲטִיא אֶת הָרַבִּים, אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה. משֶׁה זָכָה וְזִכָּה אֶת הָרַבִּים, זְכוּת הָרַבִּים תָּלוּי בּוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים לג) צִדְקַת ה' עָשָׂה וּמִשְׁפָּטָיו עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל. יָרָבְעָם חָטָא וְהֶחֱטִיא אֶת הָרַבִּים, חֵטְא הָרַבִּים תָּלוּי בּוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מלכים א טו) עַל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם (בֶּן נְבָט) אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וַאֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל:

**Whoever makes the many meritorious, no sin comes through him. And whoever causes the many to sin, they do not give him the means to repent. Moses was meritorious and made the many meritorious; the merit of the many rests on him, as it is said, Deuteronomy 33: "He performed the righteousness of the LORD, and His judgments with Israel." Jeroboam sinned and caused the many to sin; the sin of the many rests on him, as it is said, 1 Kings 15: "For the sins of Jeroboam (son of Nebat), which he sinned and which he caused Israel to sin."**

Literal: all the-causing-merit [obj] the-many, not sin coming upon his-hand; and-all the-causing-to-sin [obj] the-many, not they-give-means in-his-hand to-do repentance; Moses merited and-caused-merit [obj] the-many, merit-of the-many hanging in-him, as-it-is-said (Deuteronomy 33) righteousness-of YHWH he-did and-his-judgments with Israel; Jeroboam sinned and-caused-to-sin [obj] the-many, sin-of the-many hanging in-him, as-it-is-said (Kings I 15) upon sins-of Jeroboam (son-of Nebat) which sinned and-which caused-to-sin [obj] Israel

Grammar:

- זִכָּה (Piel/causative of זָכָה) 'made meritorious, caused to have merit' contrasts with the Qal זָכָה 'was meritorious': Moses was meritorious and made others so.
- הַמַּחֲטִיא (Hiphil of חָטָא) 'one who causes to sin' parallels הַמְזַכֶּה; both are participles with the article used as 'whoever'.
- אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ is an impersonal plural: 'they do not enable him' (Heaven does not supply him the means); the verb is Hiphil of ספק, 'supply, suffice', here 'give the opportunity'.
- תָּלוּי בּוֹ, 'hangs on him', means 'depends on him / is credited to him'; it is the passive participle of תָּלָה.
- The two proof-texts are Deuteronomy 33:21 and 1 Kings 15:30; the Hebrew's brackets give the chapter (and the optional name 'son of Nebat'). The Vilna text has the references in the margin as כא and ל.

Note: 'Merit' (זְכוּת) is kept as one English word through the mishnah for the pun on זָכָה / זִכָּה. תָּלוּי בּוֹ is rendered 'rests on him' to keep the sense 'depends on, is attributed to'; 'hangs' is given in the literal line. The impersonal 'they do not give him the means' is kept as an impersonal plural, as in the Hebrew. The pack lists no entry for the verb חָטָא or for the Hiphil of ספק, so those tokens carry no sense.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: no sin comes through him, so that he not be in Gehinnom while his disciples are in the Garden of Eden.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: they do not give him the means to repent, so that he not be in the Garden of Eden while his disciples are in Gehinnom.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'caused the many to be meritorious' - he taught Torah to all Israel.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the judgments that are with Israel are credited to him as if he had made them.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: since the verse does not say 'for the sins of Jeroboam and Israel', learn that everything depends on Jeroboam.
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): so that his disciples not be in Eden and he in Gehinnom, as it is written 'You will not leave my soul to Sheol, nor give Your pious one to see the pit' (Psalms 16:10).
- Rabbeinu Yonah (records): Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): 'the righteousness of the LORD he did' - he completed and kept the whole Torah, he and all Israel with him.

Apparatus:

- Deuteronomy 33:21: צִדְקַת יְהוָה עָשָׂה וּמִשְׁפָּטָיו עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל.
- 1 Kings 15:30: עַל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וַאֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל. The mishnah text has בֶּן נְבָט in brackets.
- Vilna reads וזיכה for וְזִכָּה (5:18.21), and gives the references כא (Deut 33:21) and ל (1 Kings 15:30) as words.
- וְזִכָּה: Vilna reads וזיכה (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads כא (word)
- —: Vilna reads ל (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:19

> כָּל מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים הַלָּלוּ, מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ. וּשְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים אֲחֵרִים, מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע. עַיִן טוֹבָה, וְרוּחַ נְמוּכָה, וְנֶפֶשׁ שְׁפָלָה, מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ. עַיִן רָעָה, וְרוּחַ גְּבוֹהָה, וְנֶפֶשׁ רְחָבָה, מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע. מַה בֵּין תַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ לְתַלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע. תַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ, אוֹכְלִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְנוֹחֲלִין בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (משלי ח) לְהַנְחִיל אֹהֲבַי יֵשׁ, וְאֹצְרֹתֵיהֶם אֲמַלֵּא. אֲבָל תַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע יוֹרְשִׁין גֵּיהִנֹּם וְיוֹרְדִין לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תהלים נה) וְאַתָּה אֱלֹהִים תּוֹרִידֵם לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת, אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים וּמִרְמָה לֹא יֶחֱצוּ יְמֵיהֶם, וַאֲנִי אֶבְטַח בָּךְ:

**Whoever has these three things is of the disciples of Abraham our father; and three other things, of the disciples of Balaam the wicked. A good eye, a humble spirit, and a modest soul: of the disciples of Abraham our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit, and a broad soul: of the disciples of Balaam the wicked. What is the difference between the disciples of Abraham our father and the disciples of Balaam the wicked? The disciples of Abraham our father eat in this world and inherit in the world to come, as it is said: "To bequeath to those who love me substance, and I will fill their treasuries." But the disciples of Balaam the wicked inherit Gehinnom and go down to the pit of destruction, as it is said: "And You, God, will bring them down to the pit of destruction; men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in You."**

Literal: all who that-there-is in-his-hand three things these, from-his-disciples of Abraham our-father. and-three things other, from-his-disciples of Balaam the-wicked. eye good, and-spirit lowly, and-soul low, from-his-disciples of Abraham our-father. eye evil, and-spirit high, and-soul broad, from-his-disciples of Balaam the-wicked. what between his-disciples of Abraham our-father to-his-disciples of Balaam the-wicked? his-disciples of Abraham our-father eat in-the-world the-this and-inherit in-the-world the-coming, that-it-was-said (Proverbs 8) to-bequeath those-who-love-me substance, and-their-treasuries I-will-fill. but his-disciples of Balaam the-wicked inherit Gehinnom and-go-down to-pit-of destruction, that-it-was-said (Psalms 55) and-you God you-will-bring-them-down to-pit-of destruction, men-of blood and-deceit not they-will-halve their-days, and-I I-will-trust in-you.

Grammar:

- The mishnah first states the matter in general terms (whoever has these three things) and then names the things; Rabbeinu Yonah draws from this that these three things are the whole of what makes one a disciple of Abraham or of Balaam.
- The two lists are exact opposites, member for member: good eye / evil eye, lowly spirit / high spirit, low soul / broad soul. The two sets are given in parallel clauses with no verb: 'a good eye ... of the disciples of Abraham'.
- מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל is the Mishnaic genitive with שֶׁל ('of') and a pronominal suffix anticipating the owner: lit. 'from his disciples, of Abraham'. The מִ is partitive.
- The two proof texts are Prov 8:21 and Ps 55:24. In the second the verse is cut after וַאֲנִי אֶבְטַח בָּךְ, which does not describe Balaam's disciples but ends the verse as written.
- Aramaic-style plural participles in -ין (אוֹכְלִין, נוֹחֲלִין, יוֹרְשִׁין, יוֹרְדִין) are normal Mishnaic Hebrew; the mishnah is Hebrew, not Aramaic.

Note: Translation choices. עַיִן טוֹבָה / רָעָה are kept as the literal 'good eye' / 'evil eye', with the commentators' definitions (Bartenura, Rambam: contentment vs. greed) given in the notes. רוּחַ נְמוּכָה 'humble spirit', נֶפֶשׁ שְׁפָלָה 'modest soul' (Bartenura: restraint and abstinence from desires; Rambam: restraint (זְהִירוּת), above all in sexual matters), נֶפֶשׁ רְחָבָה 'broad soul' (great craving). אֹהֲבַי is 'those who love me' (Bartenura reads the verse as naming Abraham 'the lover', Isa 41:8). בְּאֵר שַׁחַת is 'the pit of destruction'; שַׁחַת is both 'pit' and 'destruction/corruption'. Gehinnom is left in Hebrew form per the decisions.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'of his disciples' means one who learns from him and walks in his ways. The English keeps 'of the disciples' with that sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: a good eye is being content with what one has and not coveting others' money; proof Gen 14:23 (Abraham to the king of Sodom: not a thread or a sandal-strap). The English keeps the idiom and the notes give the sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: רוּחַ נְמוּכָה is extra humility (עֲנָוָה יְתֵרָה), as Abraham says 'I am dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: נֶפֶשׁ שְׁפָלָה is caution and abstinence from desires; Abraham 'knew' Sarah's beauty only late (Gen 12:11) out of modesty. He adds that Balaam's evil eye shows in his going for payment (Num 22:18).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Balaam's haughty spirit, shown by 'the utterance of one who hears the words of God and knows the knowledge of the Most High' (Num 24:16).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: נֶפֶשׁ רְחָבָה is great appetite; otherwise Balaam would not have advised exposing the daughters of Moab to immorality; the sages say he lay with his ass (Sanhedrin 105a). The English 'broad soul' is literal and this is the sense.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Abraham is called 'lover' (Isa 41:8); יֵשׁ is the world to come and 'their treasuries I will fill' is this world. The English takes יֵשׁ as 'substance' with this reading noted; the order of worlds in the verse is the reverse of the mishnah's.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: Balaam is called a 'man of blood' because by his counsel twenty-four thousand of Israel fell. The English 'men of blood' keeps the verse's plural.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: disputes for the sake of truth endure. His comment on 'this' in 5:17 about reward and punishment; it does not bear on the wording of 5:19.
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam: whoever makes others righteous is rewarded by being kept from sin, and whoever leads others astray is punished by being kept from repentance. A comment on the previous mishnah; no bearing on the English here.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: a good eye is contentment (הַהִסְתַּפְּקוּת), a lowly soul is restraint from desire (הַזְּהִירוּת), a humble spirit is extra humility; their opposites are greed for money (evil eye), great lust (broad soul) and pride (haughty spirit). He finds each trait in Abraham (Gen 14:23; 12:11; 16:6; 21:11; 18:27) and in Balaam, and explains 'men of blood and deceit' of Balaam.

Apparatus:

- Prov 8:21: לְהַנְחִיל אֹהֲבַי יֵשׁ וְאֹצְרֹתֵיהֶם אֲמַלֵּא.
- Ps 55:24: וְאַתָּה אֱלֹהִים תּוֹרִידֵם לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים וּמִרְמָה לֹא יֶחֱצוּ יְמֵיהֶם וַאֲנִי אֶבְטַח בָּךְ.
- Variant 5:19.32: Vilna reads גבוה (masculine) for גְּבוֹהָה; with רוּחַ (feminine) the base is the regular agreement.
- Variant 5:19.58: Vilna reads הבאין (plural 'those that come') for הַבָּא; the base reads 'the world to come'.
- Variant 5:19.63: Vilna reads אוהבי (full spelling) for אֹהֲבַי. Variant 5:19.65: Vilna reads ואוצרותיהם for וְאֹצְרֹתֵיהֶם.
- The pack also lists two position-less variants (Vilna reads כא and כד) with no base text; they appear to be verse markers and bear on no word.
- גְּבוֹהָה: Vilna reads גבוה (word)
- הַבָּא: Vilna reads הבאין (word)
- —: Vilna reads כא (word)
- אֹהֲבַי: Vilna reads אוהבי (spelling)
- וְאֹצְרֹתֵיהֶם: Vilna reads ואוצרותיהם (spelling)
- —: Vilna reads כד (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:20

> יְהוּדָה בֶן תֵּימָא אוֹמֵר, הֱוֵי עַז כַּנָּמֵר, וְקַל כַּנֶּשֶׁר, וְרָץ כַּצְּבִי, וְגִבּוֹר כָּאֲרִי, לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן אָבִיךָ שֶׁבַּשָּׁמָיִם. הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, עַז פָּנִים לְגֵיהִנֹּם, וּבֹשֶׁת פָּנִים לְגַן עֵדֶן. יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנֶיךָ יְיָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ שֶׁתִּבְנֶה עִירְךָ בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ וְתֵן חֶלְקֵנוּ בְתוֹרָתֶךָ:

**Judah son of Tema says: Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and strong as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven. He used to say: The bold-faced to Gehinnom, and the shamefaced to the Garden of Eden. May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You rebuild Your city speedily in our days, and give us our portion in Your Torah.**

Literal: Judah son-of Tema says: be bold like-a-leopard, and-light like-an-eagle, and-running like-a-deer, and-mighty like-a-lion, to-do the-will-of your-Father who-in-the-heavens. he was saying: bold-of face to-Gehinnom, and-shame-of face to-garden-of Eden. may-it-be will from-before-you YHWH our-God that-you-build your-city in-speed in-our-days, and-give our-portion in-your-Torah.

Grammar:

- The four animal similes are parallel, each of the form adjective + כְּ + animal: bold / leopard, light / eagle, swift / deer, strong / lion. A single purpose phrase, 'to do the will of your Father in Heaven', governs all four.
- The second saying is an elliptical antithesis with no verb: 'bold of face (goes) to Gehinnom, shame of face to the Garden of Eden'. עַז פָּנִים and בֹּשֶׁת פָּנִים are construct chains: עַז is the adjective 'strong, bold' in the construct ('bold of face'), בֹּשֶׁת the noun 'shame' in the construct.
- יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנֶיךָ is the standard petition formula ('may it be Your will') and shifts the form to second person address to God: 'Your city, Your Torah'.
- שֶׁתִּבְנֶה is a purpose/content clause: 'that You build'. In the Mishnaic petition, the verb is in the imperfect after the formula; חֶלְקֵנוּ בְתוֹרָתֶךָ 'our portion in Your Torah' is the second request.
- The words עַז כַּנָּמֵר, וְקַל כַּנֶּשֶׁר, וְרָץ כַּצְּבִי, וְגִבּוֹר כָּאֲרִי pair a trait with its image; the first plays on עַז as both 'fierce' and 'brazen' (cf. עַז פָּנִים below).

Note: עַז פָּנִים is rendered 'bold-faced' and בֹּשֶׁת פָּנִים 'shamefaced' to keep the paired construct chains; the sense is 'the brazen' and 'the bashful'. Rambam and Bartenura read the first saying as boldness in learning and in rebuke for the sake of heaven; the second as the condemned shamelessness. The Tetragrammaton is rendered 'Lord'.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: the leopard is born of a forest boar and a lioness, so being a bastard it is brazen though not truly mighty; so be bold and do not be ashamed to ask your teacher what you do not understand, as 'the shy do not learn'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'light as an eagle' is to hasten after your learning without wearying (Isa 40:31: they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they run and do not grow weary).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'swift as a deer' is to pursue the commandments.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'strong as a lion' is to overcome your inclination away from transgressions.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: brazenness shows on the face (Prov 21:29: a wicked man hardens his face), hence 'bold of face'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'as You have graced us with this trait' (shame, the mark of Abraham's seed: bashful, merciful, doers of kindness; Yevamot 79a), so may it be Your will to rebuild Your city. The English takes this as the link between the two sayings.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: though he says 'the bold-faced to Gehinnom', he commands boldness for reproof, as teachers must reprove, and the like: use a vice in its place for God's will ('with the crooked be subtle'), on condition that the aim is truth, 'to do the will of your Father'. Shame is a gift to this nation (the seed of Abraham is bashful, merciful, kind); so he prays: as You granted us this trait, grant that Your city be rebuilt.

Apparatus:

- Isa 40:31 is cited by Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah for the eagle and the deer; not quoted in the mishnah.
- Variant 5:20.31: Vilna reads ה for the Tetragrammaton written יְיָ in the base text.
- The first saying ('Be bold ...') and the second ('bold of face to Gehinnom') use the same root עַז in different senses; the commentators reconcile them (Rambam: boldness for truth is permitted).
- יְיָ: Vilna reads ה (word)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:21

> הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, בֶּן חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים לַמִּקְרָא, בֶּן עֶשֶׂר לַמִּשְׁנָה, בֶּן שְׁלשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה לַמִּצְוֹת, בֶּן חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה לַתַּלְמוּד, בֶּן שְׁמֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה לַחֻפָּה, בֶּן עֶשְׂרִים לִרְדֹּף, בֶּן שְׁלשִׁים לַכֹּחַ, בֶּן אַרְבָּעִים לַבִּינָה, בֶּן חֲמִשִּׁים לָעֵצָה, בֶּן שִׁשִּׁים לַזִּקְנָה, בֶּן שִׁבְעִים לַשֵּׂיבָה, בֶּן שְׁמֹנִים לַגְּבוּרָה, בֶּן תִּשְׁעִים לָשׁוּחַ, בֶּן מֵאָה כְּאִלּוּ מֵת וְעָבַר וּבָטֵל מִן הָעוֹלָם:

**He used to say: At five years old, for Scripture; at ten, for Mishnah; at thirteen, for the commandments; at fifteen, for Talmud; at eighteen, for the wedding canopy; at twenty, for pursuit; at thirty, for strength; at forty, for understanding; at fifty, for counsel; at sixty, for old age; at seventy, for gray hair; at eighty, for might; at ninety, for stooping; at a hundred, it is as if he had died and passed away and ceased from the world.**

Literal: he was saying: son-of five years to-Scripture, son-of ten to-Mishnah, son-of thirteen to-the-commandments, son-of fifteen to-Talmud, son-of eighteen to-the-canopy, son-of twenty to-pursue, son-of thirty to-strength, son-of forty to-understanding, son-of fifty to-counsel, son-of sixty to-old-age, son-of seventy to-grey-hair, son-of eighty to-might, son-of ninety to-stoop, son-of hundred as-if dead and-passed and-ceased from-the-world.

Grammar:

- Each stage is an elliptical clause of the form 'son of N (years) to X': the verb 'is fit' is understood. The ל prefix is 'for' (fit for, ready for).
- The ages count by tens from twenty to a hundred; בֶּן שָׁנִים is a fixed idiom for age. Gender of the numerals follows the noun they do not name: שָׁנָה (feminine) takes חָמֵשׁ, עֶשֶׂר, שְׁלשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה, etc.
- Each ל-noun is a stage of life or a pursuit: מִקְרָא (Bible), מִשְׁנָה (oral teaching), מִצְוֹת (commandments), תַּלְמוּד (study), חֻפָּה (marriage), רדף (pursuit), כֹּחַ (strength), בִּינָה, עֵצָה, זִקְנָה, שֵׂיבָה, גְּבוּרָה, שׁוּחַ.
- The last clause is a full sentence: כְּאִלּוּ מֵת וְעָבַר וּבָטֵל מִן הָעוֹלָם, with three Qal perfects (מֵת is the perfect of the stative מות): 'as if he had died and passed and ceased from the world'.

Note: Translated with the plain sense of each stage. Bartenura derives the first stages from the law of orlah (Lev 19:23-25) and the Levites (Num 8). For לִרְדֹּף I keep 'pursuit' and record both of his readings (livelihood; or being pursued by the heavenly court) in the notes. לָשׁוּחַ is 'stooping' (Bartenura: walking bent and bowed).

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: five years for Scripture is learned from orlah (Lev 19:23-25): three years of nothing, the fourth year 'holy', when the father teaches the shape of the letters and the vowel points, and from the fifth 'you shall eat its fruit': from then on 'feed him (Torah) like an ox' (סְפֵי לֵיהּ כְּתוֹרָא).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: five years Scripture, five Mishnah, five Gemara; a student who has seen no sign of success in five years will not (Hullin 24a); the Levites learned the laws of service five years (Num 8:24).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: thirteen for the commandments: Num 5:6 'a man or woman'; Levi at thirteen is called 'man' (Gen 34:25).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: nineteen occurrences of 'adam' in the first section of Genesis; one for the body itself, eighteen remain for the derashah (the wedding canopy).
- Bartenura (records): Bartenura: at twenty, to pursue a livelihood, after learning, marrying and having children. Another reading: to be pursued from Heaven, since the heavenly court does not punish before twenty. The English keeps the neutral 'pursuit'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: thirty for strength: the Levites set up and dismantled the tabernacle and carried it from the age of thirty.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: forty for understanding: after forty years in the wilderness Moses said 'the Lord has not given you a heart to know until this day' (Deut 29:3).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: fifty for counsel: the Levites retired from service at fifty and 'served' their brothers, which is giving counsel (Num 8:25).
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: sixty for old age: Job 5:26, 'you shall come to the grave in ripe age' (בכלח), whose numerical value is sixty.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: seventy for gray old age: David died 'in good old age' (1 Chr 29:28) and lived seventy years.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: eighty for might: Ps 90:10, 'and if by reason of strength eighty years'.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: ninety to stoop: one walks bent and bowed. Others: from the word for a deep pit (שׁוּחָה).
- Rambam (not-applicable): Rambam (anchored from 5:23): reward is according to toil; knowledge learned with labor and awe lasts. It concerns Ben He He's saying in 5:23, not this mishnah.

Apparatus:

- Bartenura's proof texts: Lev 19:23-25; Num 8:24-25; Gen 34:25; Deut 29:3; Job 5:26; 1 Chr 29:28; Ps 90:10.
- Variants (spelling only): 5:21.20 שמונה, 5:21.22 לחופה, 5:21.25 לרדוף, 5:21.42 שמונים, 5:21.49 כאילו.
- Rabbeinu Yonah on לָשׁוּחַ: from שיח 'speech' (one speaks only words of Torah) or 'pit/cave' (fit for burial).
- שְׁמֹנֶה: Vilna reads שמונה (spelling)
- לַחֻפָּה: Vilna reads לחופה (spelling)
- לִרְדֹּף: Vilna reads לרדוף (spelling)
- שְׁמֹנִים: Vilna reads שמונים (spelling)
- כְּאִלּוּ: Vilna reads כאילו (spelling)

#### Pirkei Avot 5:22

> בֶּן בַּג בַּג אוֹמֵר, הֲפֹךְ בָּהּ וַהֲפֹךְ בָּהּ, דְּכֹלָּא בָהּ. וּבָהּ תֶּחֱזֵי, וְסִיב וּבְלֵה בָהּ, וּמִנַּהּ לֹא תָזוּעַ, שֶׁאֵין לְךָ מִדָּה טוֹבָה הֵימֶנָּה:

**Ben Bag Bag says: Turn it and turn it, for everything is in it; and in it you will see, and grow old and worn in it, and do not move from it, for you have no quality better than it.**

- The saying mixes Hebrew and Aramaic: הֲפֹךְ בָּהּ וַהֲפֹךְ בָּהּ is Hebrew; דְּכֹלָּא בָהּ וּבָהּ תֶּחֱזֵי וְסִיב וּבְלֵה בָהּ וּמִנַּהּ לֹא תָזוּעַ is Aramaic; שֶׁאֵין לְךָ מִדָּה טוֹבָה הֵימֶנָּה is Hebrew again.
- The feminine בָּהּ refers back to the Torah, as the commentators say (the mishnah does not name it: it follows the previous saying).
- The imperatives הֲפֹךְ, סִיב, בְּלֵה are paired: turn it over and over; grow old and wear out in it.
- The negation לֹא תָזוּעַ is a prohibition in Aramaic style ('do not move'); the final clause gives the reason with שֶׁאֵין לְךָ 'for you have not'.
- מִדָּה 'measure, quality'; the English 'quality' also allows 'virtue' or 'standard'.

Note: The pronoun 'it' is the Torah (Bartenura, Rambam). The Aramaic words are translated without comment in the English; the notes and grammar record where the Aramaic begins and ends.

Commentary:

- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'turn it and turn it': in the Torah. The English 'it' is the Torah.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: 'for everything is in it': that you will find everything in it.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: even to old age and gray hair do not abandon it.
- Bartenura (follows): Bartenura: do not say you have learned the wisdom of Israel and will go learn Greek wisdom; it may be learned only at a time when thought of Torah is forbidden (bathhouse), or in the hour that is neither day nor night (R. Joshua), since 'you shall meditate on it day and night'. The English keeps 'do not move from it'.
- Rambam (follows): Rambam: turn it and meditate in it because everything is in it; 'and in it you will see' means you will see the truth with the eye of the intellect (as the Targum renders 'and he saw' with 'and he chazah'); then grow old in it and do not turn from it to another.

Apparatus:

- Rabbeinu Yonah (anchored 5:22.5-6): review words of Torah, for all the wisdom of the world is included in it.
- Variants: 5:22.5 הפוך, 5:22.7 והפוך (Vilna), 5:22.9 דכולה, 5:22.16 ומינה (Vilna spellings).
- Aramaic is in the Hebrew of the base text; בָהּ/בָּהּ vary in dagesh only.
- הֲפֹךְ: Vilna reads הפוך (spelling)
- וַהֲפֹךְ: Vilna reads והפוך (spelling)
- דְּכֹלָּא: Vilna reads דכולה (word)
- וּמִנַּהּ: Vilna reads ומינה (spelling)

- The saying is in Aramaic and has no verb: 'according to the toil, the reward'.
- לְפוּם is lit. 'to the mouth of' and is an idiom for 'in proportion to'; it takes the following noun in the emphatic state.
